## Problem

The current DeepSeek V4 Flash model (~81GB compressed) doesn't fit in consumer AMD GPUs with limited VRAM.

## Hardware tested

- **AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395** (Strix Point)
- **GPU**: Radeon 8060S (62GB VRAM)
- **System RAM**: 128GB

## Implementation

I've started implementing AMD HIP/ROCm support in a fork:

- **Fork**: https://github.com/darchidev/ds4-hip
- **Files added**: `ds4_hip.c`, `ds4_hip.h`, plus Makefile / `ds4.c` changes

## Current situation

| Configuration            | Model | VRAM needed        | VRAM available | Result        |
|--------------------------|-------|--------------------|----------------|---------------|
| Apple Silicon 128GB      | Q2    | ~81GB (RAM only)   | 128GB RAM      | ✅ Works      |
| AMD 62GB VRAM            | Q2    | ~81GB              | 62GB           | ❌ Doesn't fit |

GPU detection works, but the model weights (81GB) exceed available VRAM (62GB), so it falls back to CPU.

## Requests

1. Are there smaller versions of the model? (e.g., 30–40GB that fits in 62GB VRAM)
2. Is it possible to have a Q4 version with more aggressive MoE quantization?
3. Advice on how to proceed with layer-by-layer decompression on GPU?

Any guidance would be very helpful. Thanks!

Update: I found the root case, it is tool calling canonicalization issue. This is a real pain, we have to translate the LLM protocol back and forth from the JSON API format, and especially during long tool calls like huge edits, it is easy that there is some mismatch in the canonicalized form. And there was a bug during rewinding. But I want a larger fix for this stuff: instead of trying to canonicalize and hope it will match, each time we perform a tool call, we can *check immediately* if the tool call will fail the canonicalization round-trip, and in that case we can build an hash table with the actual LLM sampled text, and substitute the exact one. Problem: the client (pi, opencode, ... in this case) need to pass the right tool call ID and behave as well, but they should AFAIK. I'll probably start with a quick fix, and later provide this more advanced system.

No, it’s that every use of `$TOKEN` is already properly quoted — unless you’re talking about the `TOKEN=$1` (I forget the semantics off the top of my head).

With all due respect, looking at line 112 in download_model.sh, the variable $TOKEN is NOT quoted:
​curl -fL ... -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -o "$part" "$url"
​In Bash/Sh, when a variable is inside double quotes but not individually quoted or escaped, and if the variable itself contains spaces or shell metacharacters (like ;), the shell will expand it before passing it to the command.
​If a user provides a token like abc; touch HACKED;, the command becomes:
curl ... -H "Authorization: Bearer abc; touch HACKED;" ...
​The semicolon acts as a command separator. This is a textbook Command Injection. If you think this is 'properly quoted,' I suggest running a simple PoC locally before dismissing a security report.
​Security isn't about assumptions; it's about what the code actually executes.

It does *because* it can't find a match, so this checkpoint is not reusable by definition. @jamez-bondos important, your Pi is configured with the default `requiresReasoningContentOnAssistantMessages: true`?

Additional retest results and answers to the questions above:

- Yes, my pi local ds4 provider is configured with `requiresReasoningContentOnAssistantMessages: true`.
- The same provider config also uses `thinkingFormat: "deepseek"`.
- I retested with a fresh KV cache directory and a much larger disk cache budget:

```sh
rm -rf /tmp/ds4-pi-kv

./ds4-server \
  --ctx 100000 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000 \
  --kv-disk-dir /tmp/ds4-pi-kv \
  --kv-disk-space-mb 32768
```

With the larger budget, the worst-case fallback to `4096` did not reproduce. The next user message did reuse a substantial prefix:

```text
0510 22:33:13 ds4-server: chat ctx=31937..33659:1722 gen=2457 TOOLS finish=stop 109.032s
0510 22:33:18 ds4-server: kv cache stored tokens=36116 trimmed=0 reason=evict size=497.09 MiB save=95.5 ms
0510 22:33:18 ds4-server: kv cache hit tokens=24576 quant=4 load=63.3 ms file=/tmp/ds4-pi-kv/02ba530d31e2d13b4b4f7fcabc078e8ec99a7217.kv
0510 22:33:18 ds4-server: chat ctx=24576..36148:11572 TOOLS prompt start
```

So the original `4096` fallback appears to be amplified by the smaller `8192 MiB` disk cache budget and eviction pressure. However, the larger-cache run still did not reuse the newest final-response checkpoint as the longest prefix. In the snippet above, `36116` was stored immediately before the next prompt, but the lookup matched `24576`, not something close to `36116`.

**Forward-compat heads-up while you're rebasing:** there's a latent compressor-APE interaction between this PR and Q8_0 ape ingestion (e.g. for stock-recipe GGUFs like cyberneurova's). On M5 Max:

1. `kernel_dsv4_compressor_store_one` (in `metal/dsv4_kv.metal`, upstream) only handles F16/F32 ape — Q8_0 falls through to the F32 branch and reads garbage.
2. A naive Q8_0 GPU dequant kernel for the prefill APE byte-strided path produces silently wrong output on M5 Max for compressor APE shapes (4 rows × 1024 cols). CPU-side dequant into a *per-call private* `MTLBuffer` is what works — a shared scratch loses writes when the same buffer is reused inside one command buffer (Metal kernels run in encode order; CPU writes don't participate in that ordering when the scratch is reused).

The bug only manifests when both your MPP work and Q8_0 ape branches are present, so nothing to fix in this PR in isolation. Just flagging in case #60 (the stock-recipe loader PR) lands — the fix at [`audreyt/ds4` `m5-support-q8_0-token-embd`](https://github.com/audreyt/ds4/tree/m5-support-q8_0-token-embd) (commit [`79b08bb`](https://github.com/audreyt/ds4/commit/79b08bb)) would need to land alongside it. Removed the template system and background flusher. Both were redundant with the KV disk cache's SHA1-based continued checkpoints, which already store aligned frontiers (10K, 20K, 30K...) during prefill for cross-session reuse.

Pool L2 (session-id addressed) now only saves after generation completes and on eviction/shutdown. Fixed two bugs: continued frontier files were being deleted after first load (`cold_max_tokens` consume logic), and partial pool prefix matches were being discarded in favor of worse KV cache hits.

DeepSeek v4 has native MTP head, not included in the GGUFs but loadable as a secondary GGUF that you can download. The problem is that DeepSeek v4 is a model that is hard to optimize very well for speculative decoding, it requires N=2 kernels that are able to do the whole computation and verification in parallel and be cheap enough even in the case the token is rejected. There is likely no need for a second model: the problem is making it cheap to compute+verify for N=2. Also you can use a different model only if the tokenization aligns well.

Another fundamental point is that **the current MTP** of DeepSeek v4 is the cheap part, the implementation in this repository is fast. That's not the problem. Hit rate is ~73% in my tests. The expensive part is the target verification.

In short **there is no simple way in DeekSeek v4 Flash** AFAIK to have a small batch that is much faster then sequential decoding with cheaper rollback.

Going through some tests, Q4 > Q2 on logic, but so far the two are quite comparable for coding and more qualitative work. Here's the logic question: 

> Six paintings labeled A, B, C, D, E, F are hung in a single row, positions 1 (leftmost) through 6 (rightmost).  Each painting occupies exactly one position; positions are not repeated.
> 
> Constraints:
>   1. A is strictly to the right of D but strictly to the left of E.
>   2. F is strictly to the right of B.
>   3. The painting immediately to the right of C is either A or E (so C cannot be in position 6).
>   4. D and A are not adjacent (their positions differ by more than 1).
>   5. B is at one end of the row (position 1 or position 6).
> 
> Determine the exact left-to-right ordering.  Reason one position at a time: each step must cite which numbered constraint forces that placement.  Where a step requires case analysis, walk through every case and show where the contradiction arises.  Do not guess; do not skip steps.  Conclude with the final ordering as a single line, e.g. "Final ordering: X Y Z W V U".

Both correctly deduced B=1 from constraints 2+5 and started enumerating D/A/E triples. But that's where the similarity ends. 

- Q2 found one valid ordering (B,D,C,A,E,F)
- Q4 systematically enumerated all four valid (D,A,E) triples, found multiple valid orderings (B,D,C,A,F,E and B,D,F,A,C,E from the (2,4,6) triple alone), and was still going when it hit the limit. Q4 correctly identified that the puzzle is underspecified — it has 5 valid solutions, not 1. 

So my conclusion is that I'm as smart as Q2, but I'm dumber than Q4. Faced with an ambiguous problem, Q2 stopped at "I found one that works" while Q4 kept verifying uniqueness. So there is value in pushing for Q4, even with half the throughput due to thunderbolt constraints.

My reasoning is more about the server side that receives the calls, even if they are local, to protect it from possible anomalous or malformed inputs.

That said, this is probably a relatively minor aspect. If another agent calls the DS4 server, we can decide between two scenarios:
- Protect ourselves: if an LLM calls DS4 with a malformed request, it receives an explicit error. In an agentic loop, I would expect it to understand the error, fix the formatting, and retry. In this case, yes, upstream sampling/grammar would help reduce these cases.
- Be less formal: if DS4 can still understand the intent even with inputs that are not perfectly formatted, then this validation can be considered too rigorous.

Based on the 6 benchmark runs, here is the **optimal context window sizing recommendation** for running deepseek-v4-flash on the M3 Max 128GB:

---

## 📊 Core Finding: There is a Clear Performance Cliff at ~30K Tokens

The data reveals a sharp inflection point where generation speed collapses. Using the **max fan** runs (4–6) as the reliable baseline:

| Zone | Context Range | Gen Speed | User Experience |
|------|-------------|-----------|-----------------|
| 🟢 **Smooth** | 0 – 22K | ≥ 20 TPS | No perceptible latency |
| 🟡 **Acceptable** | 22K – 35K | 18–20 TPS | Slight delay, still fluid |
| 🟠 **Slow** | 35K – 70K | 15–18 TPS | Noticeable waiting |
| 🔴 **Sluggish** | 70K – 102K | < 15 TPS | Significantly impacts UX |

---

## 🎯 Two "Sweet Spots" Depending on Your Use Case

### **Sweet Spot A: Speed-First (~28K tokens)**
- **Gen:** 19.53 TPS | **Prefill:** 218.5 TPS | **KV Cache:** 0.39 GB
- This is the last data point before the performance cliff. The decay rate accelerates dramatically after 28K (losing ~4–5 TPS per 1K token increase).
- **Best for:** Code completion, interactive writing, chatbots, any scenario where low latency matters more than massive context.

### **Sweet Spot B: Balanced (~65K tokens)**
- **Gen:** 15.09 TPS | **Prefill:** 148.8 TPS | **KV Cache:** 0.86 GB
- Still above the 15 TPS "sluggishness threshold." The memory footprint is trivial on a 128GB machine.
- **Best for:** Long-document RAG, analyzing 50–80 page PDFs, cases where context breadth outweighs pure speed.

---

## 📋 Practical Recommendations by Scenario

| Scenario | Recommended Context | Why |
|----------|---------------------|-----|
| **Chat / Conversational AI** | 8K – 16K | Gen ~20.5 TPS, memory footprint negligible (~0.2 GB) |
| **Code Completion / Copilot** | 24K – 28K | Right at the edge of the cliff; safest high-speed zone |
| **Long Document Analysis / RAG** | 48K – 65K | Acceptable 15+ TPS, enough for substantial documents |
| **Book-length / Extreme Cases** | 80K – 100K | Only when absolutely necessary; Gen drops to ~14.5 TPS |
| **> 100K** | ❌ Not recommended | Diminishing returns; speed too slow for good UX |

---

## ⚠️ Key Insight: Memory is NOT the Bottleneck

On the M3 Max 128GB, the KV Cache at 102K context is only **1.33 GB** — completely negligible. The constraint is **compute bandwidth**, not RAM capacity. The generation speed decays because the attention mechanism must traverse an increasingly large KV cache per token, not because the system is running out of memory.

> **Bottom line:** Set your context window based on **latency tolerance**, not memory limits. For this machine, **28K** is the hard ceiling for fluid interaction, and **65K** is the practical maximum for productive use.

## Current Experimental State The stack is reviewable as infrastructure plus CUDA MTP enablement, but the MTP performance work should still be treated as experimental. The best validated result so far is that the harness and verifier tooling now let us measure MTP against both fast-MTP and no-MTP baselines without repeatedly paying full model load cost. The VMM weight server path was validated on DGX Spark with full base+MTP raw tensor sharing, and the proof runner can now report exact byte comparisons plus steady-state throughput. For runtime MTP itself, the main conclusion is that exact MTP is no longer dominated by startup or measurement artifacts. It is dominated by the target verifier pass. Results summary across 2k-64k context, 128 greedy generation tokens per point: | Run | Prefill mean | Generation mean | Generation first | Generation last | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | no-MTP | 342.20 t/s | 12.68 t/s | 14.00 t/s | 11.63 t/s | | exact MTP | 341.02 t/s | 12.62 t/s | 12.53 t/s | 11.68 t/s | Currently MTP is basically a wash; the curves are effectively tied. Exact MTP trails on the first cold row, then tracks no-MTP closely and is slightly ahead at the largest contexts. Validated wins: - Q8 pair batching is useful for verifier-sized batches, but must stay limited to `n_tokens <= 2`. Applying it to normal long prefill regressed prefill from about `402 t/s` to `261 t/s`; after gating it, default prefill returned to `401.51 t/s`. - The exact decode2 top2 output-head path is the cleanest exact CUDA-side win so far. It reduced forced decode2 verifier averages from roughly `145-148 ms` to `130-134 ms` while preserving exact byte parity against no-MTP. - The acceptance gate helps low-acceptance prompts by falling back toward ordinary decode. On prose, exact MTP steady-state became nearly equivalent to no-MTP after warmup. - The VMM weight server materially improves proof iteration time by keeping raw weights loaded across isolated workers. What remains experimental: - Non-strict / fast MTP can show speedups on favorable prompts, but outputs should be compared before treating a run as an exact speedup. - Decode3, batch-first verifier, and candidate-certified logits are promising research paths, but not yet proven default wins. - The reverted attention-output-B N2 Q8 path did not meet the proof bar as a default optimization; shadow infrastructure remains useful for further localization. Best current leads: 1. **Purpose-built exact decode2 layer kernels.** The current verifier still runs a target-model layer pass over the drafted suffix. Profiling shows about `103 ms` of synchronized verifier layer work per cycle on GB10. 2. **Attention output projection.** This is one of the largest remaining single costs, about `27 ms` per verifier cycle. 3. **Routed MoE gate/up.** Routed MoE is about `30 ms` per verifier cycle, and most of that is gate/up rather than the already-optimized down/sum side. 4. **Q path folding.** The Q path is about `15 ms` per verifier cycle. There may still be savings by folding projection/RoPE/bookkeeping work for the fixed decode2 verifier shape. 5. **Candidate-certified logits.** This could be a major win if it can prove acceptance without full vocabulary logits in common cases, but it needs a higher proof bar before becoming default. The practical reading is: this stack makes CUDA MTP safe and measurable, fixes the known prefill regression, and lands a few exact verifier improvements. The next performance frontier is reducing exact target verifier layer cost, especially attention output projection and MoE gate/up.

`
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from pathlib import Path
import sys

src = Path(sys.argv[1])
dst = Path(sys.argv[2])

text = src.read_text()

old = "const float alpha = rsqrtf((float)head_dim);"
new = "const float alpha = 1.0f / sqrtf((float)head_dim);"

count = text.count(old)

if count != 2:
    raise SystemExit(
        f"Expected exactly 2 host alpha rsqrtf occurrences, found {count}. "
        "Refusing to generate ROCm source."
    )

text = text.replace(old, new)

dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
dst.write_text(text)

print(f"Generated {dst} with {count} ROCm host rsqrtf fixes")
`

Hey @vstath — thanks, not naive at all, that's exactly the right axis to probe.

**Short answer: neither.** The lever isn't attention sweep optimization, and speculative decoding is orthogonal (could layer on top of any of these architectures, but it's not the design driver). The chip-side lever is **whole-model weight residency**: V4-Flash's 142 GB INT4 stays statically resident in 28nm ReRAM-CIM, so per-token inference does zero DRAM round-trips. Today's wall-clock bottleneck in LLM inference isn't attention compute — it's HBM↔compute bandwidth. We're eliminating that physically.

V4-Flash is ~90% MLP/MoE FLOPs and only ~10% attention per token (MLA + multi-query attention keeps KV small — ~6.7 GB on-die SRAM at 256K context, no dedicated attention hardware needed). ReRAM-CIM is a clean physical match for the MoE side: 256 experts × 4-bit weights resident, Top-6 routing dispatching across 6 chip layers in parallel.

Just added a physical-anatomy section in the repo README mapping 5 architectures side-by-side (Traditional GPU+HBM / Cerebras / Taalas / Groq / Ours) with per-token energy + distance numbers — probably faster than I can explain in a comment: https://github.com/michaelhuo2030/millisecond-era#how-a-token-physically-computes--and-where-our-240-960-lives

Re geopolitical / lithography: yes, 28nm bypassing EUV is a real driver — supply chain is fully domestic (华虹 logic + 昕原 ReRAM + 通富/长电 packaging), no SMIC 14nm yield risk. Happy to go deeper on any of this.

More precisely, the possible rules are:

1. What we do right now: dot product (vector, activations) * vector, so that we try to "undo" the component in that direction.
2. Something with a threshold (not implemented): check the dot product to see how much component we have, and when we see the component is over a given threshold, apply a fixed steering.
3. Additive steering. Always do activations += vector.

I believe what we do right now is the most interesting but... There are cool uses at least for "3", and "2" could preserve quality of inference in a more conservative way. About "3", imagine you want a model that always focuses on certain ideas for an artistic experiment, that would be quite interesting to see. Like the Anthropic experiment where the model would always try to talk about the Golden Bridge.
Of course "2" was already done: CAST: conditional activation steering; apply steering only when activations indicate the relevant context. Source: Lee/IBM, 2024 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05907)

The idea is not that large files without hits aren't as valuable, it is that **`continued` is less valuable than `evict` and `cold`** regardless of size.

Cold would be if we started a new conversation from that same client again. (Cold hits)
Evict would be if we resumed an existing conversation that was interrupted by some other conversation.

On main, before #174 (#175) and #176 (#177) the kv cache looks like:

- conversation A cold
- conv A contine 10k
- conv A contine 20k
- conv A contine 30k
- ...

Then when conversation b comes in the kv cache adds:
- conv A evict ##k

Then conv b starts writing continues and the A-evict and A-cold has an equal weighted chance of being unlinked as A-continued.

If we were to resume conv-A after conv-B and the A-evict had been unlinked the cache has failed us.

With #174/#175, when conv-B starts writing continues, the cache would look like because A-continue n-1 gets unlinked at the time A-continue n gets written:

- conversation A cold
- conv A contine 30k
- conv A evict ##k
-

With #176/#177 the conv-A continue-biggest would be unlinked first, preserving the conv-A evict at least until conv-B starts writing continues > the size of conv-A's biggest continue.

A note on the 2 remaining `Invalid` cases and how they relate to [PR #197](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/197).

These two PRs address the same class of problem from opposite sides:

- **PR #197** — **input side**: prevents structural tokens (`<|im_start|>`, role markers, etc.) from entering the prompt via user content, stopping context contamination at the source.
- **This PR (#192)** — **output side**: repairs malformed DSML that the model has already produced, regardless of how the contamination happened.

The 2 unrecoverable `Invalid` cases were observed when I first returned to the ds4 codebase to work on these fixes. At the time, the conversation context was saturated with DSML fragments — code discussion, tag syntax, partial repair logic. The model encountered malformed and discussed-but-not-executable DSML patterns in its own context and began hallucinating broken tool calls in turn. Two of those were structurally damaged beyond repair (likely invoke tags completely missing with additional corruption), and they remain the only cases the repair layer cannot salvage.

The root mechanism is the same as #197: the model’s output structure is influenced by structural patterns present in its context. #197 closes one contamination vector; this PR ensures that when contamination does happen (from any source — context discussion, tool output, rare sampling failures), the agent loop survives.

Just to clarify my point: what I was wondering is whether ds4 could eventually make better use of the parallelism available on NVIDIA Spark, in a way closer to what vLLM does with continuous batching / concurrent requests.

Maybe I misunderstood the current implementation, so please correct me if I’m wrong: from what I understand, ds4 can handle multiple clients/sessions, but the actual decoding is still mostly serialized, so it does not really exploit concurrent inference in the same way vLLM does.

My interest is not necessarily to force full vLLM-style serving into ds4, but to understand whether there is room in the future to better utilize the Spark hardware when multiple agents are connected, especially for coding-agent workflows where several agents may alternate between reasoning, tool usage, and generation.

I’m also thinking about the case of a small cluster with two DGX Spark systems connected together. In that scenario, would ds4 be able in the future to take advantage of both machines for multi-agent workloads, or is the intended direction mainly to run separate ds4 instances on each Spark and route agents between them?

From your point of view, what would be a realistic and interesting result on this kind of hardware? For example, how many coding agents could reasonably work at the same time on one Spark, or on a two-Spark setup, assuming they are not all continuously decoding but are alternating between tool calls and generation?

I understand that DeepSeek V4 Flash being MoE makes this much harder, and that serious batching would be required to really benefit from expert grouping and reduce memory bandwidth pressure.

So my question is mainly: does ds4 already exploit this kind of parallelism as much as is practical on one Spark or even on a two-Spark setup, or is this an area that could improve later after the current implementation is stabilized?

Thanks again!

My current feeling is that it is very complicated. For once: while there is a prefill in progress, to mix generation in the same kernel is going to be not really practical, so the current approach would be to have prefill mini batches that interleave with generations mini batches. But the generation mini batches for a few sessions will reach a very low level of MoE parallelism. So we don't try to exploit this at all as it would gain little and, in order to work, the mini batching would slow down single session usage.

What you instead say about having *two* DGX Spark is a bit different and could work in theory, but the problem is the bandwidth between the two systems. You could load both the DGX with 2 bit quants, so that both have a copy of the model, and out of the 6 experts you have to route you could send 3 in one box, 3 retained in the "main" box together with the shared expert, in order to speedup the generation. If the wins are burned by the IPC is to be seen... :)
My idea is that locally, by frequently reusing the same prompts across multiple agents that start identically, we can leverage the KV cache to skip most of the initial inference overhead.

Good point about re-injecting the schema. I think it targets a real but different failure mode than what I was hitting in testing.

The failures I saw happen during long single-turn generation (50K+ tokens into one response). By that point the model has already seen the schema during prefill, so adding it again to the input wouldn't help — the issue isn't that it's too far, it's that the autoregressive hidden state encoding the DSML state machine tool_calls → invoke → parameter → close gradually degrades over tens of thousands of steps with no training distribution support at that length. The repair layer catches that output-side drift.

Schema re-injection makes more sense for a different case: when the prompt itself is very long and the current turn's schema sits far behind in the context. That's worth fixing separately, and I can follow up with a PR if you'd like.

I've pushed some DS4/Pi agent workflow updates:

   1. **Dynamic prefill chunking**
      - This keeps small deltas responsive while still using larger batched chunks for bigger tool outputs.

   2. **Stateful sessions in DS4-server**
      - DS4-server can now bind a `session_id` + revision to the live KV-cache.
      - After the first full request, Pi can send only appended tool results as a `delta`.
      - DS4 validates the revision, keeps using the existing KV prefix, and only tokenizes/prefills the new delta.
      - This avoids rebuilding/replaying the same conversation KV after every tool call.
      - If the live KV state is unavailable, DS4 returns `409` and Pi retries with a full reset.

   3. **Pi extension/package**
      - Registers:
        `ds4-stateful/deepseek-v4-flash`
      - Uses the stateful DS4 endpoint.
      - Adds guardrails for agentic workflows, including duplicate/covered read blocking and tool-output prompt-injection guidance.

Install: 
   ```sh
   pi install /path/to/ds4/pi-ds4-stateful -l
 ```

 Then select:

 ```text
   ds4-stateful/deepseek-v4-flash
 ```

 Useful commands:

 ```text
   /ds4-stateful status
   /ds4-stateful off
   /ds4-stateful on
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import openai
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1"
API_KEY = "not-needed"
MODEL = "default"
TOOL_NAME = "record_calendar_event"


class CalendarEvent(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")

    name: str
    date: str
    participants: list[str]


def main() -> None:
    client = openai.OpenAI(base_url=BASE_URL, api_key=API_KEY)
    tool = {
        "type": "function",
        "name": TOOL_NAME,
        "description": "Record the extracted calendar event.",
        "parameters": CalendarEvent.model_json_schema(),
        "strict": True,
    }

    print(f"[so-test-ts] base_url={BASE_URL}")
    print(f"[so-test-ts] model={MODEL}")
    print(f"[so-test-ts] calling responses.create with strict tool={TOOL_NAME}")

    response = client.responses.create(
        model=MODEL,
        instructions=(
            f"You must call the {TOOL_NAME} function. Do not answer with text. "
            "Extract only facts from the user message."
        ),
        input="Alice and Bob are going to a science fair on Friday.",
        tools=[tool],
        tool_choice="auto",
        parallel_tool_calls=False,
        temperature=0.0,
        max_output_tokens=500,
    )

    call = next(item for item in response.output if item.type == "function_call")
    print(f"[so-test-ts] tool={call.name}")

    event = CalendarEvent.model_validate_json(call.arguments)
    print("[so-test-ts] parsed object:")
    print(event.model_dump_json(indent=2))
    print("[so-test-ts] raw response id:", getattr(response, "id", None))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

| KV dtype | kvcache_bytes  | vs fp8    |

Thank you. From my side, this is yet not actionable. Compressing only the raw SWA ring can only cause correctness problems without winning us any memory savings: I guess everybody can agree on that, and indeed it was the first step. So the real saving happens once we have the full kv cache compressed, that right now is CUDA only in the next PR, so I can't test it easily. So here the things to take in mind are the following:

* DeepSeek KV cache is already compressed by a factor 4 or 128 factor depending on the layer (apart from non compressed layers). So we are already working with a model that is already runnable with a large context with the use of little memory compared to the memory used by the weights.
* The compression likely makes the kv rows more quantization sensible, since quantization exploits some entropy inefficiency that DS4 is likely to exploit as well. So it is possible that we will see issues.
* This could be mostly interesting for 96GB systems. At the same time, it creates issues from the POV of a different representation for KV cache files, and maintenance complexity.

However there is to say that we could work with other models in the future that don't have the same compression that DeepSeek features, so it could be more useful than it is now. Basically: this could be merged only if we can see that 3 bit compression of the *full* kv cache does not create correctness problems, otherwise why to risk? We already have a 2 bit compressed model, and a model that uses little KV cache. At the same target the natural targets are 128GB systems. So it could be wiser to simply don't attempt kv cache compression.

**PR updated since the last comment:**
- Four-PR stack collapsed into this one (turbo3 + turbo4 + h8/sparse-V + comp_cache + HISA, eight commits)
- Title narrowed to `opt-in KV cache compression`

**Evidence summary**

Teacher-forced PPL on `tests/long_context_story_prompt.txt`, 511 scored tokens, GB10 sm_121, Qwen3.6-A3B IQ2XXS:

| KV config                            | ppl       | KLD vs fp8 | top-1   | top-5   |
|--------------------------------------|-----------|------------|---------|---------|
| fp8 (baseline)                       | 15.736332 | —          | —       | —       |
| turbo3 (SWA only)                    | 16.559995 | 0.076420   |  86.89% |  99.61% |
| turbo3 + comp_cache turbo3 (full KV) | 16.351816 | 0.079748   |  87.08% |  99.80% |
| turbo4 + comp_cache turbo3           | 16.135470 | 0.053660   |  89.04% |  99.61% |

KV memory at 256K context, same model and backend:

| KV config                            |          bytes |      GB | vs fp8 |
|--------------------------------------|---------------:|--------:|-------:|
| fp8 (baseline)                       |  3,632,145,808 | 3.38 GB |   100% |
| turbo3 alone (SWA only)              |  3,623,245,840 | 3.37 GB |    99% |
| turbo3 + comp_cache turbo3 (full KV) |  1,004,230,672 | 0.94 GB |    28% |
| turbo4 + comp_cache turbo3           |  1,004,538,896 | 0.94 GB |    28% |

The raw-only `turbo3` row saves essentially nothing on its own (the engine caps the raw SWA ring at 4352 rows regardless of context, so shrinking each row barely moves the total).  The real win lives in `--comp-cache turbo3`, which trims the compressor pool that dominates at long context.

`./ds4_test --long-context` passes with `--kv-cache turbo3`.  The four-question `ds4-eval` gate passes 3/4 with full-KV compression; Q4 (the GPQA Diamond physics chain) regresses from `C` to `A`, which is the same answer your `CONTRIBUTING.md` records as the historical fp8 failure mode on that question — not a new failure shape.

**Where this fits**

Since you mentioned that other models will be supported in the future, this is probably more relevant to DwarfStar's eventual support for models that don't handle their KV cache as well architecturally.  So I'd think of this PR as an experiment log to come back to once those land — or for 96 GB DeepSeek users running multiple applications who are essentially resource-constrained on unified memory.

I resolved this in my `ds4go` Golang bindings and install tool (which depend on custom shared library `ds4` builds; I've been rebasing daily). Here's a summary of the thinking that got me through, but smaller chunks helped. ``` The HF 400 error — model downloads were getting HTTP 400 from HuggingFace's Xet CDN (cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co). Root cause (two-part): 1. The CDN rejects open-ended Range: bytes=N- (or missing-Range) GETs on large objects. 2. It also refuses any single Range spanning more than ~200 GiB. This blew up on the 432 GiB DeepSeek V4 Pro file. Fix (commit 8baf1ff, internal/models/manager.go:469): - Always send a closed range (bytes=N-M), never open-ended. - Cap each GET at downloadChunkSize = 16 GiB, so the 432 GiB file streams over ~27 chunks. - .part resume still works at any byte offset. ``` Here's the spot in the commit where I fixed it: * https://github.com/NimbleMarkets/ds4go/commit/80f139890597dcc587598280c6bf835579272adb#diff-9ba1198f1da4320b34c5c2bd5584e3efdd2338db5fcb204778893bd4f41346b5R472-R481 You can use `ds4go model download` to get the model without using the rest of the tooling. I'm at the stage where I can share and hopefully get some help with other configurations. Here's the deets (some AI produced text for better formatting):

The pipeline is wired end-to-end on my fork at [https://github.com/cchuter/ds4](https://github.com/cchuter/ds4) — single-tier behavior is bit-equivalent to upstream, GPU-only multi-tier placements run, and `--gpu-vram 44,44` produces real numbers on my 2× RTX 6000 Ada box.

I'm hitting two reproducible bugs that I'd love eyes on from other people with multi-GPU NVIDIA boxes. The biggest single thing slowing this down is having only one piece of hardware to test against.

## TL;DR

| | |
|---|---|
| What | Multi-GPU pipeline-parallel for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPU-only execution path |
| Fork | `cchuter/ds4` `main` |
| Works | 44,44 GiB split across 2 GPUs at sm_89 (Ada) — ~225 tok/s prefill, ~37 tok/s gen |
| Bug 1 | **session_create OOM** with larger budgets (47/47, auto) even when weights fit |
| Bug 2 | **`cudaMemcpyPeer` flakiness** on RTX 6000 Ada — flickers DIRECT ↔ BOUNCE between runs |

## Bench numbers (mine)

Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS (~80 GiB on disk), 2× RTX 6000 Ada (48 GiB each, PCIe NODE topology, no NVLink), driver 570.207, CUDA 12.

```
config        ctx   prefill_tps   gen_tps   kv_cache
--gpu-vram 0  2048         1.94      1.59    -
--gpu-vram 44,44 2048    225.00     37.85    52 MB
--gpu-vram 44,44 4096    219.50     37.14    80 MB
--gpu-vram 44,44 6144    219.36     37.13   109 MB
--gpu-vram 44,44 8192    218.17     36.22   137 MB
```

~116× speedup on prefill, ~24× on gen, throughput essentially flat across context size up to 8K. Layout:

```
multi-GPU layout:
  GPU0: layers 0-21 + embedding         (41.6 / 44.0 GB)
  GPU1: layers 22-42 + output head      (39.4 / 44.0 GB)
ds4: peer access matrix (validated): 0->1 BOUNCE 1->0 BOUNCE
```

(Peer access falls back to a pinned-host bounce buffer here because of bug 2 below.)

## Bug 1 — session_create OOM at "obviously fits" budgets

`--gpu-vram 47,47` and `--gpu-vram auto` both place the entire model successfully (model + cache log shows ~80 GiB registered, layout printed with several GiB slack per device), then **the session_create call OOMs allocating the KV cache for ctx=4096**:

```
multi-GPU layout:
  GPU0: layers 0-23 + embedding       (45.3 / 47.0 GB)
  GPU1: layers 24-42 + output head    (35.7 / 47.0 GB)
ds4: CUDA (no-copy) registered 80.76 GiB model mapping for multi-tier selective cache
ds4: CUDA tensor alloc failed: out of memory
ds4: CUDA tensor alloc failed: out of memory
... (×many)
ds4-bench: failed to create session
```

KV cache for ctx=4096 × 43 layers shouldn't need >10 GB. Single-tier engine in the same `--ctx-max 4096` config initializes fine. **Something in the multi-tier per-layer KV allocation is over-allocating or not respecting the device budget after weight upload.** Suspected files: `ds4.c` around `ds4_session_create` graph allocation walking the placement table.

## Bug 2 — `cudaMemcpyPeer` flakiness on RTX 6000 Ada

The runtime validation we put in `ds4_gpu_init_multi` flickers between **DIRECT** and **BOUNCE** on the same hardware minutes apart. Same driver (570.207), same workload state. Multi-size probe (4 KiB / 256 KiB / 1 MiB / 16 MiB × 4 iters) correctly catches both states and falls back to a pinned-host bounce buffer when validation fails — but the underlying driver behavior is genuinely non-deterministic. This might be a driver bug.

I'd love to know whether other Ada / Ampere / Hopper pairs show the same flicker or are deterministic.

### What output to capture in a reply

Paste:
1. Output of `nvidia-smi -L`
2. Driver + CUDA version (`nvcc --version`, `nvidia-smi | head -3`)
3. The bench output for `--gpu-vram <your-split>`
4. The bench output for `--gpu-vram auto` (whether it OOMs or runs)
5. The peer-access log line from the init: `ds4: peer access matrix (validated): 0->1 ... 1->0 ...`

## Other things to know

-  If your combined VRAM doesn't fit your chosen quant, the engine cleanly refuses rather than silently falling back.
- MTP (multi-token prediction) is disabled in multi-tier mode for now.

I may be very cautions in the future to merge other CUDA changes that are not tested for correctness in a very deep way, because unfortunately correctness changes tend to create many problems. For instance in this case HBM instead of mmap() for certain parts of the model created pressure and as soon as the Q8->F16 buffers where created, not sure why, but instead of receiving out of memory I started to see bad logits. So new changes targeting the Spark especially and CUDA in general need to pass every kind of test before being accepted.

Mmap() appears to be a lot safer, I had other issues in the past. At least in the Spark, but the DGX Spark is the primary target in the CUDA world for DwarfStar.

Hi, there is no need to benchmark Q2 vs Q4 vs Q2-Q4. Q4 follows token-exact more continuations from the official API, and Q2-Q4 has less logits drift compared to Q2. So for sure it's better if you have the memory. It's a tradeoff. Benchmarking this subtle difference is almost impossible, even if we have ds4-eval. You would need to repeat the benchmark at non zero temperature, and is still a narrow test.

Hi @loge-gh,

I've opened PR #305 — x86 AVX2/AVX512 SIMD fast paths for the CPU quantized dot products (Q2_K, Q4_K, IQ2_XXS). This should speed up CPU-only inference on x86 machines since the routed MoE expert dot products were previously pure scalar.

Since you have x86 hardware with enough RAM to run the model, would you be willing to benchmark it?

**How to test:**

```bash
# Checkout the PR branch
gh pr checkout 305 --repo antirez/ds4
# Or without gh:
git fetch https://github.com/hexxyan/ds4.git cpu-simd-dot-kernels:pr-305
git checkout pr-305

# Step 1: Run unit tests
make quant-dot-test

# Step 2: Build and compare speed
# First, build and test current main for baseline:
git stash
git checkout main
make cpu
# Run your usual benchmark with ds4-server, note tok/s
./ds4-server -m path/to/model.gguf --cpu ...

# Then build the PR branch:
git checkout pr-305
git stash pop
make cpu
# Run the same benchmark, compare tok/s
./ds4-server -m path/to/model.gguf --cpu ...
```

If your CPU supports AVX2 or AVX512, you can also try the explicit ISA builds:

```bash
make cpu-avx2          # for AVX2-only CPUs
make cpu-avx512        # for AVX512BW CPUs (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+)
make cpu-avx512-vnni   # for AVX512BW+VNNI CPUs
```

These produce separate binaries (`ds4-avx2`, `ds4-avx512`, etc.) so they won't overwrite your normal build.

**What's useful to report:**
- CPU model and `lscpu | grep -i avx` output (so we know which SIMD path is active)
- Model quant format (q4-imatrix, q2, etc.)
- Whether `make quant-dot-test` passes
- tok/s before and after on the same model + prompt
- Whether output looks correct (no garbage, no crash)

Any testing would be very helpful — I don't have enough RAM to run E2E benchmarks myself. Thanks!

Hi @ngt1999 — I opened PR #317 that addresses the full-GGUF registration issue you reported.

**Root cause:** `ds4_gpu_set_model_map_spans()` was passing the full file size to every fallback path. Even though the span calculation was correct, all downstream code (`cuda_model_range_ptr`, `cuda_model_range_is_cached`, `cuda_model_direct_fallback_ptr`, Q2 tail expansion) assumed the full mmap was accessible — which is why Q2 "worked" (80.76 GiB registered ≈ whole file) but Q4 OOMed (150 GiB > 128 GB).

**Fix:** Added `g_model_span_cover_offset/end` to track the actual page-aligned span cover, and a `cuda_model_range_in_span_cover()` helper that gates all direct/full-file fallback paths. The new log line makes it immediately visible:

```
ds4: CUDA span cover 78.21 GiB of 150.00 GiB model (48 spans, offset 72.00 GiB)
```

**CUDA compile verified** with `nvcc -arch=sm_90` (zero warnings/errors).

Some back of the napkin calculation for feasibility:

Pipelining of prefills is already an existing mechanism, the only additional overhead is shipping KV cache for earlier (or all layers) to the machine doing the inference. It makes sense to do that per chunk alongside the layer activation data being pipelined anyway. If full 1M tokens context is taking 26GB (from README), then assuming context chunking by 4096 tokens, full context is 244 chunks with ~106MB per activation chunk. Practical bandwidth of 2.5GbE connection is around 280Mbytes/s with 1-2ms RTT. Activation chunk itself is around 64MB (4096 tokens × hidden size 4096 × 4 bytes FP32). Sending 170MB (chunk + KV cache) instead of 64MB over that link adds only extra 0.4-0.5s latency. Since inference is strictly feed-forward, and assuming efficient pipelining implementation, that 0.5s latency should be added only once per prefill.

This makes it feasible.

On Thunderbolt 5 vs 2.5Gbps, I'm yet to test this, but I suspect practical difference is negligible here. It's reported (from README) that setting `--dist-activation-bits` to a smaller value doesn't provide significant improvement despite cutting the payload size in half (if set to 16), from which I conclude that distributed inference at this scale is not bandwidth-bound. Will report back after practical testing once some hardware arrives later this week.

## Follow-up (2026-06): `--routed-metal-dynamic` + `F_RDADVISE` across all paths

  Since the original post I added a third path (gen experts on the **GPU**) and
  found the single biggest lever was prefetch. Same 153 GiB Q4 model, M4 Max /
  128 GiB. Full writeup with charts (budget sweep, thermals, vm_stat):
  https://github.com/tkhr-sait/ds4/blob/main/cpu-moe-memo/02-routed-metal-dynamic/README.md

  **`F_RDADVISE` is the key lever (all three paths).** On Darwin
  `posix_madvise(WILLNEED)` is only a vm hint and issues no I/O; `F_RDADVISE`
  issues a real read-ahead, so the SSD page-in overlaps compute. (Priority is
  encoded by *repeat count*, so the prefill lookahead deliberately re-hints the
  current layer.)
  - prefill (per-layer phases N=43 + next-layer prefetch): **111.9 → 182–222 t/s** (1.6–2.0×)
  - CPU gen (prefetch the selected experts): **5.4 → ~10 t/s**
  - GPU dynamic path: I/O cap lifted (per-expert `make_buffer` warmed)

  **`--prefill-metal-phases auto` now resolves to N=43** (one layer per phase,
  ~3.38 GiB swap each) with lookahead prefetch — instead of the old N=2 (two
  82 GiB swaps, no prefetch).

  **New `--routed-metal-dynamic` (gen experts on GPU).** Instead of the gen-time
  expert GEMV on CPU, wire only the experts the router actually selected (6 of
  256, ≈13.5 MiB each on Q4) into a per-expert Metal residency set; an LRU keeps
  the recent working set resident up to a byte budget and evicts the tail. Reuses
  the existing `mul_mv_id` kernels. Requires `--cpu-moe`, Metal-only, default off;
  budget via `DS4_ROUTED_METAL_BUDGET_MIB` (default 40 GiB).
  - Q4 gen, 32 GiB budget: **10.58 (Normal) / 10.91 (High Power) t/s ≈ 2× the cpu-moe baseline (5.37)**
  - Scales with budget via LRU hit%: 8→80 GiB = ~7.8→~12.6 t/s (High Power), hit% ~41→~94%

  **Thermals govern both CPU and GPU.** gen t/s ≈ thermal headroom (cooling −
  accumulated heat). At a large budget dyn drives the GPU hard, so Normal
  throttles and High Power recovers +10–14% (72–80 GiB). Equalise the starting
  die temp when comparing runs, or most of the delta is thermal-history noise.

  **CPU vs GPU — opposite RAM trade-offs:**
  - `--cpu-moe`: tiny wired (~13 GiB), rides the page cache → portable, runs on
    less RAM, no raised `iogpu.wired_limit_mb`; speed rides free-RAM-for-cache.
  - `--routed-metal-dynamic`: the **wired budget *is* the speed knob** (predictable,
    tunable t/s) but pins RAM and needs a raised `iogpu.wired_limit_mb`. Overshoot
    swaps — **validate `swap-out = 0` at your longest context**, not a short prompt
    (80 GiB wires at the default limit).

  **Q2 (fits in RAM):** dyn lands **between full Metal (22.13) and cpu-moe (7.96)**
  — 24–40 GiB ≈ 17 t/s (≈78% of full Metal). Even when the model fits, dyn is a
  useful **cap on wired memory** (most of full-Metal speed at a smaller footprint).

  **Tried, no effect here:** MTP (speculative draft/verify) did not speed gen in
  this setup.

  Still alpha quality / personal fork, Metal-only — sharing the measurements in
  case they're useful.

EDIT18:57 GMT+2:
By inserting a `return;` immediately after entering the `ds4_acquire_instance_lock` function in order to bypass it, I was able to run two instances on the same server in **worker–coordinator** mode.

The `q2-q4-imatrix` model does not fit within two A40 GPUs, so I added a third server connected over **25 Gbit Ethernet** (average ping latency is around **0.035 ms**) with two additional A40s, splitting the model as follows:

- **Server A**
  - Layers `0:15`
  - Layers `16:31`

- **Server B**
  - Layers `32:output`

```bash
./ds4-bench \
  --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
  --ctx-start 2048 \
  --ctx-max 32000 \
  --step-incr 2048 \
  --gen-tokens 128
```

Performance results:

- ~440 TPS during prefill
- ~21 TPS during generation

I have been working on my fork of `ejpir`'s `rocm-upstream-shape-cyberneurova` branch to measure and reduce drift between the ROCm backend and the CPU implementation. With the help of my butler (Antigravity/Gemini 3.1), I [updated the test harness](https://github.com/kyuz0/ds4/commit/740e8ba349e2e2c047c9b388a5740cb32582342a) to track KL Divergence and Top-20 token overlap.

I found two changes that reduce early-token drift (*WARNING*: I haven't had time to dig into these explanations and they might very well be hallucinated AI slop):
1. **`-ffast-math`:** The CPU implementation uses `-ffast-math`, but ROCm did not. Enabling it allows the GPU to use native FMA instructions, preserving intermediate precision during matrix multiplications.
2. **Hardware rounding:** The manual bit-shifting approach (`f32_to_f16_bits_hip_round`) yields worse probability distributions than using the hardware's native `__float2half` intrinsic.

By applying these changes (see commit [2d3cb1f](https://github.com/kyuz0/ds4/commit/2d3cb1f7cfcbe334409daaec67a5e55925e1c00b)), KL Divergence drops (e.g. from 0.177 to 0.050 at 8 tokens), and Top-20 overlap improves.

@lobanov Thanks a lot for testing this on M5 Max — the numbers are very clear.

The stage profile confirms it: this mini-GEMM path spends ~0.76 ms/layer in gate+up and ~0.54 ms/layer in down, totaling ~1.36 ms per MoE layer. Across 43 MoE layers that's ~58.7 ms, which already exceeds the baseline's full per-token budget of ~33 ms. So the 2× slowdown is fully explained.

The root cause is that the baseline decode path is already highly specialized — fused gate+up+SwiGLU matvec (`kernel_mul_mv_id_iq2_xxs_pair_swiglu_f32`) plus direct 6-expert down accumulation (`kernel_mul_mv_id_*_sum6_f32`). This prototype forces batch=1 matvec into 64×8 MMA tiles, paying dequantization → threadgroup store → barrier → tile load → barrier per K-step, which can't be amortized at M=1.

The hypothesis was wrong for single-token decode. I'll close this as a useful negative result. The MMA approach may still make sense for batched decode / continuous batching where tile overhead gets amortized, but that's a future direction, not this PR.

Dug into this — it looks like a **regression from `116b3fb`** ("Fix SSD streaming map and auto cache defaults"), and the q4-vs-q2 difference is exactly as you suspected (low-offset F16 non-routed tensors).

### Root cause

In `ds4_engine_open` (`ds4.c`), the SSD-streaming initial model map has two branches:
- **distributed (`load_slice`)** → maps token + the full non-routed static slice (what `116b3fb` fixed).
- **single-machine (`else`)** → `weights_model_map_token_spans()`, i.e. **token embedding only** (~0.99 GiB). This is the `restricted to token embedding` line you saw.

The routed experts (`ffn_*_exps`) stream/cache on demand, but every **non-routed** tensor must stay resident in the mapped views for the whole forward pass. The token-only initial map happened to work for **q2-imatrix** because its non-routed tensors are small Q8 and got incidentally covered by the overlapping token-embedding view. For **q4-imatrix** the HC/compressor/indexer are **F16** and sit at low offsets (~0.01–3.4 GiB) — outside the token-only view — so `ds4_gpu_wrap_model_range` rejects them and prefill fails with `... not covered by mapped model views`. So the single-machine branch never got the same treatment `116b3fb` gave the distributed branch.

### Fix

Map the **full non-routed static set** up front in the single-machine branch too (layout-independent; uses the same span helper that already computes the 8.2 GiB non-routed budget). q2 then maps a strict superset of what it mapped before (so it keeps working); routed-expert streaming/caching is unchanged.

```diff
--- a/ds4.c
+++ b/ds4.c
@@ ds4_engine_open: SSD-streaming initial model map
+            const bool map_all_non_routed =
+                weights_have_output_head(&e->weights);
             if (load_slice) {
                 spans_ok = weights_model_map_decode_static_slice_spans(
                         &e->weights, slice_first, slice_last, true, map_output, &spans);
             } else {
-                spans_ok = weights_model_map_token_spans(&e->weights, &spans);
+                /* Single-machine SSD streaming: every non-routed tensor (token
+                 * embedding, attn, shared experts, HC/compressor/indexer, norms,
+                 * output head) must be resident. Token-only worked for q2's small
+                 * Q8 non-routed tensors but not q4's larger low-offset F16
+                 * HC/compressor/indexer (#341). Match the distributed path. */
+                spans_ok = weights_model_map_decode_static_spans(
+                        &e->weights, true, map_all_non_routed, &spans);
             }
```
(The `restricted to token embedding` log line is also updated to `token + all non-routed weights[ + output]`.)

### Caveat / what I could and couldn't verify

I'm on AMD **gfx1151 / Strix Halo (ROCm)**, where `--ssd-streaming` is gated to Metal (`ds4.c:24572`, the view machinery is Metal-only), so I **couldn't run this end-to-end** — it's build-verified and traced through the source + the `116b3fb` history only. Would you be able to confirm on your M5 Max, same flags, only swapping in a build with the patch?

- **Before:** `initial … model map restricted to token embedding (0.99 GiB)` → `Metal model range 0.01..3.39 GiB is not covered by mapped model views` → `metal prefill failed`.
- **After:** `initial … model map restricted to token + all non-routed weights + output (… ~8 GiB span)`, no "not covered" error, prefill + generation proceed (q2 unchanged).

One thing worth watching on a 128 GB box: the initial resident set grows from ~0.99 GiB to ~8.2 GiB of non-routed weights — the auto-cache already subtracts non-routed bytes from its target, so it should be fine, but it's the one interaction I can't exercise here.

I've been working on sparse expert caching to run models that don't fit in ram, much like the --ssd-streaming.

 Architecturally, it works like this:

 1. Skip full startup model caching for models that are too large.
 2. Keep always-needed/non-routed tensors resident.
 3. Keep a configurable resident routed-MoE layer budget.
 4. Keep a configurable per-layer expert cache.
 5. For routed experts not resident/cache-hit:
     - read expert tensor ranges from the GGUF
     - stage them through CPU memory
     - upload only selected expert weights into GPU sparse expert buffers
 6. Dispatch MoE in this order:
     - resident layer cache
     - expert cache
     - sparse selected expert load
     - fallback full range when required

**Correction — withdrawing the original justification.** On a clean re-test (gfx1151, 96 GB-VRAM split, GPU exclusively free, idle-sleep disabled), managed ON vs OFF are within noise at every practical context (16k: off 186.9 / on 195.2 prefill tok/s; both succeed; 32k both ~185). **The "16k OOMs without managed" I first reported was a VRAM-contention artifact** (a concurrent GPU consumer), not deterministic — my mistake.

managed OFF does genuinely OOM only at very large KV allocation (`--ctx-alloc 1048576` → ~30.8 GiB context buffers > ~15 GiB VRAM headroom). But managed ON doesn't rescue that on this split: with ~32 GB OS-visible RAM, the ~30 GiB managed spill exhausts host memory (process OOM). So on a large-VRAM carve-out this override has no usable window — it just trades a device OOM for a host OOM. Its real benefit is the opposite config (small VRAM + large OS RAM, à la #313), which I can't exercise on this BIOS split.

The change is still gated/opt-in/zero-overhead-when-unset and correct in principle, but **I can't substantiate a benefit on the hardware I have, so treat this as unvalidated** — happy to close it, or leave it for someone who can test the small-VRAM UMA config. Sorry for the noise.

**Correction:** clean re-testing (GPU exclusively free, idle-sleep disabled) shows the high-context OOM I described is **not at 16k** — main handles ≤32k fine without any flag (16k ~187 prefill tok/s). The earlier 16k OOM was VRAM contention from a concurrent GPU consumer, not deterministic.

A real device OOM does occur, but only at very large KV allocation: `--ctx-alloc 1048576` → ~30.8 GiB context buffers, exceeding the ~15 GiB headroom of the 96 GB VRAM carve-out. And `DS4_CUDA_MANAGED` does **not** fix it on this split (the ~30 GiB managed spill exhausts the ~32 GB OS RAM → host OOM). So this is really a "very-high-ctx exceeds the carve-out, and this BIOS split lacks the OS RAM to spill" situation, not a 16k bug. It reuses the existing visible-key continuation rather than adding a new mechanism: after each finished turn the server remembers the transcript the next request is expected to render — transient spans (`<environment_details>`, `<system-reminder>`) stripped — keyed to the live frontier, so the next user turn continues from live KV with no reprefill and no KV rewrite. **Proposal: make the drift check that debugged this thread a first-class `ds4_test` gate**

The bug class that bit this thread twice — the disabled indexer / expert-selection instability behind the SWE-bench looping, and the `-ffast-math` + f16-rounding drift @kyuz0 measured — shares one property: every smoke test passes while quality silently degrades. The tools that actually caught it live outside the tree: the teacher-forced CPU-vs-GPU check @antirez described ("ask your preferred butler to replicate this"), and @kyuz0's `check_drift.sh` (KL divergence / top-20 / argmax at depths 4→128). So forks ship without them — @alantsev already flagged the missing `ds4_test` suite in the forks as the correctness blind spot.

In-tree today, `--local-golden-vectors` checks top-k overlap and max-abs logit delta at a single prompt frontier. What caught the real bugs is per-step **decode** drift, where the numerical error compounds.

I'd like to build (small, following the existing local-golden pattern, no env knobs):

1. A `ds4_test --decode-drift` track: teacher-force a fixed continuation (long prompt + N committed tokens), record per-step top-k logits, and report KL divergence / top-20 overlap / argmax-match at depths 4/8/16/32/64/128 — @kyuz0's metric set, with tolerant thresholds in the spirit of the existing local-golden comment (catch substantial backend drift, not tiny floating-point noise).
2. A dump/compare fingerprint file like `local-golden.vec`: the reference gets generated once on Metal and committed, so any ROCm/CUDA/CPU build — including forks — can be checked against it with one command.

That makes backend correctness portable: a future kernel change on any backend gets a red/green answer in minutes instead of an overnight SWE-bench run, and it slots into per-commit CI.

@alantsev agreed on enabling `ds4_test` for ROCm — today the `strix-halo` target only builds the five binaries and the Linux `ds4_test` link rule goes through `nvcc`, so it's the link rule plus one target line. That and the decode-drift gate are complementary: one makes the existing checks run on gfx1151, the other adds the per-step decode metric none of the current tracks measure.

I can also confirm your q2 logprob failure on Metal+ssd-streaming, and it turned out to be a useful datapoint. On an M5 Max 128GB, latest main (91bafb5), IQ2XXS quant:

| config | result |
|---|---|
| full residency (no streaming) | PASS |
| `DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1` (auto budget → 72.5GiB cache, 11008 experts) | PASS |
| `DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1 DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING_CACHE_GB=16` (2427 experts) | **FAIL**, deterministic |

So the failure is keyed to expert-cache pressure, not to your machine: on a 128GB Mac the auto budget caches nearly everything and hides it, with less RAM the auto budget streams more and you hit it out of the box.

The failing assert is a near-tie argmax flip at a **decode** step (`short_code_completion` step 1): the official vector selects `c`, streaming-under-pressure ranks `C` at logprob -0.63 vs `c` at -0.76 — a ~0.13-nat shift on two near-tied tokens. Two more observations that localize it:

- Deterministic: identical mismatch across repeated runs, so not an eviction race.
- Prefill is clean: `--local-golden-vectors` (single prompt-frontier) reports *identical* metrics for streaming-16GiB and full residency, down to `top20_max_abs=3.2229`. The divergence only appears after decode steps, i.e. in the streamed-expert decode path (the resident/missing split path is the natural suspect — the down/sum pass is already order-stable by design, per the comment in ds4_metal.m, so the masked gate/up stage or the missing-expert staging).

Repro one-liner on any Mac (the 16GiB budget simulates a small-RAM machine):

```
DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1 DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING_CACHE_GB=16 ./ds4_test --logprob-vectors
```

This is also a concrete preview of what the decode-drift gate would buy: the single-frontier golden check is blind to this by construction, and the official-vectors argmax assert only trips when the drift happens to cross a near-tie. A per-step KL/top-k track would have shown the streaming decode drift directly, with a number attached, on any backend — including a ROCm `ds4_test` run once it's enabled there.

Third-party verification of #371 (+#381) on Apple M5 Max 128GB, macOS Darwin 25.5, Metal backend, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ8-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix.gguf` + `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-MTP-Q4K-Q8_0-F32.gguf`, base `91bafb5`.

Three build states: **A** = main `91bafb5`, **B** = A + #381 (clamp), **C** = B + #371 (continuous). Each built clean (`make clean && make`, 0 warnings).

## Correctness

| check | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `./ds4_test --logprob-vectors` | OK | OK | OK |
| `DS4_TEST_MTP=... ./ds4_test --mtp-verify-depth` (incl. #371's new continuous tests on C) | OK | OK | OK |

## Committed-token identity (greedy, `-n 256 --temp 0 --nothink`, fixed prompt, sha256 of output)

| config | hash class | note |
|---|---|---|
| A no-MTP (pure greedy) | **G** | reference |
| A `--mtp-draft 2` | M | main's margin-gated verifier is near-greedy by design (deviates from G at token ~20) |
| A `--mtp-draft 2` + `DS4_MTP_STRICT=1` | **G** | strict = bit-identical to greedy |
| B `--mtp-draft 2` | M | identical to A — #381 changes nothing here, as claimed |
| C `--mtp-draft 2` (env unset) | M | identical to A — #371 inert without `DS4_MTP_CONTINUOUS`, as claimed |
| C continuous `--mtp-draft 1` | **G** | lossless on this prompt |
| C continuous `--mtp-draft 2` | M′ | deterministic (re-run hash-identical); a different near-greedy sequence than M, same class |
| C continuous `--mtp-draft 2` + `DS4_MTP_STRICT=1` | **G** | strict correctly defers to the exact verifier |

Determinism: repeated runs of A-draft2 and C-continuous-draft2 produced byte-identical outputs.

## Speed (median of 3 interleaved runs, min–max in parentheses, default `--power 100`, idle machine, 60s cooldowns)

`-n 256 --temp 0 --nothink`; short = one-line prompt, long = 20kB (~5k tokens) of `promessi_sposi.txt`.

| config | short gen t/s | long gen t/s | long prefill t/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| A no-MTP | 39.13 (39.08–39.18) | 31.73 (31.71–31.76) | 413.2 |
| A `--mtp-draft 1` | 38.98 (38.97–38.99) | 31.70 (31.68–31.75) | 413.7 |
| A `--mtp-draft 2` | 37.63 (37.63–37.64) | 32.94 (32.91–32.96) | 413.6 |
| B `--mtp-draft 2` | 37.62 (37.59–37.64) | 32.94 (32.93–32.97) | 413.7 |
| C `--mtp-draft 2` (env unset) | 37.60 (37.55–37.61) | 32.96 (32.93–32.98) | 413.8 |
| C continuous `--mtp-draft 1` | 39.01 (38.90–39.05) | 31.72 (31.71–31.74) | 413.7 |
| C continuous `--mtp-draft 2` | **39.41** (39.39–39.42) | **37.32** (37.31–37.32) | 413.8 |

On this hardware the continuous path is a clear win: long-prompt generation **+13.3% over main's `--mtp-draft 2`** (37.32 vs 32.94) and **+17.6% over no-MTP** (vs 31.73). It also removes draft-2's short-prompt penalty: main's draft-2 is *slower* than no-MTP on short prompts (37.63 vs 39.13, −3.8%) while continuous draft-2 edges it out (+0.7%). Draft-1 in both flavors is within noise of no-MTP here — the acceptance gains roughly cancel the draft cost.

Long-prompt prefill is flat (~413.7 t/s) across all configs.

Non-MTP regression check: canonical `ds4-bench` sweep (2048→65536 step 2048), each state run twice in opposite order with cooldowns — **no measurable delta** (best-of-2 per frontier: gen mean −0.3%, prefill mean +1.6%, both inside same-state run-to-run variance). Worth noting for anyone comparing sweeps back-to-back: run order is a real confound — the same C binary measured 30.4 t/s gen at ctx 2048 when started immediately after a full A sweep, and 36.8 t/s when run first after a cooldown.

## Notes

- Timing-wise, B ≡ A and C-with-env-unset ≡ A within the min–max bands, consistent with #381 being a correctness guard and #371 being fully inert when disabled.
- Since `DS4_MTP_CONTINUOUS=1` stayed in the same output class (near-greedy, deterministic; strict mode bit-exact to greedy) and never regressed in our runs, the data may support making continuous the single fixed behavior rather than an env knob (with `--quality`/`DS4_MTP_STRICT` keeping the exact path) — leaving that call to the maintainer.

m5 max with 36gb of ram is wild lol, anyway this issue is about uneven bit distribution across layers within a single GGUF. Your build streams fine because all its routed experts share one quant type, so the expert cache's single-size-class assumption holds. The failure only appears when a few layers' experts are upcast (Q4_K islands in an IQ2 sea): those tensors fall outside the cache's slab size and the mapped-views fallback doesn't cover them, so every request 500s.

A field note after running this collector for a few days of benchmark serving (on my fork's implementation, but the property comes from the hook design itself so it applies to any version of this proposal).

The collector is not output neutral. With --imatrix-out enabled the generated tokens can differ from collector-off serving, same prompt, same flags, greedy at temperature 0.

The reason is that the streaming prefill fast path never materializes the per-layer activations the collector needs to read, so enabling it routes prefill through the layer-major readback path (the same reason for the ~+31% prefill cost). Different kernels and accumulation order means the logits come out different at float rounding scale. Usually irrelevant, but when the top two logits are nearly tied the argmax flips, and from that token on the whole greedy generation diverges.

I hit this in practice and confirmed it with a single variable A/B: I had a generation produced with the collector on, tried to reproduce it with the collector off and it failed a token-exact prefix check right at a near tie. Re-running with the collector on reproduced the original token by token. So determinism holds perfectly per configuration, the collector is simply part of the configuration.

Not a correctness bug, both outputs are legitimate greedy results under slightly different arithmetic. But it deserves a line in the docs, something like: "with the collector enabled, generated tokens may occasionally differ from collector-off serving; benchmark with the same collector state you serve with". Without it anyone comparing capture-on vs capture-off runs token by token will chase phantom non-determinism. I did, for a whole evening :)

Following up with a purely technical angle prompted by ecosystem activity:

PR #374 (mcmalayalam's `/health` for llama-swap integration) landed recently — it adds a minimal health endpoint specifically because llama-swap needed a way to know when DS4 is ready to serve. That's independent, third-party confirmation that these endpoints aren't hypothetical: the ecosystem already hit the wall without them.

This PR extends beyond #374's scope in two ways that matter for production deployments:

**`/info`** — Client-side model discovery without hitting `/v1/models`. Any orchestrator (llama-swap, OpenRouter-style routers, multi-instance load balancers) needs to know `context_length` and `default_max_tokens` before sending requests. Currently they have to either parse CLI flags or probe via a chat completion — both fragile.

**`/config`** — Configuration-drift detection across multi-instance fleets. In any deployment with >1 server instance, you need to verify that all instances share identical config. Without a read-only config reflection endpoint, the only way to check is comparing launchd plists or CLI invocations — error-prone and unobservable at runtime.

All three endpoints remain zero-cost (no inference, no allocations beyond buf, no model access) — same footprint as the existing dispatch logic.

If you'd prefer a narrower merge, I can rebase to just `/info` and `/config` since #374 already covers the basic health-check. Either way, the code is written and tested.

Tried this on GB10 (DGX Spark) and wanted to share the numbers, since the hardware + content mix might be a useful data point.

**Environment**: GB10 / DGX Spark, sm_121, 128 GB unified (~273 GB/s). DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Q2 imatrix GGUF, MTP head Q4K/Q8_0. Branch `cont-depth1` @ `205f146`.

**Method**: decode tok/s measured via streaming chat-completions, isolated from prefill (timed first-token -> last-token; token count from `usage.completion_tokens`). Greedy (temp 0). Modes interleaved per round, warm-up round discarded, 8 samples per cell, 95% CI bootstrapped.

| workload | plain AR | `--mtp-draft 2` | continuous | cont vs draft-2 | cont vs AR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| code reproduction (high acc) | 15.42 | 16.00 | 17.05 | +6.5% [+5.9, +7.1] | +10.6% |
| agent / tool-echo (high acc) | 15.51 | 15.44 | 16.88 | +9.4% [+7.5, +10.7] | +8.8% |
| technical prose (med acc) | 15.53 | 14.81 | 15.47 | +4.4% [+3.8, +5.2] | -0.4% |
| free prose, English (low acc) | 15.52 | 14.92 | 14.39 | -3.6% [-4.7, -2.7] | -7.3% |
| chat, Chinese (low acc) | 15.56 | 14.99 | 14.44 | -3.7% [-3.9, -3.4] | -7.2% |

On high-acceptance content (code, tool-echo) continuous is a solid win here — +6.5%/+9.4% over draft-2, and byte-identical to plain AR (argmax-exact). On low-acceptance free generation it comes in a bit below plain AR on this setup.

I checked two things that might explain the low-acceptance behavior:
- **Language**: English free prose and Chinese chat behave the same (-7.3% / -7.2%), so it tracks draft acceptance rather than language.
- **Abliteration**: my base is abliterated with a stock MTP head, so I re-ran on a vanilla (non-abliterated) q2-imatrix base with the same head and got the same pattern (code +10.3%, free prose -5.9%, Chinese -9.4%). The head pairs fine with the vanilla base, so it does not look abliteration-specific.

So on this engine/quant it seems tied to draft acceptance: once acceptance is low, removing the standalone base decode does not offset the wider verify. Might be quant-recipe sensitive (mine is IQ2_XXS / Q2_K). On prose, continuous only diverges from AR at logit ties (chars 21-178), consistent with the argmax-exact note. Happy to share raw JSON + the harness if helpful.

## Update 3: Confirmed client-worker race condition

After adding a global mutex to serialize all client request handling (eliminating client-client concurrency), the server ran for **2.5 hours** before crashing — a 5x improvement from the ~20-30 minutes without it. This strongly points to a **race condition between the client thread and the worker thread** on shared KV cache / tool memory state.

### Latest crash stack (with global client mutex):
xrealloc (ds4_server.c:79) → stop_list_push → id_list_push_unique → collect_tool_call_ids → kv_cache_restore_tool_memory_for_messages → parse_chat_request (ds4_server.c:2776) → client_main

### Key observations:
1. Without client serialization: crash in ~20-30 min
2. With client serialization: crash in ~2.5 hours (5x improvement)
3. Crash site varies (json_string realloc → bpe_emit_piece calloc → stop_list_push realloc) — all detecting the same underlying heap corruption at different allocation points
4. All crashes happen during tool-call-heavy workloads with disk KV cache enabled

### Likely root cause:
Heap corruption from concurrent access to shared session/KV cache/tool memory state between client_main (kv_cache_restore_tool_memory_for_messages, tool_memory_attach_to_messages) and worker_main (generate_job → kv_cache_maybe_store_continued, ds4_session_sync).

### Possible fixes:
1. Add a mutex around KV cache and session state operations shared between client and worker threads
2. Move kv_cache_restore_tool_memory_for_messages() out of the client path and defer it to the worker
3. Disable disk KV cache as a workaround (reduces shared state surface)

I reversed engineered the MTP drafter released with the flash version and created with Opus 4.8 this file. 

**With mtp-margin 2.5 and mtp-draft 2 it achieves better results by 1.2 seconds in the test which I used.**

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
gen_spec.py — generate the authoritative ds4 MTP tensor/metadata spec from the
geometry formulas (derived from ds4.c validate_layout + DS4_SHAPE_*), for either
the Flash or Pro shape.

Why a generated spec instead of value-substituting the Flash file: several Flash
dims collide (e.g. 1024 is BOTH n_lora_q and n_lora_o; 4096 is BOTH n_embd and
n_head_dim*(n_head/n_out_group)). A blind value-substitution Flash->Pro would be
WRONG. So we compute every ne from the shape params.

Usage:
  python3 gen_spec.py flash               > spec_flash.json
  python3 gen_spec.py pro                 > spec_pro.json
  python3 gen_spec.py flash --check FLASH_MTP.gguf   # validate formulas vs the shipped file
"""
import sys, json, struct, argparse

# ---- ggml type ids (subset we use) ----
F32, F16, Q2_K, Q8_0, Q4_K = 0, 1, 10, 8, 12
TYPE_NAME = {F32: "F32", F16: "F16", Q2_K: "Q2_K", Q8_0: "Q8_0", Q4_K: "Q4_K"}
# ds4 allows only these for routed experts (ds4.c tensor_is_routed_expert_type)
EXPERT_TYPES = {"q4_k": Q4_K, "q2_k": Q2_K}

# ---- shape presets (mirror ds4.c DS4_SHAPE_FLASH / DS4_SHAPE_PRO) ----
SHAPES = {
    "flash": dict(n_embd=4096, n_head=64,  n_head_dim=512, n_lora_q=1024,
                  n_lora_o=1024, n_out_group=8,  n_expert=256, n_ff_exp=2048, n_hc=4,
                  name="DeepSeek V4 Flash MTP support"),
    "pro":   dict(n_embd=7168, n_head=128, n_head_dim=512, n_lora_q=1536,
                  n_lora_o=1024, n_out_group=16, n_expert=384, n_ff_exp=3072, n_hc=4,
                  name="DeepSeek V4 Pro MTP support"),
}

def build_spec(shape_key, expert_type=Q4_K):
    s = SHAPES[shape_key]
    E   = s["n_embd"]
    H   = s["n_head"]
    HD  = s["n_head_dim"]
    LQ  = s["n_lora_q"]
    LO  = s["n_lora_o"]
    OG  = s["n_out_group"]
    NE  = s["n_expert"]
    FF  = s["n_ff_exp"]
    HC  = s["n_hc"]

    hc_dim  = E * HC                       # 16384 flash / 28672 pro
    hc_mix  = 2 * HC + HC * HC             # 24 (both)
    q_dim   = H * HD                       # 32768 flash / 65536 pro
    out_low = OG * LO                      # 8192 flash / 16384 pro
    oa_d0   = HD * (H // OG)               # 4096 (both)

    # (name, ggml_type, ne)  — order matches the shipped Flash MTP GGUF dump.
    T = [
        ("mtp.0.hc_head_base.weight",  F32,  [HC]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_head_fn.weight",    F32,  [hc_dim, HC]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_head_scale.weight", F32,  [1]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_attn_base.weight",  F32,  [hc_mix]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_ffn_base.weight",   F32,  [hc_mix]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_attn_fn.weight",    F32,  [hc_dim, hc_mix]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_attn_scale.weight", F32,  [3]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_ffn_fn.weight",     F32,  [hc_dim, hc_mix]),
        ("mtp.0.hc_ffn_scale.weight",  F32,  [3]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_sinks.weight",    F32,  [H]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_q_a.weight",      Q8_0, [E, LQ]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_q_b.weight",      Q8_0, [LQ, q_dim]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_q_a_norm.weight", F32,  [LQ]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_output_a.weight", Q8_0, [oa_d0, out_low]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_kv.weight",       Q8_0, [E, HD]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_kv_a_norm.weight",F32,  [HD]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_output_b.weight", Q8_0, [out_low, E]),
        ("mtp.0.attn_norm.weight",     F32,  [E]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_norm.weight",      F32,  [E]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_gate_shexp.weight",Q8_0, [E, FF]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_up_shexp.weight",  Q8_0, [E, FF]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_down_shexp.weight",Q8_0, [FF, E]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_gate_exps.weight", expert_type, [E, FF, NE]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_up_exps.weight",   expert_type, [E, FF, NE]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_down_exps.weight", expert_type, [FF, E, NE]),
        ("mtp.0.ffn_gate_inp.weight",  F32,  [E, NE]),
        ("mtp.0.exp_probs_b.bias",     F32,  [NE]),
        ("mtp.0.e_proj.weight",        Q8_0, [E, E]),
        ("mtp.0.h_proj.weight",        Q8_0, [E, E]),
        ("mtp.0.enorm.weight",         F32,  [E]),
        ("mtp.0.hnorm.weight",         F32,  [E]),
        ("mtp.0.norm.weight",          F32,  [E]),
    ]
    meta = [
        {"key": "general.architecture",            "type": "str", "value": "deepseek4_mtp_support"},
        {"key": "general.name",                    "type": "str", "value": s["name"]},
        {"key": "deepseek4.nextn_predict_layers",  "type": "u32", "value": 1},
        {"key": "deepseek4.mtp_layer_count",       "type": "u32", "value": 1},
        {"key": "deepseek4.expert_count",          "type": "u32", "value": NE},
    ]
    tensors = [{"name": n, "type": t, "type_name": TYPE_NAME[t], "ne": ne} for (n, t, ne) in T]
    return {"shape": shape_key, "metadata": meta, "tensors": tensors}

# ---- raw GGUF header reader (for --check), no deps ----
def read_gguf_header(path):
    f = open(path, "rb")
    def rd(n): return f.read(n)
    def u32(): return struct.unpack("<I", rd(4))[0]
    def u64(): return struct.unpack("<Q", rd(8))[0]
    def gstr():
        n = u64(); return rd(n).decode("utf-8", "replace")
    def skipval(t):
        # only needs to traverse; we don't keep most values
        simple = {0:1,1:1,2:2,3:2,4:4,5:4,6:4,7:1,10:8,11:8,12:8}
        if t in simple: rd(simple[t]); return None
        if t == 8: return gstr()
        if t == 9:
            ct = u32(); n = u64()
            if ct == 8:
                vals = [gstr() for _ in range(n)]; return vals
            sz = {0:1,1:1,2:2,3:2,4:4,5:4,6:4,7:1,10:8,11:8,12:8}.get(ct,4)
            rd(sz*n); return None
        raise ValueError(f"bad type {t}")
    assert rd(4) == b"GGUF"
    u32()  # version
    nt = u64(); nkv = u64()
    meta = {}
    for _ in range(nkv):
        k = gstr(); t = u32(); v = skipval(t); meta[k] = v
    tensors = []
    for _ in range(nt):
        name = gstr(); nd = u32(); ne = [u64() for _ in range(nd)]; tt = u32(); u64()
        tensors.append({"name": name, "type": tt, "ne": ne})
    return meta, tensors

def check(spec, gguf_path):
    _, got = read_gguf_header(gguf_path)
    want = spec["tensors"]
    gi = {t["name"]: t for t in got}
    ok = True
    print(f"checking {len(want)} generated tensors against {gguf_path} ({len(got)} tensors)")
    for w in want:
        g = gi.get(w["name"])
        if not g:
            print(f"  MISSING in gguf: {w['name']}"); ok = False; continue
        if g["type"] != w["type"] or g["ne"] != w["ne"]:
            print(f"  MISMATCH {w['name']}: gen type={w['type']} ne={w['ne']} | gguf type={g['type']} ne={g['ne']}")
            ok = False
    extra = set(gi) - {w["name"] for w in want}
    for e in sorted(extra): print(f"  EXTRA in gguf (not generated): {e}")
    print("RESULT:", "PASS — formulas reproduce the shipped file" if ok and not extra else "FAIL")
    return ok and not extra

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("shape", choices=list(SHAPES))
    ap.add_argument("--experts", choices=list(EXPERT_TYPES), default="q4_k",
                    help="routed-expert quant type (default q4_k)")
    ap.add_argument("--check", metavar="GGUF", help="validate generated spec against a real MTP gguf")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    spec = build_spec(a.shape, EXPERT_TYPES[a.experts])
    if a.check:
        sys.exit(0 if check(spec, a.check) else 1)
    json.dump(spec, sys.stdout, indent=2)
    print()
```
