Why the stall you sampled does not show up here: the two branches have
opposite defaults for the async selected load. On `main`,
`metal_graph_use_iq2_selected_async_load` is on for every streaming run
(env is opt-out), so the miss advise mostly lands on the async worker: in
our sample ~95% of the fcntl frames sit on
`metal_graph_selected_async_load_worker_main` and fcntl is ~0.5% of the eval
thread. On `glm5.2`, `glm_graph_use_streaming_selected_async_load` is
opt-in, so by default the GLM advise is synchronous on the eval thread,
which is exactly where your 40% sample lives and why skipping it pays there.

So the miss advise is not the problem, issuing it on the eval thread is.
Suggestion: keep the advise default on `main` (or gate the skip on the
synchronous path only), and on the glm5.2 line fix it by moving the advise
off the eval thread (or enabling the async load) rather than dropping the
prefetch. Happy to re-run any variant on this box.

And the "scale of hours" problem is avoidable: the score is a function of the header plus now (last_used), and everything the scorer reads (tokens, hits, ctx_size, reason, created_at, last_used, payload_bytes) is already in the .kv header. So you can replay real cache metadata through the real evict-lowest-until-under-budget loop with a synthetic clock and assert which files survive. Deterministic, instant.

My workload (8 weeks, 702 files, 129 GiB at the time):
- 638 files (91%) never reused (hits=0). Only 64 were ever hit; 13 hit ≥2 times.
- Reuse is concentrated in a handful of small cold session-prefixes (533–2940 tokens, 30–60 MiB) shared across independent sessions, hit 4–16 times each on a daily-to-monthly cadence.
- The bytes are dominated by large one-shot conversations (73k–139k tokens, ~1 GB each) that are never resumed (hits 0–1).
- Density cuts exactly the wrong way: a 533-token prefix costs ~57 KiB/token to store, a 92k-token snapshot ~14 KiB/token. So tokens/file_size ranks the dead 1 GB snapshot ~4x above the live prefix.

Real-world before: I dropped the budget 256 GiB → 32 GiB. When ds4-server launched, the kv-cache went from 702 files to 26, and it evicted every reused prefix (3× hits=16, one hits=9, one hits=4, one hits=2) while keeping 25 one-shot ~1 GB conversations at hits 0–1. The only prefix that survived was one hit 369 times: i.e. hit so constantly that the 6h decay never bit it. That's the failure in one sentence: on a 6h clock, a prefix reused weekly is indistinguishable from a never-hit file by the time eviction runs.

Replay result: The 26 real survivors (headers read off disk) + the 6 evicted prefixes (tokens/hits/size recovered from the eviction log), ran through the real eviction loop.
- current scorer: keeps 0/6 prefixes at 29 GiB: reproduces the real purge exactly.
- new scorer: keeps 6/6: at every budget I tried (10/15/22/29 GiB) and every idle age (3/7/14/30 days), so it isn't an artifact of one assumed age.

Score crossover at 10 days idle: the weakest surviving 1 GB snapshot goes 1.4e-4 to 9.0e-16, while the prefixes go 3.4e-5…9.1e-5 (all below it) to 1.1e-4…7.3e-4 (all above it). The ranking inverts.

On reusing the existing 6h constant: Decaying the baseline on the 6h clock fixes half of it (a dead conversation stops riding its raw size forever). But the hit evidence needs a slower clock, or a prefix reused weekly/monthly still has its hit count annihilated between uses (30 days is around 120 half-lives) and lands right back on the density floor. There are two different reuse processes here: "will this conversation be continued" is genuinely a recency thing measured in hours; "will a new session reuse this shared prefix" is an arrival rate, not a recency. One constant can't express both: that's why I split it in PR #550 rather than tuning the 6h.

The issue fundamentally remains as follows. Vendored DSpark tensors quantized to Q4_K yield average acceptance ~2.2 tokens on a broad prompt corpus. Optimized DSpark drafter + shipped batch verifier (BTW it's not greedy-exact, ~0.6% top-1 logits flip) make it approximately equal to baseline decode on M5 Max. Since my last report I tried a couple of things.

Firstly, I had a hypothesis that vendored DSpark tensors are trained on the full-pecision V4-Flash target model and fail to propose long-enough prefixes on our IQ2XXS version. I [tested earlier](https://github.com/lobanov/ds4/blob/dspark-research/issue468/archive/leads/lead_03_acceptance_statistical_power.md) with a PyTorch oracle on a substantial prompt corpus that there is no acceptance gains if the drafter is kept in higher precision, even BF16 proposes blocks with the same quality, but I could not rule out that higher precision *target model* could be more efficient because it'll feed the drafter with different residuals. To test that, I rented 2xH200 from Modal.com and run a patched vLLM to capture residuals and greedy tokens on full-precision V4-Flash with 300 prompts at 128 anchor points (fewer on shorter responses), totalling ~20k anchors. Then I ran the PyTorch oracle to simulate acceptance, and it **did show** 8-10% uplift headroom potential, but it's unclear how much of that is recoverable in IQ2XXS target model version. Cautious estimate is around 5% with custom-trained adaptation, but that alone won't make a big difference. Full report is [here](https://github.com/lobanov/ds4/blob/dspark-research/issue468/archive/leads/lead_04_fp_ceiling_capture.md). I didn't follow further leads yet.

Besides, I also captured top-128 logits, so this could be used in future for verifying quantized V4-Flash model output quality. If anyone is interested, I can upload the captures as a HuggingFace dataset.

Second thing I tried is investigating confidence-based scheduling. DSpark has it's own built-in confidence head which sort-of predicts the level of confidence of the drafter. It's useless for stopping drafting earlier, because it needs to be batched for efficiency, but it's useful for scheduling the verifier to look at fewer tokens in a batch. DSpark paper also describes a fitted STS-based scheduler, which I replicated. I've got oracle-based 5% speedup figure, which in itself isn't a decisive win again, but it could stack up nicely. Full report is [here](https://github.com/lobanov/ds4/blob/dspark-research/issue468/archive/leads/lead_02_confidence_scheduled_verification.md).

memory, sm_121, CUDA 13.0, driver 580.159.03) — the unified-memory
open question raised earlier is now resolved with real data.

`cudaMemGetInfo` reports the full system memory correctly on this
hardware-coherent unified-memory system:

  ds4: SSD streaming auto cache budget
  ds4:   cuda recommends 121.69 GiB working set
  ds4:   using 80% total for model + cached experts: 97.35 GiB
  ds4:   non-routed weights: 8.20 GiB
  ds4:   routed expert size: 6.75 MiB
  ds4:   cached expert count: 11008 (72.56 GiB)

The initial plan (11008 experts) is then correctly refined at runtime
by the existing capping logic based on actually available memory:

  ds4: CUDA streaming expert cache capped from 11008 to 4747 experts
  (available 47.29 GiB, reserve 16.00 GiB, 6.75 MiB/expert)

With the auto-sized cache, generation reaches 8.4 t/s once the expert
cache is warm (q2 model, short prompts, no manual tuning flags at
all). The same binary auto-sizes correctly on an 8GB discrete laptop
GPU and on this 128GB unified-memory system.

So the PR is validated on both memory architectures: discrete VRAM
(RTX 4070 Laptop 8GB) and hardware-coherent unified memory (GB10).

Tested on NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, Grace Blackwell, 128GB unified
memory, sm_121, CUDA 13.0, driver 580.159.03) to verify behavior on
hardware-coherent unified-memory systems.

As expected on this architecture, the fallback never triggers:
`cudaMalloc` draws from the single unified pool, so the OOM condition
that activates the fallback on discrete GPUs (device memory exhausted
while system RAM is available) cannot occur — the model's non-routed
weights (8.20 GiB) allocate directly without ever reaching the
fallback path. No behavioral change, no overhead, no regressions
observed on this hardware.

Worth noting for completeness: if the unified pool itself were
exhausted (e.g. a model larger than total system memory), the
fallback's `cudaHostAlloc` would fail too, since there is no separate
reserve to draw from on unified memory. That double-failure path is
handled: it logs both errors explicitly and fails cleanly, identical
to the pre-patch behavior (and with a more diagnostic error message).

In summary: this fallback is specifically useful on discrete GPUs
whose VRAM is smaller than a model's always-resident weights (where
it turns a hard crash into a working, if slower, run — as measured
on an 8GB laptop GPU). On unified-memory systems it is dormant and
harmless.

One correction to the staged plan above, caught while scoping stage 1
against the source.

Stage 1 was described as "dense-FFN cluster — first layers without
router". That premise is wrong for V4 Flash: all 43 layers are MoE
(`DS4_SHAPE_FLASH`: `n_expert = 256`, no dense-layer field), and the
first 3 layers are hash-routing (`n_hash_layer = 3`) — still MoE, and
actually the one place where `router_select` takes the token as a
per-token scalar. The wording was a mental leftover from V3-style
architectures.

Stage 1 is therefore retargeted to the **shared-expert FFN cluster**,
identical in every layer: `shared_gate_up_swiglu_q8_0` → `swiglu` →
`shared_down_hc_expand_q8_0`. All three shims are in the capturable set
from the audit (no per-token scalars, no routing indirection, stable
buffer pointers), which makes it the smallest cluster that still
exercises the full capture mechanics (non-blocking stream, scoped
override, warm-up, sync brackets, per-layer graph cache, eager
fallback).

Terminology note for anyone cross-reading Entrpi's decode-perf-tuning
fork: `dense_graph` there means dense *matmul* (single attention-side
projections at n_tok=1), not "dense layer". Unrelated to this cluster.

Stage 2 (routed MoE cluster with the device-side `selected`
indirection) and stage 3 are unchanged.

Corroborating this with a longer-context reproduction, plus one amplification path I don't think is described here yet.

**Setup**: ds4-server on Apple M5 Max 128GB (Metal), single slot, ~202k-token session arriving through an Anthropic-API proxy. Client is Claude Code, whose stream watchdog has a fixed deadline (600s at the time) that SSE comment lines do not reset.

**What we measured — 2026-07-14, 85 consecutive minutes on one node:**

```
15:17:52 → 15:34:28  ctx=20480..202634:182154  prefill 944.1s  finish=tool_calls gen=928
15:35:47 → 15:52:14  ctx=20480..202634:182154  prefill 937.5s  finish=error "client stream write failed"
15:52:18 → 16:08:39  ctx=20480..202639:182159  prefill 934.8s  finish=tool_calls gen=838
16:09:16 → 16:25:43  ctx=20480..202645:182165  prefill 934.0s  finish=tool_calls gen=971
16:25:46 → 16:42:08  ctx=20480..202645:182165  prefill 931.9s  finish=error "client stream write failed"
```

Five full prefills of the same conversation, back to back. The client had already disconnected in every case — its deadline is ~600s and each prefill needs ~935s. The user received **zero tokens across six attempts spanning 2.5 hours**.

Three things to add to the report:

**1. The wasted work is worse than wasted GPU time — the answers were finished.**
Three of the five runs reached `finish=tool_calls` and generated 928 / 838 / 971 tokens. The server did the work, produced a complete answer, and dropped it because nobody was on the socket. Only the other two surfaced as `client stream write failed`, so most of the damage leaves no error in the log at all.

**2. The retry doesn't just re-prefill — it can't start.**
Because the abandoned prefill keeps the single slot for another ~5 minutes after the client leaves, retry N+1 queues behind it. On the proxy side, the retry saw no `: prefill` progress comments for its entire 630s lifetime: it never got the slot, so it was guaranteed to fail before it began. The cost per disconnect isn't one wasted prefill, it's a self-sustaining queue.

**3. With a fixed client deadline shorter than the prefill, this never converges.**
It isn't "several minutes of wasted GPU work before the server is available again" — it's an unbounded loop. It stopped only when the user gave up. Past roughly 130k tokens (600s × our measured prefill rate) the failure stops being intermittent and becomes certain.

**This is reachable straight from the README.** The recommended Claude Code wrapper sets `CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=600000`, and that watchdog is not reset by the `: prefill` keepalive comments from #222 — only by a real SSE event. So on the documented setup, any session whose cold prefill exceeds 600s can never produce a token, and every retry re-enters the loop described above. We had to move the fleet to `1200000` to get long-context sessions working at all; with #333 fixed the documented 600000 would at least fail cheaply (slot released in seconds) instead of burning the node.

Collateral: unrelated requests needing 30–76s of actual work took 910s and 1445s wall-clock, queued behind the zombies.

**On the fix**: Option A (cancel flag checked between chunks) looks sufficient for all of the above, and the granularity is better than it might sound — our logs show 1024-token prefill chunks landing every ~3–5s (220–340 tok/s on M5 Max), so a per-chunk check would release the slot within about 5 seconds:

```
0714 15:00:01 ds4-server: chat ctx=0..81249:81249 TOOLS prefill chunk 11264/81249 (13.9%) chunk=314.96 t/s avg=343.45 t/s 32.797s
0714 15:00:05 ds4-server: chat ctx=0..81249:81249 TOOLS prefill chunk 12288/81249 (15.1%) chunk=319.31 t/s avg=341.30 t/s 36.004s
```

This also compounds with #62: once the retry finally runs, the token mismatch means it re-prefills from the same stuck 20480-token prefix, which is why all five runs above are byte-identical in size.

No — DS4's CUDA backend is single-GPU only. ds4_gpu_init() in ds4_cuda.cu hardcodes cudaSetDevice(0) and never enumerates or uses additional GPUs. There's no tensor parallelism, no model parallelism, and no multi-GPU CLI flags within a single process.

The only way to use both GPUs is the distributed mode — separate processes (coordinator + worker), each pinned to one GPU, communicating over TCP.

@ivanfioravanti re: "working aside on M5 but struggling a bit" — here's what we've measured on M5, in case it saves you time. M5 Max 128GB, macOS 27.0 (26A5378n), running ds4 with GLM-5.2 IQ2_XXS (197GB, SSD-streamed) and V4-Flash.

**Apple already ships a routed-MoE quantized GEMM, and it's MLX's `gather_qmm` on TensorOps.**

`MPSNDArrayQuantizedGatherMatrixMultiplication` is live and instantiable in MPS right now. It's exported in the **26.5** SDK as well as 27.0 — so it isn't a 27 thing — but there's no public header in either: private ABI, tbd export only. Its init is the whole MoE pipeline spelled out:

```
initWithDevice:leftQuantizationDescriptor:rightQuantizationDescriptor:
  isSorted:batchDims:hasLHSIndices:hasUnsortOrder:sourceCount:
```

The metallib reflection gives away the design — shader family `gather_qmm_rhs` / `gather_qmm_impl_cooperative_tile`, params struct `MPSNDArrayQuantizedGatherMultiplyParams` carrying `experts_per_token` and `w_experts_stride`, kernel args `x(half), w(uchar), scales, biases, indices(uint)` — and it runs on `__tensorops_impl_matmul2d_op_run_cooperative_b16_b16_f32_v2`.

So it's a fused affine expert-loader on the same TensorOps matmul2d engine you'd target yourself on M5 — not new silicon. Its ceiling is TensorOps. That was the useful part for us: it told us where the roof is.

**It's affine-only, by hard assert.** Hand it a LUT/codebook descriptor:

```
MPSNDArrayQuantizedGatherMatrixMultiplication.mm:592: failed assertion `Only RHS affine quantization supported'
```

So it can't take ds4's IQ2_XXS (codebook magnitudes + separate sign channel + per-K-block scales). MLX-style affine (q·scale + bias) only. Its affine scale blocks also run along **N, not K** — K-grouped layouts get `invalid block size`.

**Measured at ds4's GLM gate shape** (6144→2048, top-8-of-256), affine-u8:

```
S=  1 (rows    8):   0.295 ms   eff 385 GB/s
S=  8 (rows   64):   2.195 ms   eff 369 GB/s
S= 64 (rows  512):  24.062 ms   eff 132 GB/s
S=256 (rows 2048): 110.430 ms   eff  33 GB/s
```

Note the efficiency collapse as fan-out saturates all 256 experts. Caveat: the one gather config that encodes cleanly mis-computes on this build (the same descriptor is exact to 8.8e-8 on the non-gather QMM), so treat those as timings only. We killed it for our format.

**One more for your M5 work:** Metal 27 adds `MTLTensorDataTypeInt2`/`UInt2`, `MetalFloat4E2M1`, `MetalFloat8E4M3`/`E5M2`, `Float8UE8M0` — none in 26.5. And the OS upgrade brings the command-line tools to SDK 27.0, so you can compile against them without beta Xcode.

Stage 1 complete: shared-expert FFN cluster capture/replay — correctness validated, performance neutral as expected

Stage 1 is done on [`riccardo-galbani/ds4`, branch `cuda-graphs-stage1`](https://github.com/riccardo-galbani/ds4/tree/cuda-graphs-stage1) (stacked on `cuda-graphs-stage0`, PR #566). Full stage 1 diff (excluding stage 0): [compare view](https://github.com/riccardo-galbani/ds4/compare/cuda-graphs-stage0...cuda-graphs-stage1). Five commits:

C1 — process-global NonBlocking capture stream, created in ds4_gpu_init under the DS4_CUDA_GRAPHS gate (value, not presence).
C2 — scoped thread-local stream override (enter at BeginCapture, exit at EndCapture).
C3 — per-cluster state machine (EMPTY → WARMED → CAPTURED), key on 8 fields, bidirectional sync brackets, invalidation on arena generation.
C4 — wiring at the resident call site of metal_graph_encode_decode_layer. Two findings corrected the plan:
the default fused cluster is TWO shims (gate_up_swiglu → down_hc), and the output pointer alternates per token parity (43 layers, odd), so
slots are 4-way set-associative per layer, full-key match, deterministic policy, CAPTURED ways never evicted.
C5 — arena pre-warm: cuda_tmp_alloc sized to the computed session maximum at both graph-creation points (session and sessionless
paths), so the arena never grows after t0 — no cudaMalloc can fall in a capture bracket and the generation stays stable for the whole
session. The dominant prefill site verified exactly linear at 96 KiB/token across two decades of prefill_cap.

Correctness (GB10, sm_121): logits bit-identical to upstream in all graphs × MTP combinations; counter signatures stable across -n 40, ~900 and ~2000-token runs (non-MTP: 86 captured / 86 eager, one capture per way, zero re-captures; MTP: 88/88); arena generation 1 for the whole session. Gate off: byte-identical output to upstream behavior.

We implemented the per-token verify checkpointing proposed in this thread and can report measurements. (Disclosure: this work was done with heavy AI assistance — Claude — driving a Mac Studio; all numbers below are from real runs on that hardware, and the branch passes `--server`, `--metal-kernels`, and `--logprob-vectors`.)

**What was built** — the N=2 `prefix1` mechanism generalized to K slots (`DS4_SPEC_CKPT_MAX 8`), ~200 lines in `ds4.c`, no new Metal kernels: during the batched verify encode, the compressor/indexer frontier state (~32 KB/layer) is blitted into slot *t* after each suffix position (same in-stream `ds4_gpu_tensor_copy` pattern as the existing prefix1 captures at the two `t == 0` sites). A partial accept of *k* tokens then commits slot *k−1* and reads its already-computed spec-logits row — no snapshot restore, no second batched pass, no anchor replay. The anchor-only miss unifies with the general partial case (slot 0, row 0).

**Measured on M3 Ultra 256 GB (60-core bin), Flash q4-imatrix, greedy, ctx 32768**, with prompt-lookup (#396) as the drafter so partials occur naturally:

- partial-accept verify cost: **178–186 ms (restore + second pass) → 111–114 ms (single pass)**
- greedy output **byte-identical** across baseline / old partial path / checkpointed path (same SHA-256 for all three)
- extract-style workload throughput 54.6 → 56.6 t/s (CLI); the larger effect is that partial-heavy acceptance patterns stop being punished — exactly the block>2 economics problem quantified upthread

Code: https://github.com/robotnursenyc/ds4/commit/a6252fb79d (branch `dsv4-speculative-stack`, which stacks on #555 + #396). Happy to rebase this into a standalone PR against `main` wired to whichever consumer is preferred — MTP N>2 or the #396/#502 paths — and to drop the `DS4_SPEC_CKPT` diagnostic switch per AGENT.md's no-permanent-flags rule if it lands as default behavior.

Measurements for this PR on M3 Ultra 256 GB (60-core bin), Flash q4-imatrix, greedy, ctx 32768, merged onto the #555 branch. (Disclosure: AI-assisted — Claude driving the box; branch passes `--server`, `--metal-kernels`, `--logprob-vectors`.)

| Workload | Baseline | Prompt-lookup | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| extract/copy-heavy | 37.4 t/s | **54.6 t/s (+46%)** | 85.7% acceptance, 6.0 tok/verify |
| classify w/ repetitive output | 37.2 | **45.3 (+22%)** | drafts from output history win |
| novel prose | 37.8 | 37.5 (neutral) | 220/220 no-match; scans cost 0.02 ms *total* |

Greedy output byte-identical to baseline in all three (same SHA-256). The no-match path is effectively free — the risk is only miss-heavy *matching* workloads burning verify passes.

Two follow-ups on our branch (https://github.com/robotnursenyc/ds4/tree/dsv4-speculative-stack), offered if useful:

1. **Adaptive economics guard** (commit b6e3ce5): a verify pass costs ~4 baseline tokens of weight streaming, so we track an EMA of per-event value in baseline-token units and latch prompt-lookup off per session when it goes negative, re-probing every 256 tokens; the server then falls back to the MTP drafter while latched (commit 4808b68 prefers PL over MTP for greedy spans since measured upside is much larger). This bounds the downside on adversarial workloads without giving up the copy-heavy win.

2. **A server-side finding that affects this PR's reach** (commit 66b50d5): with think-mode enabled, `ds4_server.c` forces `temperature = DS4_DEFAULT_TEMPERATURE` (1.0) for the whole request, which disables every greedy speculative path — this PR *and* the MTP drafter — for think-mode chat requests, and silently overrides an explicit client `temperature: 0` for the final answer. Restoring client sampling once the thinking span closes re-enables speculation for the answer span: measured server answer-span chunks 44.7–47.8 t/s vs 34.5 before, thinking spans unchanged. If that behavior change is wanted upstream we'd propose it flag-free as the default for explicit client temp<=0, per AGENT.md.

Reproduced this on an M5 Pro (48 GB) and looked into it with Claude. Sharing the root cause; I couldn't fully validate a fix on this machine, so it's analysis rather than a PR.

### Reproduce

```
DS4_TEST_MODEL=./ds4flash.gguf DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1 DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING_CACHE_GB=8 ./ds4_test --tool-call-quality
```

The exact path fails with `Metal model range ... not covered by mapped model views` → `decode_ok` assertion.

### Root cause

Under `--quality`, `g_quality_mode` turns off `fuse_pair_swiglu` and `direct_down_sum`. Both `use_q4_selected_slots` and `use_iq2_selected_slots` are gated on those flags, so quality decode never enters the streamed-slot branch and falls through to the generic branch, which wraps the full per-layer routed tensor via `ds4_gpu_wrap_model_range`. Under `--ssd-streaming` that range isn't a mapped model view (the error), and mapping the whole routed pool to satisfy it OOMs a machine smaller than the pool.

### Note

Relaxing the gate so quality decode enters the slot branch removes the error and passes the suite, but quality's decode output then drifts from the fast path more than a fusion-only change would explain — plausibly because quality's other paths (sort, indexer, router) differ too, or because the slot path needs quality's expert ordering. I can't tell which without a ground-truth quality baseline, and I can't get one on 48 GB (resident quality needs the full model). So I didn't want to open a fix I couldn't verify.

The clean direction is probably to gather the exact non-fused quality encode from the resident slots instead of the full pool, keeping quality's math while staying within the streaming budget.

Here are a few data points from our independent research on this issue that may help focus the remaining effort. We did a deep dive on lobanov's research branch (docs 00-24) cross-checked against the actual M5 Max binary and RAM budget, and found several things worth sharing:

## 1. The F32-accum gathered-dense kernel infrastructure already exists

The `kernel_q4_gather_slots6` and `kernel_mul_mv_slots6_q4_K_pair_swiglu_f32` kernels are present in lobanov's metal/moe.metal on the dspark branch. They implement the F32-accumulation path over unchanged Q4_K weights — the fix that recovers the 2.79→1.53 collapse. However, the C-side toggle/env-var plumbing was never completed (no `DS4_METAL_ENABLE_Q4_GATHER_SLOTS` in ds4.c). The infrastructure is there and could be wired with ~50 lines of C — no new Metal kernels needed. This is a concrete path to recovering the ~1.53→~2.2 Metal acceptance.

## 2. Memory budget for higher-precision drafter quants

Verified on the M5 Max 128GB: real headroom is ~29 GiB (the GGUF is reclaimable mmap page cache, not resident). Q8_0 drafter (+9GB) and Q6_K (+3.8GB) both fit. Only F16 (+26GB) breaks the budget. This means Q8_0 is a viable option for anyone wanting to test whether higher drafter precision improves acceptance — it doesn't require a RAM upgrade.

## 3. The +1 token recovery quantification

The guaranteed +1 token/cycle was dropped from the terminal table in doc 23. Restoring it changes the economics materially:
- greedy+1: +9% at 64k
- B2 (A≈1.82)+1: +22% at 64k
- oracle+1: +64% at 64k

This is now partially captured in confidence scheduling (the "bonus token" from failed verifies), but explicitly accounting for the +1 across all cycles may reveal additional headroom.

## 4. Structured lever ranking

From our doc 24 review, ranked by effort/impact:
1. F32 accumulation over Q4_K — memory-neutral, no GGUF rebuild, ~1.53→~2.2 Metal acceptance
2. imatrix at Q4_K — must be collected from drafter's real activations, not target's
3. Q6_K/Q8_0 — only if offline Pareto sweep justifies new routed kernel
4. Target-distillation fine-tuning — highest ceiling, costliest

The key enabler: under F32 accumulation the numpy oracle IS the production model, so the entire quant×imatrix frontier is measurable offline in Python with zero new Metal kernels. This lets you answer "does higher drafter precision help" in ~hours, not weeks.

## 5. Measured cost curves (M5 Max)

For reference, our measurements of the component costs:
- Plain decode: 31.3→35.5 ms/tok (7k→64k, +11% SWA-flat)
- Batch verify (L=5): ~75 ms, context-flat
- Drafter backbone (3 layers, 5 tok): 5.0 ms; total draft ~7.2 ms

These match closely with the numbers others have reported and confirm the verifier-dominated regime.

The acceptance ceiling (~2.2 on broad prompts) and verifier cost (~80ms/cycle) remain the hard constraints. The most promising paths forward given current understanding appear to be: (a) wiring the existing F32-accum kernel to recover Metal acceptance, (b) per-token verify checkpointing (which robotnursenyc implemented) to eliminate the partial-commit replay tax, and (c) exploring whether Q8_0 drafter moves acceptance on the verifier-dominated workloads where it matters most.

Heads up: the Q4_K DSpark GGUF on the HF bucket (`ds4flash-dspark.gguf`, uploaded 2026-06-30) silently disables the drafter on upstream main, so any test using it measures pure overhead, not speculation.

## What's happening

The GGUF's three small-head tensors are stored as bf16:
- `mtp.2.markov_head.markov_w1.weight`
- `mtp.2.markov_head.markov_w2.weight`
- `mtp.2.confidence_head.proj.weight`

This matches the source model — audreyt noted above that the small heads are bf16/fp32 by design. The problem is that upstream main's `dspark_markov_probe_ready()` in ds4.c only accepts F16/F32/Q8_0 for `DS4_DSPARK_LAYOUT_DENSE`:

```c
case DS4_DSPARK_LAYOUT_DENSE:
    return type == DS4_TENSOR_F16 ||
           type == DS4_TENSOR_F32 ||
           type == DS4_TENSOR_Q8_0;
```

bf16 fails the check, so `markov_ready` stays false, `markov_ok` never becomes true, and `dspark_draft_valid` never gets set. The speculation entry gate then hits:

```c
if (!s || !s->dspark_draft_valid || s->dspark_draft_len == 0) {
    s->dspark_stats.no_draft++;
    return n_accept;   // returns 0 accepted
}
```

## Evidence

Running on M5 Max / upstream main `427e281` with `DS4_DSPARK_STATS=1`:

```
DSpark stats cycles=119 first_tokens=119 proposed=0 accepted_draft=0
accept_rate=0.00% avg_accept=0.000 full=0 partial=0 miss_first=0
no_draft=119 no_room=0 invalid=0
verify=0.000 verify_layer=0.000 replay=0.000
```

`proposed=0` across every flag combination I tried (`--dspark`, `--dspark-confidence 0.9`, `--mtp-draft 2/5`, `DS4_DSPARK_SCHEDULER=1`). The verifier never runs because the drafter never produces tokens. The -5% to -15% regressions I measured are the cost of carrying a dormant drafter (target-hidden capture on layers 40-42 + scheduling bookkeeping), not the verifier economics.

Forcing the drafter with `DS4_DSPARK_FAKE_ARGMAX_PROPOSAL=1` confirms speculation can run — `proposed=28, accepted=28, accept_rate=100%` — but that's the target's own argmax, not DSpark.

## Why this likely affects others

- @lobanov's +5% milestone is on the `dspark-research` branch, which has a different DSpark path (no `dspark_markov_probe_ready` gate — I checked, the function doesn't exist there). His results are real but on his branch, not upstream main.
- @machiabeli built their own GGUF ("47/47 byte-exact"), which likely casts bf16→F16 during conversion, so it works on main.
- @deathcoder's "~12% slower than baseline" matches the dormant-drafter overhead pattern exactly — possible they're hitting the same silent disable.

## Two fixes

1. **Re-quantize** the bucket GGUF casting the three small-head tensors bf16→F16 (they're ~70 MB total, negligible).
2. **Or** add bf16 to the accepted `DS4_DSPARK_LAYOUT_DENSE` types in upstream main — the engine already has bf16 support elsewhere (`ds4q_bf16_to_f32` exists in gguf-tools).

Either way, until one lands, anyone testing DSpark on upstream main with the bucket GGUF is measuring overhead, not speculation — which may explain why the negative results across participants are so inconsistent.

Happy to PR the type-check fix if that's the preferred direction.

@elkaix
The freshness grace is a good fix for fresh waypoints evicted before they earn a hit, but it misses one case, and for that case it's slightly worse than main.

Keeping a cache entry is a bet on future reuse, and past reuse is the best signal for it. A COLD reused a hundred times will likely be reused again; an EVICT or CONTINUED idle a few days probably won't be, no matter what size it is.

#489's activity-scaled anchor bonus strips a COLD entry's bonus once it goes idle, so a COLD that is reused often but on a slow cadence (mine gets hit dozens of times every couple of weeks) loses protection right when it needs it, and ranks below a much larger, but days-old conversation.

#550 keeps the 6h half-life for conversation snapshots (continued/evict) but stretches it to weeks for COLD, so a repeatedly-reused entry point's reuse count survives the gap instead of collapsing to zero.

▎ Heads up: this change produces incorrect output on DGX Spark (GB10) — I built it and the model emits pure garbage tokens (endless repeated CJK/random tokens) where main answers coherently, same prompt with --temp 0.

▎ The problem is that the kernels only get their row index rewritten, but the reduction is still full-warp. In e.g. matmul_q8_0_preq_warp8_kernel the row becomes

▎ uint64_t row  = (uint64_t)blockIdx.x * 16u + (threadIdx.x >> 4u);
▎ uint32_t lane = threadIdx.x & 31u;      // unchanged
▎ ...
▎ for (uint64_t b = lane; b < blocks; b += 32u) { ... }   // stride 32, unchanged
▎ acc = warp_sum_f32(acc);                // full 32-lane __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, ...)
▎ if (lane == 0) out[row] = acc;          // unchanged

▎ With >> 4, two adjacent output rows now share one physical 32-lane warp (row R on lanes 0–15, row R+1 on lanes 16–31). warp_sum_f32() reduces across all 32 lanes, so it sums the partials of two different rows together, and because only lane == 0 writes, out[R] gets the corrupted mixed sum while out[R+1] is never written at all. Same issue in the MoE gate_up path (rr<8, blockIdx.x*256 + row_lane + rr*16 feeding a still-32-lane reduction). The benchmark table looks great because ds4-bench measures t/s, not output correctness.

▎ To do 16 rows/block correctly the reduction has to become per-16-lane too: lane = threadIdx.x & 15, stride b += 16u, a 16-wide shuffle reduction (offsets 8→1), and if ((threadIdx.x & 15) == 0) for the write. Whether that's actually faster than the current 8-rows/block (half the lanes per reduction) would need re-measuring — with a correctness check this time.

- **Hardware**: GMKtec EVO-X2 — AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), iGPU Radeon 8060S, `gfx1151`, 128 GB unified LPDDR5X
- **OS**: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, HIP 7.1, ROCm (hipcc `/usr/bin/hipcc`)
- **GPU memory**: UMA BIOS 2 GB + `amd-ttm --set 115` → ~117 GB GTT dynamic
- **Model**: DeepSeek-V4-Flash IQ2_XXS (w2Q2K, AProj/SExp/Out Q8, chat-v2 imatrix), 80.76 GiB — fits entirely in GTT (no SSD streaming)
- **Corpus**: `speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt` (SHA `f53e0d80`, 1.3 MB)
- **Build**: `make strix-halo` (gfx1151, HIPCC), commits `80ebbc3` (baseline) vs `efdadd4` (HEAD)

### Bisect

The ROCm equivalent of `173a9a3` is commit **`ef8d923`** ("Add ROCm GLM 5.2 support"). `80ebbc3` is the direct parent — same clean bisect as the Metal side.

### Benchmark results (Promessi Sposi, 16K→100K sweep)

```bash
/usr/bin/time -v ./ds4-bench -m ./ds4flash.gguf \
    --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
    --ctx-start CONTEXT --ctx-max CONTEXT \
    --step-incr 2048 --gen-tokens 64
    
```

| Context | `80ebbc3` prefill t/s | `efdadd4` prefill t/s | Δ prefill | `80ebbc3` gen t/s | `efdadd4` gen t/s |      Δ gen |
| ------: | --------------------: | --------------------: | --------: | ----------------: | ----------------: | ---------: |
|     16K |                215.21 |                209.22 |     −2.8% |         **14.18** |          **8.15** | **−42.6%** |
|     32K |                210.77 |                199.54 |     −5.3% |         **13.53** |          **7.94** | **−41.3%** |
|     65K |                193.81 |                171.14 |    −11.7% |         **12.58** |          **7.60** | **−39.6%** |
|    100K |                177.04 |                138.33 |    −21.9% |         **11.66** |          **7.27** | **−37.7%** |

**Generation is consistently ~40% slower across all context sizes.** Prefill is roughly unchanged at 16K but degrades at longer contexts (−22% at 100K), likely due to the new KV-cache compression overhead.

### Root cause: fast-path decode Q8_0 `n_tok==1` removed in `ef8d923`

`ef8d923` rewrote `rocm/ds4_rocm_matmul.cuh`. The diff shows the single-token decode fast-path being deleted:

**Before** (`80ebbc3`, `ds4_rocm_matmul.cuh` ~line 248):

```c
if (n_tok == 1 && !cuda_runtime_config()->q8_prequant_decode) {
    // Dedicated decode kernel: matmul_q8_0_preq_rows_w32_kernel
    uint32_t rows_per_block = cfg->q8_decode_rpb;
    matmul_q8_0_preq_rows_w32_kernel<<<...>>>(out, wptr, xq, xscale, ...);
    return;
}
```

**After** (`efdadd4`): the entire `n_tok == 1` branch is gone. Decode (`n_tok==1` = generation phase) now falls through to the generic batch prefill path, which is much slower for single tokens.

This is the exact same pattern as the Metal regression — but for ROCm.

### Why `427e281` doesn't help us

On Metal, `427e281` ("Optimize Metal prefill and decode kernels") restored the in-RAM decode path. But in `rocm/ds4_rocm_matmul.cuh`, the same commit only adds an **empty stub** (`return 0` body, all args cast to `void`):

```c
// Added by 427e281 to rocm/ds4_rocm_matmul.cuh:
extern "C" int ds4_gpu_matmul_f16_pair_compressor_store_tensor(...) {
    (void)out_kv; (void)out_score; ...  // all args unused
    return 0;  // ← no-op
}
```

So the ROCm fast-path decode was never restored.

### Key difference from the Metal issue

- On **Metal**: model fits in RAM → `427e281` fixed it; only SSD streaming remains broken (PR #578).
- On **ROCm**: model fits in GTT (80.76 GiB of 117 GiB) → **still broken** because the fast-path was never restored.

### Reproduction

```bash
# Any Strix Halo machine (gfx1151), ROCm 7.1
cd ~/ds4-repo
make strix-halo

# Baseline (fast): checkout 80ebbc3, rebuild, benchmark
git checkout 80ebbc3 && make strix-halo
./ds4-bench -m ds4flash.gguf --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
    --ctx-start 16384 --ctx-max 16384 --gen-tokens 64
# → gen ~14 t/s

# Regressed (slow): checkout efdadd4, rebuild, benchmark
git checkout efdadd4 && make strix-halo
./ds4-bench -m ds4flash.gguf --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
    --ctx-start 16384 --ctx-max 16384 --gen-tokens 64
# → gen ~8 t/s
```

### Suggested fix

Restore the `n_tok == 1` fast-path in `rocm/ds4_rocm_matmul.cuh` (`cuda_matmul_q8_0_tensor_labeled`), equivalent to what existed in `80ebbc3`. The removed kernel `matmul_q8_0_preq_rows_w32_kernel` and its launch config are still present in the file above the deleted block.

This PR ports the lossless low-memory streaming optimizations from DS4Demo to the C Metal backend.

The main improvement is a per-layer dense-weight staging ring that reads exact GGUF byte ranges through a dedicated F_NOCACHE file descriptor. This avoids repeatedly walking large non-routed tensors through the macOS page cache during every generated token.

On an Apple M1 Pro with 16 GB of unified memory, the optimized C path improves decode throughput from approximately 0.225 token/s to 0.61 token/s, or about 2.7x, while preserving the selected tokens and top-20 logprobs byte for byte.

This PR deliberately excludes the lossy DS4Demo .q4dense cache.

Motivation

The existing C SSD-streaming implementation already streams routed experts and supports an expert cache. However, non-routed weights are still accessed through mmap-backed model views.

On memory-constrained Macs, the dense working set is larger than the available page cache. Each generated token therefore causes several gigabytes of dense weights to compete with routed experts and other model data, continuously evicting useful pages.

In the controlled M1 Pro 16 GB benchmark, this resulted in approximately 4.4 seconds per generated token, despite using the same expert bundle as DS4Demo.

DS4Demo avoids much of this page-cache churn by streaming dense layer weights explicitly and overlapping storage reads with Metal execution. This PR implements the equivalent lossless strategy in the C backend.

Implementation

Per-layer dense-weight staging ring

The Metal SSD-streaming path can now load non-routed weights into a ring of shared Metal buffers.

For every decoder layer:

  1. The required dense GGUF ranges are identified.
  2. Exact bytes are read using pread() through a dedicated descriptor configured with F_NOCACHE.
  3. Disjoint ranges can be read in parallel.
  4. The Metal backend temporarily resolves the original GGUF offsets against the staged buffer.
  5. Existing kernels continue using their original model offsets and tensor formats.
  6. After the command buffer completes, the slot can safely be reused for a later layer.

The recommended configuration uses:

  • DS4_DENSE_AHEAD=2
  • three staging slots;
  • approximately 160 MiB per slot;
  • three parallel reads per layer.

The staged bytes are identical to the original GGUF data. There is no tensor conversion or requantization.

Safe model-offset overrides

A small Metal backend registry maps selected model ranges to their current staging buffer.

The override table is changed only when:

  • no command encoder is open;
  • no command buffer using the previous ranges is pending;
  • the staging slot is no longer used by the GPU.

If publication or loading fails, the optimization is disabled and inference falls back to the existing mmap-backed model views.

Expert-bundle read coalescing

When the Swift-compatible expert bundle stores gate, up and down slabs contiguously, the C backend now reads the complete record with one operation instead of three separate reads.

The previous three-read path remains available as a fallback when:

  • the buffers are not contiguous;
  • the sidecar geometry does not match;
  • a mixed tensor layout cannot use the combined record.

Swift v1 bundle compatibility

The original Swift v1 bundle writer used an incorrect FNV multiplier when generating its fingerprint table.

The C reader now:

  • continues writing canonical FNV-1a fingerprints;
  • accepts complete fingerprint tables produced by the original Swift v1 writer;
  • rejects mixed canonical/legacy tables;
  • rebuilds genuinely incompatible bundles;
  • reuses existing large Swift bundles without rewriting them.

This was validated against the existing approximately 73 GB DS4Demo expert bundle.

Reduced model-view pressure

The token embedding path now maps only the selected F16 embedding row instead of exposing the complete embedding table to Metal.

For contexts that cannot reach the sparse-attention boundary, indexer-scoring weights are also omitted from the per-token dense stream. Longer contexts automatically retain those weights.

Cold prompt prefill

Short cold prompts for narrow Flash models now use layer-major prefill by default.

The previous token-major path walked the model once for every prompt token. Layer-major prefill reads each layer once for the complete prompt.

The legacy behavior remains available for diagnostic comparisons:

DS4_METAL_ENABLE_STREAMING_COLD_DECODE_PREFILL=1

Optional residency controls

DS4_MLOCK=1 provides best-effort pinning for the output head and staging ring.

Compressor residency remains separately opt-in because testing on the 16 GB M1 Pro showed that the additional resident-memory pressure could reduce performance.

Quieter runtime output

The final version removes high-volume diagnostic messages for:

  • dense-stream initialization;
  • per-layer dense reads;
  • per-token SSD graph timing;
  • prefill layer progress;
  • expert-bundle first-use and heartbeat messages.

Generated tokens on stdout and actionable staging/fallback errors remain unchanged.

Supported hardware and scope

This optimization is intended for:

  • Apple Silicon;
  • the Metal backend;
  • DeepSeek V4 Flash models;
  • SSD-streaming mode;
  • low-memory systems where the full model cannot remain resident.

Live validation was performed on:

  • Apple M1 Pro;
  • 16 GB unified memory;
  • the existing Metal compute path;
  • an approximately 81 GB GGUF;
  • an approximately 73 GB Swift expert bundle.

The optimization does not require Metal 4 and runs on the existing M1-compatible Metal path.

Other Apple Silicon generations should be able to use the same implementation, but M2, M3 and M4 hardware have not yet been measured in this PR.

The new dense staging path is not enabled for:

  • CPU inference;
  • CUDA;
  • ROCm;
  • full-resident Metal inference;
  • unsupported model variants.

CPU/no-GPU compilation remains clean. CUDA hardware was not available for a live runtime test.

Benchmark

Configuration

  • Hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 16 GB unified memory
  • Backend: Metal
  • Mode: SSD streaming
  • Context: 1024 tokens
  • Expert cache: 344 experts
  • Cache preload: disabled with --ssd-streaming-cold
  • Sampling: greedy, temperature 0
  • Thinking: disabled
  • Expert bundle: same lossless DS4Demo bundle
  • Prompt:
Rispondi con una sola parola: Roma.

Results

Path | Decode times | Average throughput -- | -- | -- mmap baseline, DS4_DENSE_STREAM=0 | 4.430 s, 4.453 s | ~0.225 token/s lossless staging ring, ahead 2 | 1.790 s, 1.468 s | ~0.61 token/s

This is approximately a 2.7x improvement in decode throughput.

A four-slot configuration with DS4_DENSE_AHEAD=3 and four parallel reads reached approximately 0.62 token/s in one run. The small additional gain did not justify recommending the extra approximately 160 MiB staging allocation.

Absolute throughput remains sensitive to SSD temperature, page-cache state and background I/O. The numbers above are a controlled same-machine comparison.

Correctness

The baseline and optimized paths generated the same continuation:

R
oma
EOS

Rendered answer:

Roma

The top-20 logprob JSON files were byte-identical.

SHA-256 for both files:

9c56914163a2f78218d2a77ab81f470fdd78dee1ee40953b46a795b18ad0de1d

Quality boundary

This PR does not create or consume DS4Demo .q4dense files.

The .q4dense path requantizes large attention and shared-expert projections. It is faster, but it can change logits and greedy output. In the controlled test, that path produced a divergent answer.

All ranges staged by this PR are copied directly from the original GGUF and retain their original formats and precision.

Usage

DS4_EXPERT_BUNDLE=1 \
DS4_BUNDLE_DIR=/path/to/swift-bundle \
DS4_DENSE_STREAM=1 \
DS4_DENSE_AHEAD=2 \
DS4_DENSE_IO_DEPTH=3 \
DS4_LAZY_IDX=1 \
./ds4 \
  -m /path/to/model.gguf \
  --metal \
  --ssd-streaming \
  --ssd-streaming-cold \
  --ssd-streaming-cache-experts 344 \
  --ctx 1024

To restore the previous mmap path:

DS4_DENSE_STREAM=0

or:

DS4_METAL_DISABLE_DENSE_STREAM=1

Validation

  • make -j4 ds4 ds4_test expert-bundle-test
  • Expert-bundle canonical fingerprint tests
  • Legacy Swift v1 fingerprint tests
  • Mixed fingerprint rejection/rebuild tests
  • Source-tensor fingerprint invalidation tests
  • ./ds4_test --metal-kernels
  • ./ds4_test --server
  • Layer-pack tests: 97/97
  • Multi-GPU placement tests: 98/98
  • GPU argument tests
  • CLI argument tests: 44/44
  • Metal C syntax check with -Werror
  • CPU/no-GPU syntax check with -Werror
  • Objective-C Metal syntax check with -Werror
  • Live same-bundle greedy decode
  • Byte-for-byte logprob comparison
  • Removed diagnostic strings absent from the final executable

Memory and I/O trade-offs

With DS4_DENSE_AHEAD=2, the implementation allocates three shared staging buffers of approximately 160 MiB each.

The path reads approximately 6.35 GiB of dense data per generated token. It improves I/O scheduling, page-cache behavior and overlap; it does not reduce the precision or total logical model data.

DS4_MLOCK remains optional because pinning too much memory can reduce performance on 16 GB machines.

Remaining performance gap

The lossless Swift path still reaches approximately 1.25 token/s on the same machine.

The main remaining C-side limitation is the blocking command-buffer completion at the end of every decoder layer. Removing that wait safely would require:

  • one Metal event per staging slot;
  • asynchronous slot-lifetime tracking;
  • protection against CPU pread() reusing a buffer still read by the GPU;
  • updated expert-cache lifetime guarantees;
  • a final drain before logits are read.

That redesign is intentionally outside the scope of this PR.

Review focus

Reviewers may want to focus on:

  1. staging-buffer lifetime and synchronization;
  2. bounds checks for model and staging ranges;
  3. slot reuse after command-buffer completion;
  4. mmap fallback after partial initialization or read failure;
  5. Swift v1 versus canonical fingerprint validation;
  6. preservation of full-resident and non-Metal paths;
  7. correctness of the context-safe lazy indexer condition.

**Stage 2 complete** — MoE cluster expanded to 6 launches/layer (4 MoE + 2 shared FFN), ABBA benchmark neutral.

Branch: `cuda-graphs-stage2` (stacked on `cuda-graphs-stage1`, C6-C8), fork `riccardo-galbani/ds4`.

**What it does:** moves the CUDA graph capture boundary from inside the shared FFN (2 shims/layer, Stage 1) to encompass the entire MoE+shared sequence (6 launches/layer). The router stays eager outside capture (P3-b boundary: avoids the stale `token` problem on hash-routing layers, uniform perimeter across all 43 layers).

**Commits:**
- C6: housekeeping and gating — one-time warning for profiling↔capture mutual exclusion, memset→async (closes Stage 0 NOTE), `spec_capture_prefix1` gate (latent Stage 1 issue with the strict-MTP verifier)
- C7: cluster key extension (+10 MoE fields) and complete entry predicate (explicit residency guard, dump guard, defensive expert profile guard) — behavior invariant, counter signatures identical
- C8: moves `begin()` upstream of `routed_moe_one_tensor` — single file touched (ds4.c), net diff = pure relocation + 1 `cluster_rc != 1` guard on the MoE call

**Verification (GB10, sm_121, resident weights):**
- Bit-exact: logits identical to the antirez reference across all graphs×MTP combinations, strict-MTP, dump prefix — no counter deviation anywhere
- Stable counter signatures: 1505/86/86 (non-MTP), 1062/88/88 (MTP), 585/88/88 (strict)
- ABBA benchmark 10+10 (MTP draft 2, -n 2000, temp 0, ctx 4096): **generation 14.21 ± 0.23 t/s (on) vs 14.22 ± 0.19 t/s (off) → neutral within noise**, same situation as Stage 1 (14.004 vs 14.002)

**Why neutral:** the 86 sync brackets per token (cudaEvent pairs pre/post cluster) still dominate the savings from eliminated launches. The ratio improved from ~0.5:1 (Stage 1: 43 launches saved / 86 brackets) to ~3:1 (Stage 2: 258 launches / 86 brackets), but the absolute bracket cost is large enough to absorb the delta. A measurable gain arrives when brackets per token decrease: larger clusters (layer-level capture) or fewer sync points.

**Next (Stage 3):** layer-level → full-token capture. Different in nature from Stages 1-2: requires migrating all per-token scalars to the device substrate, replicating host side effects in the replay path (invariant 4), and wiring the anti-nesting guard already prepared by the Entrpi fork. The side-effect census is complete (Stage 2 triage, P7); the 11 red-shim substrate table is in the plan.

**Status note:** this work is developed on main @ [80ebbc3](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/commit/80ebbc396aee40eedc1d829222f3362d10fa4c6c). I'm aware ds4 has moved forward since then; I'm completing the graph capture work on the old base to get a clean measurement of the end-to-end improvement (Stage 3 targets the bracket reduction that should produce the first measurable gain). Once the final numbers are in, I'll evaluate whether and how to port the work to the current release — happy to discuss the best approach here or in a separate thread.

Ran the branch (`567e798`) on the same M5 Max / mixed Q2+Q4 setup. Results confirm the fix, with one tuning finding that may interest you:

- **Replay fix verified:** `replay=0.000` throughout, and the same code-gen A/B that lost on main (38.2 vs 40.0) now runs at parity on default settings — `net_saved` flipped from −149 ms to +9.6 ms.
- **Why parity and not +40% at defaults:** on this quant the drafter's confidence rarely clears the default 0.9 gate — `no_draft=120` of 147 cycles, so there was almost nothing to accelerate. Quant noise on the mixed Q2+Q4 seems to depress draft confidence relative to your Q2_K run.
- **`--dspark-confidence 0.5` unlocks it: 50.69 t/s vs 39.86 baseline (+27%), byte-identical output.** `accept_rate=80.65%`, `avg_accept=2.885`, `net_saved=+1121ms`, 40/52 cycles proposing. Without your replay fix this proposal volume would have been a heavy loss, so the win is directly attributable to this branch.
- `make dspark-acceptance`: hello fixture penalty shrank −199 ms → −19 ms (32-token prompts still can't amortize); the redis near-tie flip persists exactly as you documented — pre-existing, not this PR.

Takeaway from this datapoint: on mixed quants the default confidence gate may leave most of the branch's benefit on the table — possibly worth a note in the DSpark README section, or a quant-aware default down the line.

| **Stock `ds4` Control** | 32 GB RAM | No | Unset | **7.48 t/s** | **2.24 t/s** | Standard OS `mmap` retains dense weights in free 64 GB RAM |
| **PR #514 Staging Path** | 32 GB RAM | Yes | `1` (On) | 1.02 t/s | **0.72 t/s** | Direct `F_NOCACHE` streaming bound by external SSD speed |

Rebased onto current `main` and adapted the patch to the refactored selected expert cache path.

The change remains narrowly scoped:

* gate/up/down use three distinct staging slots;
* all three copies are enqueued on the selected upload stream;
* the stream is synchronized once after the three uploads;
* unsupported cases transparently use the existing three-copy fallback;
* pending stream work is drained on partial failure;
* cache policy, tensor layouts, kernels, and diagnostics are unchanged.

Both the current baseline (`efdadd4`) and the PR commit (`6ece876`) build successfully with CUDA 12.4 on an NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe (`sm_80`).

All validation runs produced identical deterministic output and the same normalized output SHA-256, with no CUDA staging, upload, or synchronization errors.

A targeted Nsight Systems comparison confirmed the intended effect:

* `cudaMemcpyAsync`: unchanged at 108,276 calls
* `cudaStreamSynchronize`: 108,276 → 36,092 calls (`−66.67%`)
* `cudaStreamSynchronize` API time:

  * 8GB expert cache: 1.649 s → 0.587 s (`−64.42%`)
  * 16GB expert cache: 1.742 s → 0.584 s (`−66.49%`)

This removes exactly 72,184 stream synchronizations in the profiled workload while preserving the upload count and output correctness.

End-to-end throughput remained within run-to-run noise, so the validation notes no longer claim a measurable overall throughput improvement on the current `main`.

**Short version:** the corrupted output comes from the batched prefill path, not
from decode. `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_BATCH_HC_NORM_FUSION=1` fixes it — it works on

throughput. Without it, only `--prefill-chunk 1` is correct; every batch size
\>= 2 is wrong, in both prefill implementations.

### What the trace and logprobs show




Attached: [ds4-577.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30373008/ds4-577.txt) (server `--trace`) and [logprobs-broken.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30373009/logprobs-broken.json)
(`ds4 --rocm --nothink --temp 0 --logprobs-top-k 20 --dump-logprobs`).

First, the rendered prompt is correct, so this is not a template or tokenizer
problem:

```
prompt_tokens: 9
think_mode: none
--- rendered prompt ---
<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>Explain mmap in C<｜Assistant｜></think>
```

The generation from that prompt is a coherent academic abstract on an unrelated
subject — a Chinese title followed by fluent English prose about the global
distribution of warm-water coral reefs. Well-formed text, no relation to the
prompt whatsoever.

The logprobs dump quantifies why. At step 0:

- top-1 is token 4229 `波`, logprob -3.5213, i.e. **p = 2.96%**
- **all 20** of the top-20 candidates are CJK
- the logit spread across the whole top-20 is only **1.85** (12.19 -> 10.34)
- the entire top-20 accounts for just **19.5% of the probability mass** — the
  other ~80% is spread over the remaining ~129,260 tokens. By step 50 of the
  same generation the top-20 holds 100.0%.

(These are full-vocabulary log-softmax values: `logit - logprob` is a constant
15.7065 within the step, i.e. the log-sum-exp normaliser.)

That is a near-uniform distribution over unrelated Chinese characters. For
contrast, `--first-token-test` (exact CPU whole-model pass, same prompt) gives
top logit 16.77 for `#` with the runner-up at 15.82 — a clear peak, on tokens
plausible for the prompt.

Across all 113 generated steps, however, the mean top-1 probability is
**76.19%**, with only 4 steps below 10%. So decode is healthy and confident; it
is simply conditioned on nothing. It samples an essentially arbitrary first
token and then writes a fluent document from it. That looks more like prefill
leaving the state unconditioned than subtly perturbing it.

Supporting that: the two attachments generate *different* unrelated documents.
The server run (9-token prompt) produced the coral-reef abstract; the CLI run
(14-token prompt) produced "Irregular verbs are verbs that do not follow the
standard pattern of conjugation..." — the same continuation the chunk >= 32 runs
give. Two variables differ at once there (server vs CLI, 9 vs 14 tokens) so I
cannot attribute it cleanly, but a tiny prompt change yielding a completely
different coherent document fits "the state carries no prompt information"
better than "the state is perturbed".

Minor aside: the CLI renders this prompt as 14 tokens where the server renders
9. Presumably different templates — mentioning it only in case it is not
intentional.

### Chunk bisect — it is the batch dimension, not chunk stitching

Same prompt, `--nothink --temp 0`, varying `--prefill-chunk`:

| chunk | code path logged | output |
| ----- | ---------------- | ------ |
| 1 | `chunked GPU prefill` | **correct** |
| 2 | `chunked GPU prefill` | ` </think>I'm sorry, but I need more context to` |
| 8 | `chunked GPU prefill` | `####...# Diablo3 Item` |
| 32 | `gpu prefill layer 43/43` | `波Irregular verbs are verbs that do not follow the standard` |
| 128 | `gpu prefill layer 43/43` | identical to 32 |
| 512 | `gpu prefill layer 43/43` | identical to 32 |
| 2048 | `gpu prefill layer 43/43` | same, `波Irregular verbs ...` (prefill 7.06 t/s, gen 10.17 t/s) |
| 4096 (default) | `gpu prefill layer 43/43` | same |

Three observations:

1. 32/128/512 are all >= the 14-token prompt, so they run single-pass, and they
   log a **different** code path (`gpu prefill layer 43/43`) from 1/2/8
   (`chunked GPU prefill`). Both paths are wrong for batch > 1.
2. The prompt already fits one chunk at the 4096 default, so chunk stitching is
   not involved.
3. 32/128/512 produce byte-identical output beginning with token 4229 `波`,
   so it is deterministic rather than a race or an uninitialised read.

## Update: recommendation revised → `AProjQ4-SExpQ8` (keep shared experts at Q8)

Follow-up with full data. Three findings since the original write-up — ending with a **better variant** than the one proposed above, so I'd retitle the proposal to `...AProjQ4-SExpQ8-OutQ8...`.

### 1. Dense imatrix (collector extended, gap halved)

The stock `--imatrix-out` collector only covers **routed** MoE experts, so the model's existing imatrix has no vectors for the dense tensors this requant touches. I extended the collector to also accumulate the dense-matmul inputs (attention projections + shared experts) and wired `--requant-gguf` to consume it. Imatrix-weighted Q4 cut the quality gap roughly in half: **+3.38% → +1.38%** perplexity vs Q8.

Side finding: the imatrix benefit **saturates fast at 4-bit** — going from 32k calibration tokens to 220k diverse tokens (Italian prose + English docs + C code) changed nothing (0.387 vs 0.389 avg_nll, within noise). A small calibration set is enough.

### 2. Behavioral drift found: Q4 shared experts flip the *reasoning language*

Controlled A/B (same Italian prompt, greedy, deterministic): the Q8 model **thinks in Italian**, the all-Q4 model **thinks in Chinese** (the final answer is still Italian and correct). Root cause: shared experts fire on **every token of every layer**, and the reasoning-language choice is a near-tie fork at the first thinking token — the Q4 error on the shared experts is enough to flip it, and greedy decoding cascades the flip. Invisible in aggregate metrics (top-1 stays ~86%), but very visible to users.

### 3. Fix: mixed variant `AProjQ4-SExpQ8-OutQ8`

Quantize only the 5 attention projections (215 tensors); **keep the shared experts at Q8** (copied byte-for-byte). Costs ~0.55 GiB extra resident — the expert cache still fits.

```bash
# 1. collect a dense-aware imatrix (any ~32k-token text)
./ds4 --metal --ssd-streaming --ssd-streaming-cache-experts 512 -m MODEL-Q8.gguf \
  --imatrix-dataset calibration.txt --imatrix-out dense-imatrix.dat

# 2. requant (GGUF -> GGUF, no HF source needed)
./gguf-tools/deepseek4-quantize --requant-gguf \
  --template MODEL-Q8.gguf \
  --out DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ4-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix.gguf \
  --attention-proj q4_k --imatrix dense-imatrix.dat --threads 8

# 3. run (no env flags; explicit expert cache)
./ds4 --metal --ssd-streaming --ssd-streaming-cache-experts 448 -m MODEL-AProjQ4-SExpQ8.gguf
```

### Quality — 100 official Flash continuations (2289 target tokens)

| variant | avg_nll ↓ | ppl vs Q8 | top-1 | thinks in user's language |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q8 (baseline) | 0.3732 | — | 86.1% | ✅ |
| all-Q4, no imatrix | 0.4065 | +3.38% | 85.9% | ❌ (Chinese) |
| all-Q4, imatrix | 0.3870 | +1.38% | 86.2% | ❌ (Chinese) |
| **mixed AProjQ4-SExpQ8** | **0.3831** | **+0.99%** | 86.4% | ✅ |

The mixed variant also wins 56/100 cases head-to-head against the imatrix all-Q4.

### Performance — clean 3-way, same session, no expert bundle (M1 Pro 16 GB)

| ctx | metric | Q8 | all-Q4 | **mixed** | mixed vs Q8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | decode t/s | 0.73 | 2.06 | **2.06** | **2.8×** |
| 512 | first-token | 1.90 s | 1.22 s | **1.16 s** | −39% |
| 2048 | decode t/s | 0.56 | 2.02 | **1.79** | **3.2×** |
| — | prefill t/s | 11–19 | 14–19 | 15–19 | ≥ parity |

Identical to all-Q4 at ctx 512; within variance at 2048 (it runs a slightly smaller expert cache to pay for the +0.55 GiB resident shared experts).

### Bottom line

Ship **`AProjQ4-SExpQ8-OutQ8`**: **2.8–3.2× decode**, **+0.99% perplexity**, top-1 unchanged, and **no reasoning-language drift**. The all-Q4 variant remains an option only where the extra 0.55 GiB of resident memory matters more than the drift.

Where a backend lacks a specialized Q4_K attention-output kernel, the shared graph falls back to the generic per-group dense path instead of failing the layer. The decode-TP attention split and the fused kslice paths still refuse non-Q8 projections with a clear error — never garbage. CUDA prefill reuses the same matvec kernel: correct but unoptimized (a dequant+GEMM path can follow if profiles justify it). Same class of setup here — RTX 3060 12GB, DeepSeek-V4-Flash IQ2_XXS (80.8GB gguf), CUDA, Windows native. Two measurements that might be useful, both with the exact conditions attached.

*(Edited: I first wrote point 1 as a suggestion to lower `-c`, before re-reading that your benchmarks run at ctx 256 / 2048. At those sizes the KV is a few MiB and there is nothing to reclaim — the point below only becomes relevant at long context, e.g. your 30474-token regression. Sorry for the noise.)*

**1. At long context, the KV cache competes directly with the expert cache.**

The KV is allocated at full `ctx` capacity up front, not grown on demand. Same binary, same model, same prompt, only `-c` changed:

```
                 KV allocated   expert cache          backbone evictions
ctx 150000       2011 MiB       140 slots (945 MiB)      88 - 891
ctx   8000        152 MiB       255 slots (1721 MiB)            0
```

From the server log: `context buffers 2083.06 MiB (ctx=150000, compressed_kv_rows=37502)` vs `context buffers 151.96 MiB (ctx=8000, compressed_kv_rows=2002)`.

That works out to ~13.7 KiB per token of context. On a 12GB card the budget is essentially `VRAM = backbone + expert slots + KV`, so at ctx 150000 the KV takes ~2GB that would otherwise hold ~290 expert slots.

For your 30474-token `--long-context` case that's ~409 MiB, i.e. roughly 60 expert slots — probably not what's limiting you there, but it's a term that grows linearly and is easy to miss when tuning cache size, since the cache is sized *after* the KV is already allocated.

**Not tested:** intermediate context sizes, and whether this holds on cards with different VRAM.

**2. Hit rate and read count came apart for me — might be worth checking on your tier.**

From the worker profile:

```
expert cache  40 slots    read_calls_per_token = 598.0
expert cache 140 slots    read_calls_per_token = 597.8
expert cache 255 slots    read_calls_per_token = 216.4
```

Going 40 -> 140 more than doubled cache hits (65,920 -> 146,663) and changed the number of read calls by 0.2. Only at 255 slots did the read count actually drop.

Since you report hit rates of 72-82%, it might be worth checking whether those translate into fewer actual read calls on your host-RAM tier, or only into fewer misses. On my setup the two were decoupled below a threshold, and hit rate alone was a misleading proxy for work avoided.

**Not tested:** where exactly the threshold sits between 140 and 255.

Following up with three things measured since July — all on DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, MLX, 2× M3 Ultra tensor-parallel:

1. **If your "plain decode" baseline runs on mlx-lm's `deepseek_v4` (or derived code), it decays ~4.3 µs/tok per generated token.** The compiled rope helpers take the KV offset as a python int, so every generated token mints a new `mx.compile` cache entry, and lookup is a linear memcmp scan — 12% → 29% of decode-thread wall between ~2k and ~7k generated in our `sample` profiles, plus unbounded host memory (~3 entries/token retained). Fix is passing a 0-d `mx.array` offset (byte-identical outputs): details in the ml-explore/mlx-lm#1189 comment and ml-explore/mlx#3964. Relevant here because a spec-decode A/B against a decaying baseline flatters the drafter more the longer the run.

2. **A stripped-DSpark datapoint for the economics**: we dropped the dspark heads at conversion — the July admission-law finding is unchanged on current MLX (only the ~7 ms python slice overlaps; a drafter must win on serialized arithmetic alone). After the prefill/decode work above, our *non-spec* decode is ~29–31 tok/s and flat through 256k context — that's the bar any DSpark cycle has to beat on this class of hardware. @deathcoder's serialized-verifier direction is exactly what the admission law predicts pays: don't buy overlap, buy cheaper verify.

3. Possibly useful for the batch verifier specifically: we ported the sparse gather-attention kernel so prefill-shaped blocks attend only each query's window + top-k pool rows via per-query index lists (visibility encoded as sentinel-padded sorted indices; attention sinks folded into the online softmax by seeding the running max/denominator). Verify-at-L is a small prefill block, and the "prefill-shaped kernels at decode sizes" tax from the July discussion is precisely what this removes. Kernels + campaign notes: https://gist.github.com/aidiffuser/fef1890680e4eed60d3902511b02a696

Confirming @sleepless’s observation above against the official 0731 encoder and current `main` (`54b36ed9ba42da31b24f2d1a5feb075c2475dbb1`).

Official 0731 `reasoning_effort` is text-prefix based:

- `low` (default): no prefix
- `high`: `Reasoning Effort: Absolute maximum...`
- `max`: `Reasoning Effort: Beyond maximum...`

Current DS4 behaves as follows:

- omitted / `low` / `medium` / `high` / `xhigh` / `minimal` all map to `DS4_THINK_HIGH`, which renders `<think>` with no effort prefix: official 0731 **low**
- `max` maps to `DS4_THINK_MAX`, which inserts `DS4_REASONING_EFFORT_MAX_PREFIX`; that string is the official 0731 **high** prefix
- the official `Beyond maximum...` prefix is absent from current `main`, so official 0731 **max** cannot currently be selected through the API

I reproduced the parser behavior with traced requests for omitted, `low`, `xhigh`, `max`, and `none`, and checked the rendered-prompt source. The practical implication is that current 0731 runs reported as DS4 `high` are official low, while DS4 `max` runs are official high. This affects comparison with published Max benchmark results, not just naming.

**Confirming this regression on Apple Silicon, with a bisect, memory forensics, and a test of PR #578.**

**Setup:** MacBook Pro M5 Max, 128 GB unified, macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), `iogpu.wired_limit_mb=122880`, `vm.global_user_wire_limit` ≈ 108.8 GiB. Model: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Q4KExperts-F16HC-F16Compressor-F16Indexer-Q8Attn-Q8Shared-Q8Out-chat-v2-imatrix-0731.gguf` (153.3 GiB, all 129 routed-expert tensors uniformly Q4_K). Server: `ds4-server -m <model> -c 32768 --ssd-streaming` (auto expert cache: 87.80 GiB = 6.75 prefill + 81.05 dynamic). Reproducer: 3 consecutive greedy (temp 0) 1536-token generations of the same coding prompt; tok/s is wall-clock end-to-end.

**Decode throughput (generation 1 → 2 → 3):**

| build | gen 1 | gen 2 | gen 3 | compressor peak | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `80ebbc3` (pre-regression) | 15.2 | 14.8 | 14.7 | 1.5 GiB | stable |
| `0a7ad77` (current main-ish) | 14.2 | 5.3 | 4.9 | 43 GiB | **2.9× collapse** |
| `0a7ad77`, stock flags only | 14.4 | — | — | **71 GiB** | server killed by our watchdog mid-gen-2 |
| `0a7ad77` + `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts 55GB` | ~12.4 | ~12.4 | ~12.3 | low | stable (mitigation) |
| `0a7ad77` + **PR #578** | 13.2 | 13.8 | 13.8 | **0.96 GiB** | stable |

**This also causes kernel panics.** Three on this machine in 6 days (matches #483): `watchdog timeout: no checkins from watchdogd in 92 seconds`, all with the same memoryStatus signature — `free = 0`, `pagesWanted ≈ 3200 / pagesReclaimed = 0`, compressor at 35–43 GiB. The worst run logged **820M compressions / 794M decompressions** (18× a normal day): the OS compresses the unpinned expert-cache pages, ds4 re-touches them, repeat. A watchdog killing the server at compressor > 28 GiB reliably prevents the panic.

**Bisect** (`good 80ebbc3`, `bad 0a7ad77`, probe = the 3-generation reproducer):
- `fc9efd1` **good** (14.4–14.7 stable)
- `66cbce5` **bad** (watchdog fired, compressor 70.4 GiB)
- `63d9874`, `36cd0ca`, `36ee8c1` don't build standalone on arm64 (link errors); `005afed` builds and serves but every chat request returned empty in our probe — all skipped
- so the first functional bad commit is in `63d9874..66cbce5`, and within that range `git log -S mlock -- ds4_metal.m` points at exactly one commit: **`005afed` ("Add GLM 5.2 inference…"), where mlock occurrences in `ds4_metal.m` go from 78 to 0** — consistent with your attribution here.

**PR #578 test:** applies cleanly on `0a7ad77`, `mlock` count back to 77. It fully eliminates the memory spiral (compressor peak 0.96 GiB, swap peak 361 MB over a 12-round benchmark) and the round-to-round collapse. It lands ~7% below the pre-regression build on long generations (13.7 vs 14.7 tok/s), so `80ebbc3` remains slightly faster for streaming decode on this machine — but #578 restores stability and, critically, removes the panic risk. Happy to run any variant of this if it helps validate the fix.

One more datapoint: the wire-limit concern from #437 doesn't bite here — `vm.global_user_wire_limit` (108.8 GiB) comfortably covers the 87.8 GiB auto cache. And the disk KV cache (`--kv-disk-dir`) is not involved: the collapse reproduces identically without it.

We independently ported the transport half of this PR (the streamed-upload pipelining and plain-copy default — not the resident-cache redesign, which duplicates functionality we already have on our fork) onto an NVIDIA GB10 (unified CPU/GPU memory over NVLink-C2C) + MXFP4 expert-LRU stack, and measured a consistent 11-25% regression from the pipelining change specifically (isolated via an env toggle; the plain-copy default alone was neutral; byte-identical outputs throughout). Our read: the pipelining's benefit comes from hiding host-read latency behind PCIe DMA, which doesn't exist as a mechanism on memory-unified hardware, so the ring-cursor/deferred-sync bookkeeping becomes net overhead. Between this PR's numbers on discrete PCIe cards and ours on unified memory, the right transport appears to be arch-dependent rather than one-size — worth gating the pipelined path on detected-discrete vs unified at init, especially since much of the consumer local-AI hardware trend (Mac minis, Strix Halo, DGX Spark class) is unified. finished another experiment on Apple Metal to check whether your GPU-originated I/O / persistent-kernel idea has a real bottleneck to attack in DS4 SSD streaming. I had Codex implement the opt-in instrumentation, run the experiments, and calculate the aggregate timings and statistics. I then reviewed the methodology, timing definitions, invariants and interpretation of the results. The goal was first to measure the current host-driven path inside every routed MoE layer. Setup: * Apple M4 Max, 36 GiB unified memory * DS4 upstream commit `54b36ed9ba42da31b24f2d1a5feb075c2475dbb1` * DeepSeek V4 Flash q2-imatrix, 86.7 GB GGUF * Metal SSD streaming * 128 generated tokens * greedy decoding, temperature 0 * MTP, DSpark, thinking and speculation disabled * cache sizes: 256, 760 and 1,521 experts * two complete runs per cache size * telemetry overhead: 0.36% median * telemetry ON/OFF produced identical token-sequence SHA-256 digests The telemetry was opt-in and aggregate-only. It did not change routing, cache policy, eviction, prefetch, paging or Metal kernels. It did not save prompts, generated text or token IDs. For every routed MoE layer, we marked these points: * **T0:** selected expert IDs are available on the host * **T1:** cache lookup is complete * **T2:** the first required I/O starts * **T3:** all required expert cache slots are ready * **T4:** the runtime is ready to dispatch the MoE compute The measured intervals were: * **T0→T2:** about **0.61–0.68 ms per layer with at least one miss** * **T2→T3:** about **1.30–1.66 ms** * **T3→T4:** only **0.007–0.022 ms** So the interesting target is clearly before the first I/O starts. Once all expert data is already in the cache slots, the remaining host work before compute dispatch is tiny. In our report, **host-addressable time** means host-side work that a different architecture might reduce, bypass or overlap. It includes: * making the selected expert IDs available to the host * cache lookup and slot selection * preparing the read requests * the delay before the first read starts * final host bookkeeping and synchronization It does not mean that the SSD itself becomes faster. It is therefore an upper bound on potentially redesignable time, not an expected speedup. The measured host-addressable cost was: * 26.22 ms/token with 256 slots * 26.53 ms/token with 760 slots * 23.32 ms/token with 1,521 slots That is around 17–19% of total decode time. The term **post-ready dispatch** specifically means T3→T4: all missing experts have already been loaded and all required cache slots are usable, but the host still has to finish the address-table update and synchronization before the GPU compute can launch. That phase is only around 7–22 microseconds per layer, so optimizing it alone would not matter much. The earlier host-side cost matters because most layers still contain at least one miss: * 256 slots: 99.98% of layers have a miss * 760 slots: 97.46% * 1,521 slots: 79.34% With 43 routed layers, even the largest cache still produces roughly 34 miss-bearing layers per token. So the roughly 0.6–0.7 ms delay before first I/O is repeated many times, which explains the measured total of about 23 ms/token. We also measured the average wait depending on the number of missing experts: * 1 miss: 1.09 ms * 2 misses: 1.73 ms * 3 misses: 2.12 ms * 4 misses: 2.28 ms * 5 misses: 2.53 ms * 6 misses: 2.81 ms So this is not a simple fixed “one miss blocks the whole layer” effect. More misses still increase the critical path, although not proportionally to the total number of bytes. Our current interpretation is: * your GPU-originated I/O or persistent-kernel idea has a real measurable target * the best target is the repeated 0.6–0.7 ms delay between expert selection and the first I/O * optimizing only the final post-ready dispatch would not help much * physical I/O still takes another 1.3–1.7 ms per miss-bearing layer * a persistent kernel alone is therefore not a complete solution The most promising architecture may be a combination of: * GPU-produced request descriptors * an always-ready submission path * earlier prefetch * later, possibly finer-grained paging We currently classify the persistent-kernel idea as **promising, but not yet proven**. The 17–19% host-addressable fraction is an upper bound. A real implementation may recover only part of it, and it may also consume GPU occupancy, create coherence traffic or interfere with the model’s compute kernels. The next experiment we are considering is a bounded comparison between: A. current DS4 host-driven path B. persistent CPU proxy consuming a shared request ring C. GPU-produced descriptors with a minimal CPU I/O proxy D. oracle early-submission upper bound The main GO criteria would be: * reduce T0→T2 by at least 50% * improve end-to-end throughput by at least 5% * identical output * no unbounded memory growth * no meaningful regression in GPU compute The sanitized RF-E2 collaboration bundle is now public here: https://github.com/kinderp/ds4-faro-reproducer/tree/main/rf-e2-layer-critical-path It contains the aggregate JSON results, timing definitions, miss histograms, interpretation for GPU-resident work, reproduction guidance and explicit limitations.
