@sleepless — I hit both of those. Here's what worked, in case it saves you time.

---

### 1. Breaking the preview model

**You're right, and it can't be avoided with a single fixed map.**

Preview's `max` **is** 0731's `high` string. So any map that makes `max` mean 0731's `max`
necessarily sends preview users a `"Beyond maximum…"` prefix that checkpoint never saw.

**What worked: don't choose.**

```
--reasoning-effort-map {deepseek|legacy}     # default: deepseek
```

`legacy` reproduces the current table exactly. One flag to revert.

Two things worth doing alongside it:
- assert **both** maps in `test_reasoning_effort_mapping()`, so the legacy path can't silently drift
- keep unknown strings returning `false` in both, so the HTTP 400 is preserved

---

### 2. GLM 5.2 — you don't need it locally to answer this

**GLM is independent of the DeepSeek prefix path.** From `chat_push_think_prefix()`,
`ds4.c:36310-36322` on `54b36ed`:

```c
if (DS4_MODEL_FAMILY == DS4_MODEL_FAMILY_GLM_DSA) {
    const char *effort = ds4_glm_reasoning_effort_text(think_mode);
    if (effort) { token_vec_push(out, vocab->system_id); bpe_tokenize_text(vocab, effort, out); }
} else if (think_mode == DS4_THINK_MAX) {
    bpe_tokenize_text(vocab, DS4_REASONING_EFFORT_MAX_PREFIX, out);
}
```

GLM takes the branch **first** and renders effort as a **system message**
(`"Reasoning Effort: High"` / `"Max"`). It never touches `DS4_REASONING_EFFORT_MAX_PREFIX`.

So the one-notch shift doesn't reach GLM — but **adding a tier does**, silently. See below.

---

### 3. Three landmines that produce no compiler error

| where | what happens if you miss it |
|---|---|
| `ds4_glm_reasoning_effort_text()` | `switch` with **no `default:`** → a new enumerator falls through to `return NULL`, **silently dropping GLM's effort system message** for that tier. `-Wswitch` warns, but there's no `-Werror`, so it scrolls past. |
| `ds4_think_mode_enabled()` | An explicit `==` list. Omit a tier and **thinking is silently disabled** for it at ~25 call sites — the `<think>` opener, all three streaming reasoning channels, tool-marker gating. |
| `think_mode_from_enabled()` (`ds4_server.c`) | `effort == MAX ? MAX : HIGH` — **collapses anything above MAX before the renderer sees it**. Must become a pass-through. |

I map the new tier to GLM's existing `"Reasoning Effort: Max"`, so GLM behaviour is unchanged.

---

### 4. The remap is inert until you fix the context gate

`DS4_THINK_MAX_MIN_CONTEXT` (393216) silently steps the top tier down below that context. On a
smaller `--ctx`, **every effort value except `none` renders an identical prompt** — so the remap
does nothing until this is addressed too.

If you make the floor settable, one gotcha: `parse_int_arg()` rejects `v <= 0`, so **`0` — the
value that disables the gate — is the one value that won't parse**. `parse_nonneg_int_arg()` is
the one you want.

---

While assessing rebase impact of #659 against `ds4f-mxfp4`, we analyzed 74e8f11 ("Commit partial DSpark verifier blocks without replay"). We believe the no-replay commit path there inherits the same greedy-identity mechanism described in this issue. All line refs below are on the current `ds4f-mxfp4` tip.

**Code path:**

- The verify batch projects compressor KV/score for the whole block with the batched matrix-matrix GEMM `ds4_gpu_matmul_f16_tensor` over `n_tokens` rows (`ds4.c:27473` and `ds4.c:27485`).
- 74e8f11 adds `!g->spec_capture_prefixes` to the `aligned_chunk` condition (`ds4.c:27601`), forcing the per-token compressor stepping loop — but that loop still consumes the batch-GEMM-projected rows via row views of `metal_graph_batch_comp_kv/sc` into `ds4_gpu_compressor_update_tensor` (`ds4.c:27724`), with emitted rows FP8-quantized at `ds4.c:27752`. Stepping token-by-token restores the *update order* of decode, but not its *input numerics*.
- Plain greedy decode computes the same logical rows via the fused single-vector kernel `ds4_gpu_matmul_f16_pair_compressor_store_tensor` (`ds4.c:22062`). These two projection paths differ in tiling/accumulation order — the comment at `ds4.c:~26490` in this same tree acknowledges exactly this ("mixing those two accumulation orders changes a few FP8 rounding decisions").
- The prefix snapshots captured at `ds4.c:27770` / `ds4.c:28066` therefore hold verify-GEMM-derived frontier state, and the new partial-accept block (`ds4.c:61391-61417`, via `spec_frontier_commit_prefix` at `ds4.c:49739`) commits that state directly with no target-model replay.

So on a partial accept, the committed compressor frontiers (and any FP8 rows emitted during the verify block) can differ in low bits from what non-speculative decode would have produced, and later tokens can diverge at `--temp 0`. Same mechanism as this issue, just reached through the new prefix-slot path instead of the old fast paths.

**Repro:** the temp-0 A/B from the top of this issue should reproduce it on `ds4f-mxfp4` — long greedy generations with `--mtp <support.gguf> --dspark` vs. plain decode, diff the token streams. Divergence is prompt/length-dependent since it needs an FP8 rounding decision to flip, so longer runs make it deterministic to observe.

This is a static analysis (we can't run Metal here), but the kernel-path argument is the same one that was empirically confirmed on `main` for #658, so confidence is high.

Also a heads-up: #659's replay approach rewrites the same accept path 74e8f11 touches, so it will conflict with the `ds4f-mxfp4` rewrite. Happy to re-derive the fix on top of the new prefix-slot verifier if that's the direction that lands — the prefix-slot machinery would actually pair nicely with a replay (or a fused-kernel re-projection of just the accepted tokens), which could keep partial accepts cheaper than our current full replay.

Great writeup. I have measurements on a sibling architecture — **Kimi-K3** (MLA-MoE, top-k routed, streamed IQ2 experts) — that bear directly on (1) and (2). Same family as V4 Flash (MLA + routed experts), so likely closer to it than your MiniMax numbers. Trace-replay, not live, but the *regime* matches yours.

**(1) Eviction key — your ordering holds, and static is worse than you'd hope.**
I ran the same "how good can any static policy be" check, and independently landed where you did. Static trace-derived pinning on K3 measured **34% hit vs a 62% recency baseline at matched budget — static was strictly *worse*, not just capped.** Recency (an EMA scoreboard, decay→0 = last-token) beat LFU/frequency at every budget I tried (last-1-token residency ≈ 36%, last-2 ≈ 45%, LFU ≈ 12%). So on a DeepSeek-family MLA-MoE your "8 points below recency" result is, if anything, an understatement — the primary key being the static hotlist looks like the weaker signal here too.

One step past LRU that paid: instead of a fixed decay, run **N decay candidates as bandit arms** (recency↔frequency dial) and serve from whichever arm has the best realized hit-rate, updated per token. On K3 that beat the best *fixed* decay by **+7–9 points at matched VRAM** on a non-stationary trace — same spirit as your SLRU (protect against one-pass scans) but it adapts the decay instead of the promotion rule. Cheap: it's just M scoreboards and an argmax.

**(2) Cross-layer lookahead — I have to be careful here, because I measured a *weaker* proxy than you did, and mine says less than yours.**
I measured **statistical co-occurrence** (given layer L's fired experts, predict L+1's from a learned noisy-OR), *not* running the real router early. On K3 that was weak: 15.9% vs 40.3% for recency, and only 11.2% recall on recency's misses (~base rate). So *co-occurrence statistics* are a dead end on this model.

But that is **not** what your L+2 does — you run the actual gating network on an earlier hidden state and recover 72.5% of the true top-k. That's a real router pass, a far stronger signal, and my result doesn't touch it. Your "Python interpreter cost inverts in C" arithmetic looks right to me — a router matvec + partial sort is sub-100µs in C, and on the SSD-bandwidth-bound decode regime (#627, and our 5090 in #639) two layers of lead time is exactly the lever. I'd expect it to help where a co-occurrence table can't. I don't have a reason it wouldn't work here — and I'd genuinely like to see the C version measured.

**(3) MTP union cost** — no data, but the logic is unarguable: streaming turns speculation's "one weight read regardless of γ" into "read the union of γ tokens' routed experts," and rejected drafts still pay their fetch. On a bandwidth-bound path that can go net-negative.

Pushed one more commit (ab98473) with a fix for an accounting bug we found while hardening this cache in production.

**The bug:** the LRU budget was enforced only as an entry *count* derived from the dominant slab size class, while CUDA caches every routed layer at its actual per-expert size — layers off the slab class cache entries larger than `expert_bytes`, so `N entries * slab_bytes` under-states real device consumption. On top of that, the buffer pool's free lists park real `cudaMalloc`'d memory that no accounting saw. Running a GB10 node with a nominal 100GB cache budget, we observed ~121GB of actual device memory consumed by the cache, which pushed the box into GPU-availability thrash.

**The fix:**
- valid entries are charged at their actual gate+up+down byte sizes;
- pool free-list bytes are counted as parked;
- installs make room *before* allocating — trimming parked pool buffers first (data-lossless), then evicting LRU — so counted + parked never exceeds `budget_experts * expert_bytes`, the exact dynamic-cache byte figure ds4.c plans and logs at startup. The entry-count cap remains as a secondary bound.

One subtlety: parked bytes reusable by the incoming request are treated as slack rather than new demand. A first cut that double-counted them forced a trim-then-malloc cycle on every miss at cap and cost ~30% decode throughput — exactly the alloc/free churn the pool exists to prevent.

`DS4_CUDA_STREAM_STATS=1` now also self-reports the cache's true footprint (budget / counted / pool-parked / device total / persistent pinned-host staging / entries) every 4096 fetch calls, and the end-of-generation stats call in ds4_cli.c is now compiled only into CUDA builds, which fixes `make cpu` linking on this branch.

The fix is production-verified on the same GB10 node at a 70GB budget: actual consumption stays at the nominal figure with no measurable throughput cost versus the pre-fix pooled path.

Your read matches ours: the pipelining exists purely to overlap host reads with PCIe DMA, so where that transfer doesn't exist the ring-cursor/deferred-sync bookkeeping is pure overhead. One note on how this PR is wired, in case it changes the picture on your side: the staged/pipelined path only engages on the direct-I/O read path (`g_model_direct_fd >= 0`); when the model map is host-resident (mmap/tmpfs) the default is already the plain single memcpy (`DS4_CUDA_STREAM_MISS_PLAIN_COPY` auto-defaults to 1 in that case). On a unified-memory system the model would typically be host-resident and land on the plain path out of the box — but if your port reaches the staged path anyway, gating it at init on detected unified memory (e.g. `cudaDeviceProp::integrated` or `cudaDevAttrPageableMemoryAccessUsesHostPageTables`) sounds reasonable and cheap. Happy to add that gate to this PR if the maintainer prefers it built-in, or as a follow-up.

Can independently confirm @kernelzeroday's finding — traced this myself on the same commit (`54b36ed`) before seeing this thread, same conclusion: `chat_push_think_prefix()` only injects a prefix for `DS4_THINK_MAX` (the "Absolute maximum…" string, official **high**); `DS4_THINK_HIGH` gets no prefix at all for the DeepSeek-V4 family. The official **max** ("Beyond maximum…") prefix doesn't exist anywhere in `main` — no code path can currently produce it.

One thing not yet mentioned here that compounds it: `ds4_think_mode_for_context()` silently downgrades `max` → `DS4_THINK_HIGH` if the server's `-c` is below `DS4_THINK_MAX_MIN_CONTEXT` (393216 / 384K). Since `DS4_THINK_HIGH` gets **no prefix at all**, anyone running `-c` below 384K and requesting `reasoning_effort: max` is silently getting official **low** — not even the mislabeled "high" one. A few quant setups upthread run at ctx 262144, so this is probably biting more people than just the tier-naming mismatch.

@zom-2018's remap (`THINK_HIGH` → "Absolute maximum…", `THINK_MAX` → "Beyond maximum…") looks like the right shape for a real fix, plus keeping the context gate tied to whichever mode ends up being true max. Until something like that lands, I'm running `-c 393216` (so the existing `max` codepath — official high — actually fires instead of silently dropping to no-prefix) and treating DS4's `max` as "official high," not a fourth tier.

Adding a data point from `main` rather than this branch, since it's relevant to whether the gap this PR addresses is still live in what ships today.

## Context

`ae504c9` ("Update Flash downloads and DSpark support for 0731") frames DSpark as replacing the legacy one-stage MTP support model, and ships an official `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark-support-0731.gguf`. Worth being precise about what that commit does and doesn't change: it's a packaging/download update (new dated filenames, new sidecar), not a change to the verify/accept logic. Current `main` still verifies drafts by `target_top = sample_argmax(s->logits, ...); if (target_top != drafts[0]) reject;` — a strict greedy-argmax match, same mechanism this thread has already dissected in detail for this branch.

## What I tested

Fresh build of `main` (`ae504c9`) in an isolated tree, official `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark-support-0731.gguf`, real production quant (asymmetric Q2/Q4 mix, ~98GB), `--dspark-confidence 0.7` (default). Same exact prompt both runs ("count from 1 to 150"), only `--temp`/`--top_p` changed:

**Greedy (`--temp 0`)** — decode visibly accelerates as the pattern locks in:
```
38.73 -> 45.37 -> 62.59 -> 55.58 -> 62.52 -> 62.47 -> 74.79 t/s (chunked, running avg 51.85 t/s)
```
vs ~40 t/s non-speculative baseline on this quant. Confirms the setup/sidecar/confidence threshold are all correctly wired — DSpark is doing real work here.

**Same prompt, `temp=1.0 top_p=1.0`** (DeepSeek's own documented sampling recommendation for this model, and what any real deployment running it as an assistant would use) — completely flat:
```
39.35 -> 39.28 -> 39.25 -> 39.40 -> 39.33 -> 39.39 -> 39.21 t/s
```
Zero acceleration, zero variance across 7 chunks — the signature of first-token draft rejection on essentially every cycle, consistent with comparing a proposal to the true model's argmax while the actual committed tokens are being chosen by temperature+top_p sampling instead.

## Why this thread is the relevant place for this

This PR is the only mechanism in flight that targets exactly this gap (B2 rejection sampling, "lossless by construction at any temperature"). Reading through the existing discussion here:

- @lobanov's independent device report (same hardware class, M5 Max 128GB) found the claimed speedups don't reproduce (measured regressions instead), traced to KV replay firing on 100% of cycles including full-accepts — and separately found the B2 accept/reject math isn't actually lossless as implemented, because the draft proposal is chosen by `sample_argmax` rather than being genuinely drawn from the proposal distribution `q` that `min(1, p/q)` requires.
- @audreyt confirmed the root cause and posted a fix (`machiabeli/ds4#1`, temperature-scaled categorical sampling for the draft proposal) with a statistical proof it restores losslessness (`max_dev_correct=0.0018` vs `max_dev_biased=0.1426`, N=50000).
- By @audreyt's own follow-up, the correctness fix doesn't recover throughput: B2 remains slower than non-speculative baseline on most non-repetitive workloads after the fix, with partial-commit replay dominating cost. Repetitive structured output is the one clear win.
- `machiabeli/ds4#1` (the correctness fix) doesn't appear to be merged into this branch yet — the commit list here still ends at `3efb3066`, the same HEAD @lobanov tested.

So as it stands: current `main`'s shipped DSpark (greedy-argmax verify) gives zero benefit at real sampling settings — reconfirmed above on today's official 0731 artifacts, not just on the preview build this was originally measured on back in July. This branch is where that would eventually get fixed, but per the discussion already here, it isn't there yet either (KV-replay cost, and the proposal-bias fix not yet folded in) — net win currently looks limited to highly repetitive/structured content even once correctness is fixed.

Given `ae504c9` now positions DSpark as *the* speculative path going forward (replacing MTP legacy in the download script and docs), it might be worth a maintainer look at consolidating the fixes already worked out in this thread, since right now the documented recommended sampling profile for this model gets none of DSpark's benefit either way.

@sleepless — on the preview-breakage problem you raised, that is exactly the thing that stopped
us shipping a naive fix too, and I think it is avoidable. Sharing the design and, more usefully,
the traps, since you said you may implement it yourself.

**Don't renumber the enum — append.**

Preview's `max` **is** 0731's `high` string. So any single fixed remap that makes `max` mean
0731's `max` necessarily sends preview users a prefix that checkpoint never saw. That is real and
it is why the renumbering variant in this thread breaks preview.

What worked for us: add a **fourth** tier rather than remapping the existing three.
`DS4_THINK_ULTRA` carries 0731's real `max` prefix, the existing values keep their meaning, and
preview is untouched. Then one flag to choose the table:

```
--reasoning-effort-map {deepseek|legacy}     # default: deepseek
```

`legacy` reproduces today's behaviour exactly, so it is a one-flag revert rather than a rebuild.
An env var would work just as well — the shape matters more than the mechanism.

Byte-exact against the live model, if it helps you verify your own build:

| wire value | prefix emitted | = DeepSeek tier |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | — (thinking off) | non-thinking |
| `minimal` / `low` / `medium` | none | `low` |
| `high` / `xhigh` | 476 B, sha256 `f7a24f3b…` | `high` |
| `max` (unpatched) | *same 476 B string* | **still `high`** |
| `max` (patched, ULTRA) | 528 B, sha256 `53fb31b8…` | `max` |

**Three things that bite silently — none produces a compiler warning.** These are the reason I am
posting the design rather than just a diff; they will catch any implementation, not just ours.

1. `ds4_think_mode_enabled()` is an `==` list. Omit your new tier and thinking is **silently
   disabled** at ~25 call sites — no error, the model just stops thinking.
2. `think_mode_from_enabled()` does `effort == MAX ? MAX : HIGH`, which **destroys** any tier
   above `MAX`. A new top tier collapses straight back down unless this is updated.
3. The GLM path renders effort as a **system message** rather than a prefix, and its switch has
   no `default:` — so a new enum value silently drops its effort text there. Worth checking
   against GLM5.2 specifically, since you mentioned you could not verify that one.

**On the practical question @nazeshinjite asked:** yes — on unpatched ds4, ctx above the
threshold plus `max` gets you DeepSeek's **`high`**, not `max`. The genuine `max` tier is not
reachable in any configuration, at any context length, with any flag. So a re-run on unpatched
code produces another set that is one notch below its label. Sorry — that is the answer to the
30 GPU-hours.

## Mainline llama.cpp + DSpark, tested at real production sampling

Fresh mainline build (`1c3c967`, today — includes #25784, merged 08-02), Unsloth `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF` (`UD-Q2_K_XL`, 90GB), the mainline-native DSpark checkpoint linked from #25784 (`am17an/DeepseekV4-Flash-20260731-DSpark.gguf`), `--spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 5`. Isolated instance, port not shared with anything else.

| Test | Sampling | Decode | Accept rate | Mean accepted len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline, no draft | temp=1.0 top_p=1.0 | ~34.1 t/s | — | — |
| "Count 1→150" (repetitive) | temp=0 (control) | 66.08 t/s | 89.7% | 5.48 |
| Same prompt | **temp=1.0 top_p=1.0** | **69.40 t/s** | **94.8%** | 5.74 |
| Realistic code (`merge_intervals` w/ docstring) | **temp=1.0 top_p=1.0** | **48.60 t/s** | **60.6%** | 4.03 |

Acceptance at temp=1.0 is *not* worse than greedy here — on the repetitive prompt it's actually a bit higher (94.8% vs 89.7%), and it stays substantial (60.6%) on a prompt that's just normal code, not a synthetic best case. This lines up with why: `common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` (`common/sampling.cpp`) always samples the target token through the real configured sampling chain first, and only *afterward* checks it against the draft — the committed token is never forced to argmax the way DS4's `target_top = sample_argmax(...)` comparison does. Same verification path is shared by every drafter in mainline (DSpark, DFlash, EAGLE-3, MTP), so DSpark isn't getting special treatment — it's just not hitting the failure mode this thread has been debugging.

Posting this mainly as a reference point for whichever fix path this PR (or a rewrite of the verify step) ends up taking: the "accept via true target sample" approach above is simpler than B2's probability-ratio rejection sampling and sidesteps the not-actually-from-`q` bug entirely, at the cost of a somewhat lower expected accept rate than a fully optimal rejection sampler would give (no residual-distribution correction on reject). Given DSpark's own paper benchmarks it at temp=1.0 and gets 60–85% production gains, there's real headroom being left on the table here.

# DSpark follow-up: re-test on engine `6747e77` (post bug-fix)

**Follow-up to:** yesterday's report (engine `b7e9f00`)
**Date:** 2026-08-05
**Hardware:** MacBook Pro, Apple M3 Max, 128 GB
**Main model:** `ds4flash.gguf` = DeepSeek-V4-Flash q2-imatrix, 0731 weights (~91 GiB)
**DSpark support:** `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark-support.gguf` (~5.99 GiB, the 0731-compatible file)
**Flags:** `--nothink --temp 0 -c 32768 -n 512` (greedy; required for DSpark)

---

## Context

After my yesterday's report, ds4 landed two DSpark-related fixes on `main`:

- `7fb2830` — *Replay partial DSpark accepts through ordinary decode* (Closes #658, #659)
- `af80694` — *Restore greedy identity after DSpark acceptance*

I rebuilt and re-ran the exact same A/B benchmark to see whether these fixes
change the negative result I reported. They do **not** — DSpark remains a net
slowdown on this hardware, and on the most-affected scenario the new engine is
actually worse because of added replay cost.

---

## Headline results (generation t/s, higher is better)

| Scenario | Base | DSpark | Delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| code — Python quicksort | 26.93 | 21.49 | **-20.2%** |
| chat — short story | 26.68 | 24.63 | **-7.7%** |
| struct — 3 parallelism strategies | 26.93 | 23.09 | **-14.3%** |

For comparison, yesterday (`b7e9f00`) the same three scenarios were
-1.5% / -9.3% / -45.4%. The base speed improved slightly (engine work elsewhere),
but DSpark is still slower in every case.

---

## DSpark diagnostics (`DS4_DSPARK_STATS=1`, struct scenario)

| Metric | `b7e9f00` (yesterday) | `6747e77` (today) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cycles | 405 | 434 |
| `no_draft` + `scheduler_skips` | 353 + 280 | 394 + 311 |
| draft-not-proposed share | ~87% | **~91%** |
| `avg_accept` (accepted tokens / cycle) | 0.242 | **0.159** |
| `full` accepts | 41  | 31  |
| `replay` time (ms) | 0   | **2555.693** |
| `net_saved` (ms) | -507.007 | **-3272.589** |

The diagnosis is essentially unchanged in nature but amplified:

- The draft model **still declines to propose in ~91% of cycles** (`no_draft` went
  *up* from 87% to 91%). The fixes did not improve the proposal rate on the q2
  target.
- `avg_accept` fell from 0.242 to 0.159 — on average DSpark advances <0.2 tokens
  speculatively per cycle, i.e. barely different from ordinary decode.
- The new `replay` path adds **+2555 ms** overhead on this run, turning the already
  negative `net_saved` of -507 ms into -3272 ms. This is the main reason the new
  engine scores worse here.

---

## Interpretation

The two fixes address *correctness* of partial accepts (#658/#659), not the
underlying low proposal rate. On a q2-imatrix (IQ2XXS) main model the draft
model's hidden-state alignment with the heavily compressed target is poor, so the
scheduler almost always declines to draft. The replay safeguard is correct
behavior, but it adds cost on top of an already-negative baseline.

So my earlier conclusion stands and is now stronger: **on M3 Max 128GB + q2-imatrix
0731, DSpark speculative decoding is a consistent net slowdown.** The README's
"experimental / can be slower" caveat is confirmed for this configuration. Positive
DSpark gains likely require a higher-bit main model (q4), which does not fit
resident on 128 GB.

---

## What I'd still like to know

1. Is the ~87–91% `no_draft` rate an expected/known outcome on q2-imatrix + Metal,
  or a sign the draft/target coupling needs tuning for low-bit targets?
2. For the replay path: is `replay` time expected to dominate `net_saved` like this,
  or is there a short-circuit that should skip replay when acceptance is this low?
  (e.g. auto-back-off DSpark when `no_draft` stays above some threshold.)
3. If there is any known DSpark configuration that shows a real speedup on Apple
  Silicon (specific quantization / `--dspark-confidence` / prompt class), I'm happy
  to re-test.

## Best-case content: maximally predictable numeric continuation

Greedy (`--temp 0`, `reasoning_effort: none` to rule out thinking-mode content), continuing an already-started `1, 2, 3, ...` sequence to 300 — about as repetitive as real content gets, and specifically the kind of input the README singles out as DSpark's ideal case:

- **Before this fix (measured 2026-07-20, same content type, older `main`)**: baseline 37.6 t/s → DSpark **89.3 t/s** (+137%)
- **After this fix (today)**: decode is flat, **31.67 t/s average**, no ramp-up at all across the whole generation

So it's not just prose/code that went net-negative — even the textbook best case (which used to be DSpark's strongest argument) now sits *below* the non-speculative baseline (~37-40 t/s on this quant). Consistent with your read: the replay fix is correct and shouldn't be reverted, but the scheduler's break-even estimate not counting replay means it no longer has any regime where it clearly wins on this hardware.

## Separate but related data point

Adding a code-level confirmation of @Flor1an-B's per-accepted-token reading, because it changes what I asked for in the original report.

## Replay is one full target-model forward per accepted token

At `6747e77`, accepted drafts are replayed in a sequential loop:

```c
for (int i = 0; i < replay_budget; i++) {
    ok = metal_graph_eval_token_raw_swa(&s->graph, &e->model, &e->weights,
                                        drafts[i], (uint32_t)s->checkpoint.len,
                                        row_logits);
    if (!ok) { ... }
    token_vec_push(&s->checkpoint, drafts[i]);
    accepted[n_accept++] = drafts[i];
    replayed_drafts++;
}
```

(around `ds4.c:61777` at that commit — I don't have `af80694` locally, so the line may have moved.)

One `metal_graph_eval_token_raw_swa` per accepted token is one ordinary decode. The telemetry in my original report says the same thing numerically:

```
replay 1063.1 ms / 31 accepted   = 34.3 ms per accepted token
one baseline token at 29.31 t/s  = 34.1 ms
saved = 1045.3  vs  replay = 1063.1   -> within 1.7%
```

An accepted token costs almost exactly what accepting it saved, leaving `propose` (332 ms) and `verify` (964 ms) with nothing to pay them.

## This makes my original framing too weak

I suggested the scheduler's break-even estimate should include the replay term. If savings and replay cancel by construction, that isn't sufficient: **no threshold makes speculation profitable**, and the best a perfect scheduler can do is skip every cycle and converge to baseline. That matches the flat 31.67 t/s @Flor1an-B measures on maximally predictable content, where the old behaviour was +137%.

It also explains why the opt-in timing knobs changed nothing: the dominant cost scales with *accepts*, not with *cycles*, so a high accept rate cannot dilute it the way it would dilute a fixed per-cycle overhead.

## A direction that doesn't touch the correctness fix

Batch the replay — evaluate an accepted run in a single multi-token forward instead of *k* sequential ones, so *k* accepted tokens cost ~1 forward rather than *k*. At my `avg_accept` of 0.35 this would change little, but the long-draft regime is exactly where the old speedup came from, so it is the case that stands to recover.

There is batched machinery on the prefill side (`layer_attention_raw_swa_batch`, chunked prefill), though reusing it for a mid-sequence replay against a restored snapshot is clearly not a small change.

## Minor: stale comment on the invariant under discussion

The comment on the speculative scratch fields still describes the pre-`7fb2830` design:

> Prefix slots retain the intermediate frontiers of a tiny verifier block so partial accepts do not need target-model replay.

(`ds4.c` ~15021.) That is no longer true after the partial-accept shortcut was removed.

I hit this on a DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, 121.63 GiB unified memory) with the 0731 q2/q4 hybrid GGUF (97.6 GB / 90.89 GiB of spans), and I think the root cause is narrower than "aligned artifacts are too big" — it's **arena chunk sizing**, and it's fixable with an existing env var.

### What's actually happening

With the aligned artifacts enabled, `replaces_complete` works correctly: the expert residency is replaced and the model mmap is left unpinned, exactly as designed.

```
built 456 aligned CUDA artifacts (68.58 GiB) in 18.7s; expert raw residency replaced
CUDA aligned artifacts replace expert residency; leaving the 90.89 GiB model mmap unpinned
```

The remaining non-replaced tensor spans then get cached, and that's where it goes wrong:

```
CUDA model arena allocated 1792.00 MiB (arenas 12.25 GiB)
CUDA fd-cached tensor-span:7 1152.00 MiB (total 7.88 GiB)
```

**12.25 GiB of arenas for 7.88 GiB of spans — 1.555×.** The spans on this model are **1152 MiB** and `DS4_CUDA_WEIGHT_ARENA_CHUNK_MB` defaults to **1792 MiB**, so each chunk holds exactly one span and wastes 640 MiB (35.7%).

This model needs 28.45 GiB of non-replaced spans, so at the default chunk size that's **44.2 GiB of arenas**. Add the artifacts and context and it's ~125 GiB on a 121.63 GiB box — OOM, at any context size. I confirmed context is not the variable: the failure is byte-identical at `--ctx 393216` and `--ctx 131072`, same span, same offset.

### The workaround

```
DS4_CUDA_WEIGHT_ARENA_CHUNK_MB=2304    # 2 x 1152 MiB spans per arena
```

With that, `covered 28.45 GiB of tensor spans` and the server loads and serves at the full `--ctx 393216` in ~30 s.

### A second finding, possibly worth separating

`Q8_0_ALIGNED_DENSE` is the one *additive* artifact (+6.15 GiB — the MoE kinds are byte-neutral replacements). On this box it costs more than it returns. Disabling it with `DS4_CUDA_Q8_NO_ALIGNED=1` keeps `replaces_complete` intact (artifacts 456 → 111, 68.58 → 62.44 GiB, mmap still unpinned) and **improved** things:

| | decode tok/s | free memory |
|---|---|---|
| artifacts incl. Q8 dense | 17.08 | ~0–1.5 GiB |
| `DS4_CUDA_Q8_NO_ALIGNED=1` | **18.24** | **~7 GiB** |

For reference, against the older build this machine was pinned to (`80ebbc3`), the working `ae504c9` configuration gives **prefill 373.7 → 686.2 tok/s (+83.6%)** and **decode 14.51 → 18.24 tok/s (+25.7%)** at `--ctx 393216`, same GGUF, same prompt, both cold. (Steady state over 3 reps; the first rep is a consistent warm-up outlier in every arm.)

### Suggested fix

Size the arena chunk from the span size rather than a fixed 1792 MiB default — either round the chunk up to a multiple of the largest span, or allow spans to pack across arenas. As it stands the default silently wastes 35.7% on any model whose spans don't divide 1792 MiB, and on a unified-memory box that's the difference between loading and not loading.

**The headline: at 90.7% accept rate it is still 23.8% slower than baseline.** Your case was 70.45%, and the natural objection to it is "acceptance is just too low here". On a high-acceptance prompt the loss does not go away:

The counting run proposes 86 times and gets 78 drafts accepted, and still loses a quarter of the throughput. That is consistent with your reading that the dominant term is per-cycle and not per-rejection.

**On the proposal — counting replay in the break-even so the scheduler pauses earlier.** The direction is supported, and here is a slope for it. Same binary, same prompt, three configurations ordered by how much they pause:

**But the same table bounds the gain.** The most aggressive configuration that exists today already skips 65% of cycles on the counting prompt and still lands 23.8% under baseline. For the scheduler to converge *to* baseline rather than below it, it would have to pause on essentially every cycle for this content — that is, the fix converges to "do not speculate here". That may well be the honest answer for low-bit main models, but it is a different change from correcting the estimate, and worth separating in the discussion.

Yes, read it carefully — thanks for the pointer. They turn out to be two different gaps, so this issue is not covered by #621, but your work is very relevant to us for a second reason.

**Different tensor class.** #621 touches the *dense* attention projections (Q8_0 → Q4_K). The OOM here comes from the *routed* experts of layers 37–42 in `ds4f-q2-q4`, which are Q4_K and match none of the aligned repack candidates in `cuda/mmq/ds4_repack.cu` (`iq2_candidate` → IQ2_XXS gate/up, `q2k_candidate` → Q2_K down, `q8_candidate` → dense Q8_0). Without an aligned artifact they are pulled into the device cache raw, which is what inflates the startup span phase from 8.20 GiB / 2.2 s to 28.45 GiB / 296 s. The mmq prefill path for Q4_K (`q4k_path && n_tokens > 1u`) is live in this build and works — just slower — so this is the aligned/SoA residency path, not the prefill kernels.

**It closes the objection from the opposite end.** My case was 70.45% acceptance, where the fair
pushback is "acceptance is simply too low here". Yours accepts 78 of 86 drafts and still loses a
quarter of throughput, so the loss survives across the whole acceptance range.

Putting the three reports together, the loss does not track acceptance at all:

| report | accept_rate | change |
|---|---:|---:|
| mine, prose | 70.45% | −21.5% |
| yours, prose | 78.10% | −31.0% |
| yours, counting | 90.70% | −23.8% |

That non-monotonicity is itself the argument. If the dominant cost were per *rejection*, the
90.7% cell should be close to break-even. If savings and replay cancel per accepted token, then
acceptance buys nothing either way and what remains is `propose` + `verify` as pure overhead —
which is what all three cells show.

**And my proposal was too optimistic — your sweep bounds it.** The report says a replay-aware
break-even estimate "could pause speculation earlier on low-yield content and converge to
baseline instead of below it". The second half of that is wrong. Your most aggressive existing
configuration already skips 65% of cycles on the counting prompt and still lands 23.8% under
baseline, so for the estimate alone to reach baseline the scheduler would have to pause on
essentially every cycle. That is not a corrected estimate, it is a decision not to speculate on
this content.

So the two changes are worth keeping separate:

- **Counting replay in the break-even** stops the bleeding on low-yield content, and your
  monotone slope (24.80 → 22.63 → 20.68 as pausing decreases) shows it moves throughput the
  right way. Its ceiling is baseline-minus-epsilon, approached by speculating never.
- **Batched replay** — evaluating an accepted run against a restored snapshot rather than one
  `metal_graph_eval_token_raw_swa` per accepted token — is the only change that can put DSpark
  *above* baseline again, because it attacks the per-accepted-token cost itself.

**The different drafter is more useful than it might look.** You are on an 11.5 GiB support GGUF
with `mtp.<N>.` renamed tensors rather than the 5.6 GiB 0731 file, and you reach the same
conclusion — which rules out drafter mismatch as the cause. That is worth stating explicitly,
because a mismatched drafter is exactly what corrupted my own first measurement of this: the
legacy and 0731 support files are byte-identical in size (5,989,114,272) and differ only by
sha256, so nothing on disk flags the pairing, and it produced a plausible-looking −7.7% that I
had to throw away.

**Your #658 note deserves more prominence than a footnote.** Any `--dspark` throughput number
taken before `7fb2830` compares different generated text, so a fair amount of pre-existing
comparison in this area — including some of my own early numbers, though not the ones in this
report — is not measuring what it claims to. Worth flagging wherever those figures are still
quoted.

## I added the counter you were missing

You were measuring `read_calls_per_token`. That doesn't exist in the tree — hit rate was
the only thing the engine reported, which is exactly the gap you were pointing at. So I
made it a real metric, counted at the one place every expert read passes through:

```
ds4: CUDA streamed experts over 216 decode tokens: cache 44293 hits / 55728 lookups
(79.5% hit, 2249/2249 slots), reads 34305 (158.8/token, 357.34 MiB/token)
```

Adding it immediately caught a bug in the number it replaces: misses that couldn't get a
cache slot were being left out of the total, so the hit rate looked better than it was.
Fixed in the same commit.

## Your point 2: I can't make it happen here

I swept the cache from off to full and watched both numbers together:

| cache | hit rate | reads per token |
|---|---|---|
| off | — | 774.0 |
| 2 GiB | 44.0% | 433.4 |
| 6 GiB | 63.4% | 283.0 |
| auto (14.8 GiB) | 79.5% | 158.8 |

Every row satisfies `reads = 774 × (1 − hit rate)`. 774 isn't arbitrary: it's 43 layers ×
6 experts × 3 pieces per expert, i.e. everything the model needs for one token. So on this
tier a hit removes exactly three reads, every single time. 

## Your point 1: your arithmetic is right, and it found a bug

First, your KV numbers are correct. I get 13.5 KiB per token of context against your 13.7,
and one of the internal numbers in the log (`compressed_kv_rows=37502` at ctx 150000) is
identical on my machine. That term behaves exactly as predictably as you said.

What surprised me is where it bites. On CUDA the expert cache doesn't live in VRAM at all —
it's pinned host RAM. So with default settings, growing the context genuinely does nothing
to it: 2249–2250 slots at ctx 8192, 30474 and 150000 alike.

**But if you pass a cache size explicitly, it shrinks — and that was a real bug.** The code
was subtracting the VRAM taken by the KV from the budget of a cache that lives in system
RAM. Two different pools. Same binary, same 8 GiB request, only `-c` changed:

| ctx 150000, 8 GiB budget | slots | pinned | hit rate | reads/token |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 549 | 3.62 GiB | 53.6% | 359.4 |
| **after the fix** | **701** | **4.62 GiB** | **58.7%** | **318.8** |

And the check that matters: after the fix, ctx 8192 and ctx 150000 give the *same* cache
and the *same* ~319 reads/token. Before, they didn't. That's your effect, and it's gone.
The fix is scoped so the backends where the cache really does share VRAM (Metal, ROCm) keep
the old behaviour.

## The thing that's actually costing you at long context

This is the part I'd most want to hand you, since we're both on 12 GB.

Going from ctx 30474 to ctx 150000, the read work per token doesn't move at all — 167.3 to
167.9 — and neither does the hit rate. But generation drops by about half. If the disk work
is identical and the disk didn't slow down, the lost time simply isn't in the streaming path.

I had a plausible story here — the KV squeezing the engine's q8→f16 weight cache, pushing
weights onto slower kernels — and I'm dropping it, because when I finally measured that
cache directly it turned out to work the other way round.

unchanged by construction, not by measurement. And as above, treat my tokens/s as
directional this time round; the read counts are the solid part.

Follow-up: I said above that the silicon-versus-TensorOps split could not be separated without `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_METAL4` on an M5. It can be answered from the M4 side instead, by going the other way and enabling the path here. Result: **your gate is right, and the M5 prefill lead is silicon.**

## Method

Added `"M4"` to the `default_enable` device-name list in `ds4_metal.m` and re-ran the identical sweep — same machine, same `ds4f-q2` file, same `b030961`, same command. The gate was the only variable.

First finding: **the probe passes on M4 Max.** The patched build prints

```
ds4: Metal device Apple M4 Max, 128.00 GiB RAM
ds4: Metal 4 tensor API enabled for Tensor kernels
```

so on macOS 26 the tensor API and `mpp::tensor_ops::matmul2d` compile fine on M4 — the restriction is policy, not capability.

## But enabling it loses

| ctx | prefill off → on | generation off → on |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 2048 | 331.6 → 312.2 (**−5.8%**) | 29.87 → 30.44 (+1.9%) |
| 8192 | 287.8 → 251.9 (**−12.4%**) | 29.13 → 29.41 (+1.0%) |
| 16384 | 280.5 → 273.0 (−2.7%) | 28.75 → 28.42 (−1.1%) |
| 32768 | 229.3 → 210.2 (**−8.3%**) | 25.65 → 24.28 (−5.3%) |
| 49152 | 199.2 → 200.8 (+0.8%) | 23.76 → 23.79 (+0.1%) |
| 65536 | 190.8 → 194.2 (+1.8%) | 23.28 → 23.01 (−1.2%) |

Aggregated over all 32 frontiers: **prefill −4.2%, generation −0.9%**, with prefill improving at only 10 of 32. That is exactly what the comment above `default_enable` predicts — on pre-M5 the TensorOps path maps to ordinary shader fallbacks, and here they are slower than the established kernels.

## Consequence for the M5 comparison in this PR

Enabling the path moves M4 backwards, so the M5/M4 prefill ratio **widens** rather than closes: 2.38× → 2.53× at ctx 2048 and 2.43× → 2.65× at 32768 (roughly unchanged at 64K, 2.09× → 2.05×). So the caveat in the PR description should be read as settled: the prefill gap is the M5's per-GPU-core neural accelerators, not the gating decision holding M4 back. The generation gap stays 1.19–1.34× either way, which fits — decode is bandwidth-bound and TensorOps does not touch it.

**Not proposing a change.** The gate does the right thing, and this is only evidence for it. Reverted locally.

Caveats: one run per frontier and no thermal control between the two sweeps on a laptop, so a few percent of the aggregate could be drift; the per-cell signs are mixed at the top of the range. I did not check whether TensorOps changes numerics on M4, only throughput.

Tested on a stock NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, 128 GB unified, CUDA 13.0.88, driver 580.173.02), as offered above. Short version: **the CUDA path is correct, the memory win is bigger than expected, but prefill regresses ~16x**, which is a blocker for resident use on this machine.

Setup: branch `aprojq4-dense-attention` at `41aefd2c`, `make cuda-spark`, no local changes — **builds clean in 2m52s with zero warnings**. Model is the GGUF you linked (`5ca1abfe`, 78.62 GiB). Baseline everywhere below is `IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ8-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix-0731`, run with **the same binary**, so the comparison isolates the quant rather than the code version.

One caveat up front: the AProjQ4 file is from an **older checkpoint** (no `-0731`) and I did not download a matching AProjQ8 baseline, so memory and correctness numbers are clean, but **speed and perplexity carry a checkpoint difference** that I cannot separate out.

### 1. Correctness: the CUDA path looks good

`--decode-consistency 64`:

| model | max_abs | rms |
|---|---:|---:|
| AProjQ8 (baseline) | 1.476 | 0.293 |
| **AProjQ4** | **1.118** | **0.191** |

Top-1 matches, top-10 sets match. The divergence is *smaller* than on the existing Q8_0 path, so the new kernel is not introducing numerical error.

### 2. Memory: a bigger win than the file-size delta suggests

`--inspect` shows 215 tensors moved Q8_0 → Q4_K (345 → 130 Q8_0, plus 215 Q4_K), everything else byte-identical. Startup spans and the memory plan both drop by exactly the file-size delta:

- `startup model preparation`: **8.20 GiB → 6.06 GiB**, and no time penalty (2.12s → 1.70s)
- `planned` at `--ctx 200000`: 85.21 GiB → 83.07 GiB
- aligned artifacts: 474 / 78.71 GiB → **259 / 74.16 GiB** (the Q4_K tensors get no repack builder)

But free memory after startup improves by **~11 GB**, well beyond the 2.14 GiB the file shrank:

| ctx | AProjQ8 free | AProjQ4 free |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 200000 | 9.8 GB | **21.3 GB** |
| 250000 | 8.7 GB | **20.1 GB** |
| 300000 | 8.1 GB | **19.1 GB** |

My guess is that the Q4_K tensors no longer exist simultaneously as an aligned artifact *and* a mapping, which accounts for roughly 6.7 GiB of it — I have not verified the rest, so treat the exact figure with caution. On GB10 (CPU and GPU share one 128 GB pool) this is a real change: `--ctx 300000` now starts with more headroom than `--ctx 200000` had before.

### 3. Prefill: ~16x slower, and this is the blocker

`ds4-bench`, same prompt file, 128 generated tokens per frontier:

| ctx | prefill Q8 | prefill Q4 | decode Q8 | decode Q4 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | 817.32 | **53.98** | 17.55 | 17.28 |
| 4096 | 892.89 | **54.20** | 15.08 | 14.86 |
| 6144 | 883.59 | **54.18** | 14.97 | 14.78 |
| 8192 | 877.75 | **54.17** | 14.83 | 14.65 |

**Decode is essentially free (−1.2%)** — impressive for halving the precision of the attention projections. All the cost is in prefill, exactly where your comment above `matmul_q4_K_dense_kernel` predicts it ("correct-but-unoptimized for prefill chunks"; every token re-reads the weight rows). With a 4096-token prefill chunk this dominates.

Practical effect for a long-context server: a full 194681-token prefill went at a steady 54.6 t/s, i.e. **~59 minutes instead of ~4.5** (I aborted the run at 17%). So on this machine the patch trades a context ceiling we can now afford for one we can no longer fill — a 15k-token page would go from ~17s to ~4.5 minutes.

That makes the dequant + GEMM prefill path you mention in the comment the deciding factor here, rather than a later optimization. Is that something you're planning? **If you push a prefill path, I'm happy to re-run this whole sweep on the same machine** — the harness is set up and a rebuild plus full sweep is under an hour.

### 4. Perplexity — reported for completeness only

Same 1882-token sample: AProjQ4 **12.730** (avg_nll 2.5439) vs AProjQ8-0731 **11.108** (avg_nll 2.4077). **Please do not read this as a +14.6% quantization cost** — it is dominated by the checkpoint difference, and it is inconsistent with your own +0.99% measured within one checkpoint. I mention it only so the number isn't misread if it surfaces elsewhere. If you publish an AProjQ8 GGUF from the same older checkpoint, I'll rerun and give you a clean quality delta.

Also worth noting for anyone reading this from the DGX Spark side: this is a different issue from #705, which is about *routed* Q4_K experts having no aligned repack builder. This PR touches dense tensors only and does not OOM.

**On the part you left open** — ctx 30474 → 150000 with reads/token flat and generation halving — we ran into the same shape, and what moved us forward was measuring the *rendezvous* rather than the transfer.

At ctx 150000, single request, 2250 tokens, median token 231 ms, from a counter that aggregates per window rather than emitting per token:

```
waits per token       43          (one per layer)
pickup_lag            45.2 ms/token   = 1.05 ms per rendezvous
queue                 47.0 ms/token
worker idle           85.7 ms/token   = 37% of the token
```

**The caveat that matters, and it's why I can't hand you a budget:** those are *sums over 43 overlapping per-layer waits*, not exclusive wall-clock slices. The proof is internal — the summed wait (268 ms) is larger than the token itself (231 ms). So they can't be added up. What we took from them was the ratio and one fact: decode was waiting on a worker that was itself idle a large fraction of the time. That points at hand-off latency rather than throughput, which is at least consistent with your observation that the disk work doesn't move.

If your tree has an equivalent, the two quantities I'd look at are **the delay between a route job being submitted and the worker picking it up**, and **worker idle time per token**. **`--source-gguf` works, and the result is better than I expected.** I requantized our production `-0731` model directly from GGUF — no safetensors needed — and then ran `score_official` on both. Summary: on a same-checkpoint comparison the AProjQ4 quality cost is **+0.64% avg_nll**, while decode gets *faster* than Q8_0 and the model frees ~13 GB of memory.

### 1. Requantization

```sh
./deepseek4-quantize \
  --source-gguf  DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ8-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix-0731.gguf \
  --template     <same file> \
  --attention-proj q4_k \
  --out          ...-AProjQ4-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-0731-requant.gguf
```

Converted **215 tensors** `q8_0 -> q4_K`, output **84,420,584,032 bytes** — 224 bytes off your published AProjQ4 file, so the layout matches exactly. `--inspect` confirms it: 130 × q8_0 (1.59 GiB), 215 × q4_K (2.41 GiB), everything else byte-identical to the source.

Two notes for anyone repeating this:

- The tool streams 16 rows at a time, so memory use is negligible — **it ran fine alongside a live 80 GB `ds4-server` on the same box**, only costing disk I/O.
- **No imatrix was used.** `write_imatrix_kvs` only records the imatrix *filename* and entry count in the KV block, not the vectors, so a requantized GGUF cannot recover them from its source. This is therefore a double quantization (Q8_0 → f32 → Q4_K) with unweighted Q4_K, i.e. a *worse* case than your imatrix-based path — which makes the quality numbers below a pleasant surprise.

### 2. `score_official` — as requested, plus your files for comparison

`data/flash/manifest.tsv`, ctx 4096, both env vars set to 1 (so the grouped-tok8 / QKV-pair paths from my previous comment are out of the picture):

| yours: Q4 (macOS, older ckpt) | 0.653162 | 82.88% | 41 | 3.420 |
| **mine: Q8 `-0731` (CUDA)** | 0.404811 | 85.86% | 55 | 5.150 |
| **mine: Q4 requant `-0731` (CUDA)** | 0.407383 | 85.34% | 56 | 5.540 |

Please **don't compare the absolute values across our two pairs** — the `data/flash` fixtures were collected from the official DeepSeek V4 Flash **0731** API, so they match my checkpoint and not the older one. That alone explains most of the level difference (0.405 vs 0.633). Only the within-pair deltas are meaningful, and even those differ in backend and checkpoint.

Traced the replay cost to its exact source in `ds4_session_eval_dspark_speculative_argmax` (`ds4.c`), which explains *why* it's structured this way and why the fix isn't a quick change.

**The mechanism**: verification is already correctly batched — `metal_graph_verify_suffix_tops` does one forward pass over all `draft_n` positions to get `row_tops` (the target model's greedy pick at each draft position), which is exactly how a fast verify step should work. But the code comment right after it says why the accepted tokens then get replayed one at a time (`ds4.c:61711-61714`):

> Batch verification and ordinary decode update compressor state with different kernels. Restore the pre-verify frontier and replay every accepted draft through ordinary decode, including partial accepts, so speculative decoding retains the target model's greedy token stream.

So the batched verify kernel doesn't correctly maintain the compressed-KV/indexer state per accepted position — only the normal single-token decode kernel (`metal_graph_eval_token_raw_swa`) does. The checkpoint gets rolled back after verify and then each accepted draft is replayed through that single-token path, one full target-model forward per token (`ds4.c:61777`).

**Why this cancels the savings almost exactly** (confirms @datanerdie's per-accepted-token framing with the actual cost accounting): producing N accepted tokens costs 1 batched-verify forward (~1 normal forward, wall-clock-wise, since this is memory-bandwidth bound) + N sequential replay forwards + a cheap draft-model forward. That's ~(N+1) target-model forwards to produce N tokens — at best breakeven with plain autoregressive decoding (N forwards), before even counting the draft model's own cost. There's no regime where this wins; higher accept rates just mean you pay the full (N+1) more often instead of falling back to a cheap 1-token verify-miss path.

**Why MTP stays viable with the same mechanism**: MTP's replay path has the identical split (batched-ish confidence check, then per-token replay — see the `mtp timing ... replay=...ms` log lines in the same file) but typical draft windows are small (`--mtp-draft` commonly 1-2, vs DSpark's `DS4_SPEC_PREFIX_SLOTS=4` → up to 5-token windows). Same per-token tax, much smaller absolute N, so it stays net-positive in practice where DSpark doesn't.

**External expectation check**: Unsloth's docs claim DSpark should give up to ~2x decode speedup (DeepSeek-V4-Flash "120 tokens/s on a B200 GPU compared to the original 60 tokens/s baseline"): https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/deepseek-v4#dspark-speculative-decoding. That's consistent with a correctly-batched implementation (verify *and* accept both O(1) forwards regardless of N) and sharpens the gap here — ds4's replay step currently pays the full O(N) cost speculation is supposed to let you skip.

The real fix is a batched-replay kernel that updates the compressed-KV/indexer state correctly per position the way the single-token path does, not just batched logits like verify already has — that's genuine kernel work I don't have the Metal expertise to attempt safely, but hopefully this narrows exactly what needs to change for whoever does (this lines up with @datanerdie's "batch the replay" proposal above, now with the specific reason the two kernels currently diverge).

Follow-up with a working prototype and real numbers, plus a finding that reframes the fix as a policy question rather than a pure bug.

**MTP already made this trade-off, by default, on Metal.** Tracing `ds4_session_eval_speculative_argmax`'s MTP path (draft_n==2) turned up:

```c
#ifdef DS4_ROCM_BUILD
    const bool prefer_decode2_exact = true;
#else
    const bool prefer_decode2_exact = false;   // Metal
#endif
```

`metal_graph_verify_decode2_exact` — the exact, bit-identical-to-decode verifier — is only *preferred* on ROCm. On Metal, MTP's default path uses the same batched `metal_graph_verify_suffix_tops` DSpark's verify already uses, and on a **full accept it commits directly from that batched pass with no rollback and no replay** — it only snapshots/replays when the accept is partial. That's why MTP stays net-positive: it almost never pays sequential-replay cost. DSpark, by contrast, unconditionally rolls back and replays every accepted draft, full accept or not (`ds4.c:61711-61714`, quoted in my last comment).

**Prototype**: mirrored MTP's full-accept path onto DSpark — skip the rollback + sequential replay when `commit_drafts == draft_n`, and just read the already-computed `spec_logits` row for the last drafted position directly, same as MTP's `commit_drafts == draft_n` branch already does. TP path untouched (falls through to the existing rollback+replay unconditionally, since I haven't touched or validated that path).

**Measured, same session, controlled A/B, `--dspark --mtp-draft 2 --temp 0`, same prompt**:
- Unpatched: 30.43 t/s
- Patched: 35.95 t/s (**+18.1%**)

**The catch, and it's a real one**: comparing full generated output (not just the `dspark-verify-depth` unit test, which passed clean at `worst_argmax_gap=0.000` over 128 cycles) — the patched output diverges from plain greedy decode starting at the first sentence. So I checked whether MTP's already-shipped default has the same property: it does. Same prompt, same settings, MTP's output diverges from greedy decode **at the same point, with the same inserted phrase** ("...spanning over a millennium *and leaving an indelible mark on Western civilization*..."), because it's the identical batched kernel causing the same near-tied-logit flip. This isn't a new risk my patch introduces — it's the exact trade-off MTP already ships by default on Metal, just not yet applied to DSpark.

So this isn't "here's a bug fix," it's "DSpark doesn't yet apply the speed/exactness trade-off the project already made for MTP." Whether that's the right call for DSpark too is a real decision, not something I want to sneak in as a quiet correctness-preserving patch — happy to open a PR with this behind an opt-in flag, or as the new default matching MTP, whichever @antirez would rather review.

Independent M4 Max follow-up on the narrower-repair idea mentioned in this PR (re-derive only the compressor-frontier projection instead of full replay): we now have runtime first-divergence evidence showing that compressor-only repair is not sufficient for strict decode-order identity.

Using the same true pre-verify state and the same forced proposal tokens, with an in-stream GPU snapshot harness whose non-perturbation control passes (`A0==A1`, `A0==A2` bitwise), the earliest observed generic-vs-ordinary-sequential divergence is already in layer 0 / row 0 at the Q_A projection output:

```text
CP1 normalized_attention_input: EXACT (4096 F32)
CP2-Q q_a_projection_output: MISMATCH (823/1024)
max_abs=5.2154064178466797e-08

generic:
  metal_graph_matmul_q8_0_named_tensor_attn_q_a

sequential:
  metal_graph_matmul_dense_quant_tensor_attn_q_a
```

An isolated same-input/same-weight primitive A/B reproduces the numerical non-equivalence. Then, under a diagnostic gate, making only generic Q_A use canonical sequential-equivalent arithmetic removes that divergence completely (`CP2-Q: EXACT`) while the probe controls remain PASS.

With Q_A canonicalized, the next first divergence moves immediately to:

```text
row=0 layer=0 checkpoint=CP2-KV-P subobject=kv_raw
```

This is the semantic raw-KV projection output *before* persistent raw-cache interpretation/store, so this mismatch cannot be attributed to ring-row mapping, the persistent store, compressor update, snapshot/restore, or later operators.

Current evidence:

```text
QA_CAUSAL_SOURCE              PROVEN BY TEST
QA_ONLY_SOURCE                DISPROVEN
NEXT_INDEPENDENT_DRIFT_SOURCE CP2-KV-P / kv_raw
KV_PRIMITIVE_ROOT_CAUSE       NOT YET PROVEN
```

So a narrower alternative to full replay still looks possible, but the repair set is already broader than compressor-frontier re-projection alone.

The next question is whether Q_A, raw-KV, and subsequent sites collapse to one reusable quantized-projection arithmetic family (batched vs single-row/fused), or whether independent drift appears across multiple operator families.

We are iteratively canonicalizing one proven source at a time and rerunning whole-model first-divergence to identify the minimal sufficient canonical repair set, rather than sequentializing the verifier wholesale.

Thanks @GiorgioOppo — I went ahead and ran the test. Here are the results.

## Setup

Since the prebuilt AProjQ4 GGUF on HF uses IQ2XXS experts (84 GB), which would confound the comparison against my MXFP4 baseline (different expert quantization = different replay/verify byte counts), I used the `--source-gguf` requantize tool from #621 to produce a clean version: **MXFP4 experts preserved bit-for-bit, only the 215 attention projection tensors requantized Q8_0 → Q4_K**. Same model, same experts, only attention projection precision differs.

## Token throughput

Same prompt, `--ctx 8192 --nothink --temp 0 --tokens 100`:

| Mode | MXFP4 Q8Attn baseline | AProjQ4 | Delta |
|------|----------------------|---------|-------|
| baseline (no DSpark) | 39.78 t/s | 41.77 t/s | +5.0% |
| `--dspark-strict` | 39.17 t/s | 40.74 t/s | +4.0% |
| `--dspark` (conf 0.7) | 25.47 t/s | 26.77 t/s | +5.1% |
| `--dspark --dspark-confidence 0` | 21.58 t/s | 22.09 t/s | +2.4% |

AProjQ4 is consistently a few percent faster (attention projection reads half the bytes), but the regression pattern is unchanged: **conf 0.7 is still -36% vs baseline**, identical to MXFP4.

## Telemetry comparison

The key question is whether AProjQ4 changes the per-cycle replay/verify cost. I ran control groups to isolate the variable: same binary (#621 build) running both MXFP4 Q8Attn and AProjQ4, same confidence (0, full 5-token drafts, no pruning).

**conf 0 (full drafts, cleanest comparison):**

| Per-cycle | MXFP4 Q8Attn | AProjQ4 | Delta |
|-----------|-------------|---------|-------|
| replay | 73.4 ms | 65.8 ms | -10.4% |
| verify | 81.7 ms | 81.5 ms | -0.2% |

replay improved ~10% (attention projection is part of the replay forward pass), verify essentially unchanged. Both within ±15%.

But `replay + verify` combined (3534 ms) still vastly exceeds the 1591 ms saved by accepted tokens. `net_saved = -2186 ms`.

## Conclusion

AProjQ4 delivers the expected small improvement in attention-projection-bound paths (~10% on replay, consistent with attention projections being ~4% of the model), but it does not change the DSpark cost structure. The dominant cost is reading routed experts during verify and replay, which AProjQ4 doesn't touch. The net-negative result holds across all configurations.

The bottleneck, as #695 also identified, is the replay path itself (commit `7fb2830`) and the verify kernel cost — both are structural to the current DSpark implementation, not properties of the attention quantization format.

Appreciate the suggestion and the requantize tool though — it was clean to use and the Q4_K attention path works correctly. Good luck with #621.

| target | 4322 ms | 2716 ms | 5092 ms |
| **net_saved** | **−1884 ms** | **−3136 ms** | **−1733 ms** |

Draft quality genuinely *improved* when you removed the scheduler: proposals 72 → 116, accepted drafts 46 → 77, `avg_accept` more than doubled (0.622 → 1.510). The scheduler was indeed suppressing drafts that would have been accepted — that part of your read was right.

But that isn't where the loss is. `spec_total` went from 3798 ms to **6410 ms against only 2716 ms of target decode**, so the speculative path now costs 2.4× the work it replaces. The scheduler was functioning as a *cost* limiter rather than a quality filter, and removing it let per-cycle `replay` + `verify_layer` scale unchecked.

The `--dspark-confidence 0.9` run confirms the direction: it speculates *less* (38 proposals, 80 of 97 cycles with no draft) and produces the best DSpark figure I have measured on this machine, 15.15 t/s. Every configuration that speculates less does better.

### What this implies

On this hardware the bottleneck is **per-cycle verify + replay cost, not draft accuracy**. Proposing better won't help; proposing more actively hurts. Even the best case is still net-negative: at `--dspark-confidence 0.9`, `saved=1620 ms` against `propose=1024 ms` plus verify and replay, ending at `net_saved=-1733 ms`. `replay` + `verify_layer` would need to come down by roughly 2–3× for DSpark to break even here.

So I'd suggest reverting the scheduler removal, or replacing it with a gate on measured cost rather than deleting it. If it helps, I can run a sweep of `--dspark-confidence` (0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95) so you can see the whole curve rather than three points.

Usual caveats: one synthetic and highly repetitive prompt, one machine, `--temp 0`. Run-to-run spread is small (decode within 0.5% within each pair, counters byte-identical), so the ordering is solid even though the absolute numbers aren't portable.

Follow-up with real-world agent workload benchmarks, since the earlier results used simple coding prompts. I constructed three test tiers from actual agent working materials — long system prompts and architecture documents that represent the real prefill/decode patterns when this model runs as a coding/architecture agent.

## Test tiers

| Tier | Description | Prefill tokens | Generation |
|------|-------------|---------------|------------|
| agent-startup | Full orchestrator system prompt (~16k) + task instruction | 16,057 | 200 |
| agent-analysis | Full system prompt + architecture doc excerpt (~8k) + analysis task | 23,633 | 200 |
| agent-review | System prompt §1-§3 (~7k) + design doc (~4k) + review task | 11,295 | 200 |

All Chinese input (native working language), `--ctx 32768 --nothink --temp 0`.

## Results (main vs PR #755, multiple runs per tier)

| Tier | main gen | PR #755 gen | Delta |
|------|----------|-------------|-------|
| agent-startup (16k) | 35.68 t/s | 40.38 t/s | +13.2% |
| agent-analysis (24k) | 34.91 t/s | 39.18 t/s | +12.2% |
| agent-review (11k) | 36.01 t/s | 40.52 t/s | +12.5% |

Prefill unchanged across all tiers (within noise, ±3%).

## Observations

Two things worth noting for anyone benchmarking decode optimizations:

1. **Decode throughput drops ~12% at real context lengths.** Simple ~20-token prompts give ~40 t/s on main, but realistic 11-24k agent contexts settle at ~35-36 t/s. The KV cache attention scan cost is non-trivial even within 32k context.

2. **PR #755's improvement narrows from +15-22% (short prompts) to +12-13% (agent workloads).** This is expected — the fusion optimizations benefit decode kernels, but at longer contexts the attention scan overhead grows and dilutes the kernel-level gains. Still a solid, consistent improvement where it matters.

The main takeaway: simple-prompt benchmarks overstate both the absolute speed and the relative improvement. Real agent workloads see ~12% decode gains, which is meaningful for daily use but not transformative. Prefill (the bigger daily-use bottleneck) remains untouched, as expected since this PR targets decode kernels.

Complementary angle from #756, in case cross-referencing is useful.

This PR localizes the **earliest bitwise** point where `F_gen(S,x)` and `F_seq(S,x)` diverge — the strong, future-visible-state requirement. #756 comes at the same phenomenon from the surface: it teacher-forces the committed speculative stream back through ordinary decode and reports the **rate + severity histogram** of greedy-token divergence (committed token ≠ autoregressive argmax) over real generations. Your point that argmax-match is weaker than bitwise state identity is exactly right — #756 deliberately measures only the visible greedy consequence, so its rate is a **lower bound** on the underlying state divergence you localize.

## What I think this means for the PR

This reframes the last three rounds. Both of us have been treating the cost as proportional to speculation — which is why `EXACTN` looked like the right lever, and why it was reasonable to expect that cutting `verify`/`replay` would eventually bring DSpark to parity. **On this hardware it can't**: even with the speculative path at ~0 ms, there's a fixed ~16% floor underneath it.

That's not a reason to abandon the work — it's a different target. Your flags do measurably help in the low-speculation regime (+8.2% at `conf 0.9`, as I reported earlier). But the thing standing between DSpark and break-even here isn't `verify` or `replay`; it's whatever `--dspark` changes globally on entry. The prefill improvement in the same step suggests the two are the same mechanism seen from opposite ends — something is being reconfigured for speculative execution and it happens to suit prefill and hurt decode.

If you want a starting point: whatever `--dspark` disables or reroutes in the decode path when it initializes, independent of `dspark_confidence_threshold`.

## Update (2026-08-11): root cause found — the earlier "slowdown" was a silent OOM, not DSpark

I re-ran the A/B on the current engine (commit `84cc882`) and found that **my earlier
conclusion was wrong**, and the error is worth documenting because it points at a real
usability bug.

### The real cause of the 08-05 failure

On 08-05 I reported DSpark as a consistent net slowdown on engine `6747e77`
(code -20.2% / chat -7.7% / struct -14.3%). That was misleading. My Mac had rebooted
in between, which **reset `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` to `0`**. With no wired-memory
headroom, the ~5.99 GiB DSpark support model could not be mapped on top of the ~91 GiB
main model, so ds4 **aborted at startup**:

```
ds4: Metal model warmup failed: Insufficient Memory (kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorOutOfMemory)
ds4: metal failed to map support model views; aborting startup.
```

So the 08-05 DSpark runs never actually generated a token — the harness reported the
failure as "NA / slowdown". After setting `iogpu.wired_limit_mb=120000` (the main model
alone needs ~93.5 GiB wired; DSpark needs the extra headroom), DSpark loads and runs
normally. **This is a silent, confusing failure: ds4 does not warn that wired_limit is
too low for main + support model; it just OOMs at warmup.**

### New engine `84cc882` results (generation tok/s, higher = better)

Same harness as the original report: `--nothink --temp 0 -c 32768 -n 512`, M3 Max 128GB,
q2-imatrix 0731 main model, `wired_limit=120000`.

|----------|-----:|------:|-----:|-----------------------|

commits" path from fixes `7fb2830` / `af80694` is active and the expensive `replay`
stage is gone (0 ms). That is why `net_saved` recovered from -3272 ms to roughly -500 ms.

### Revised conclusion

- On this hardware, DSpark is **no longer a clear net negative** once:
  (a) `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` is high enough to fit main + support model, and
  (b) the `84cc882` decode kernels are in use.
- It is now **prompt-class dependent**: clean/structured/code-like prompts (code) go
  positive; open chat and enumerations (chat, struct) stay a few percent negative. This
  matches the README's "low-yield prompts can be no faster" caveat, now in the
  small-negative rather than large-negative regime.
- The original issue title/§6 ("structural to q2 quantization") should be read with this
  correction: the dominant factor in the early numbers was the **reset wired_limit
  causing a silent OOM**, not DSpark's quantization interaction.

Re-ran my end of this on `84cc882`, with `0e89a0e` in. **The replay cost is gone, and on the counting prompt speculation now wins.** Since my earlier numbers are the ones in this thread, here they are again under the same protocol, so the before/after is like-for-like.

| prompt | `accept_rate` | baseline | `--dspark` | change | (same arms on `b030961`) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| counting (1..120) | 88.95% | 35.45 t/s | **39.87 t/s** | **+12.5%** | 32.53 → 24.80, −23.8% |
| prose (~200 words) | 77.22% | 35.50 t/s | **34.79 t/s** | **−2.0%** | 32.51 → 22.44, −31.0%\* |

\* One correction to my own before-column while I am at it: that prose `--dspark` cell was the one arm my protocol flagged as suspect back then (surviving cells 22.44 / 21.69 / 17.37, 3.3% spread), so −31.0% was a lower bound on the loss, not a tight estimate. The −23.8% counting figure was solid (24.80 / 24.79 / 24.78 / 24.78).

**The mechanism, measured rather than inferred:** `replay=0.000` in *every* cell of both campaigns, `replay_fallbacks=0`, and every acceptance accounted for as `direct_full`/`direct_partial` (counting `full=37 partial=5`, prose `full=35 partial=9`). Worth noting for anyone reading #746 first: the shipped default also covers **partial** accepts, which the opt-in prototype deliberately left on the old path — though reading the source rather than the counters, that direct partial path is conditional on being off TP (TP workers get no intermediate snapshots and keep the mirrored replay fallback) and on `commit_drafts <= DS4_SPEC_PREFIX_SLOTS`. Single-host Metal runs like mine take it every time; that is not the same as always.

Per-run balance (`saved − spec_total − propose`): **+863 ms** on counting, **−100 ms** on prose. So on prose the residual is no longer the replay — it is the drafter itself (`propose` ≈ 694 ms against `verify` ≈ 2836 ms). At 77% acceptance the margin does not cover the proposal.

**Two things that are easy to conflate, and one of them is mine to flag.** The non-speculative arm moved too: 32.53 → 35.45 and 32.51 → 35.50, +9.0% and +9.2%, from the MXFP4/M5 decode work and `0ad494e`. Anyone comparing a number from today against one from five days ago is adding two effects. A free provenance check on that: the greedy text hashes to the same md5 as on `b030961` **on both prompts** (`5284848e` counting, `fa10dd86` prose, recomputed from the raw logs of the earlier campaign). So the exact fast paths really are exact here — 9% faster, byte-identical output.

**The three-point scheduler series I posted above is now reversed, and it changes sign with the prompt.** Same binary, same prompts, ordered by how much the scheduler pauses:

| config | `scheduler_skips` (counting · prose) | counting | prose |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| default | 26 · 58 | 39.87 | **34.79** |
| `DS4_DSPARK_SCHEDULER_NO_DRAFT_SKIP=0` | 8 · 24 | **41.74** | 33.72 |
| `DS4_DSPARK_SCHEDULER=0` | 0 · 0 | 41.72 | 34.20 |

On counting the scheduler now **costs** 4.7%: the more it pauses, the slower it runs — the exact opposite of what it did before the fix, and the default is the worst of the three. On prose it still pays, which is consistent with its purpose (lower acceptance, pausing is worth it). So my earlier "monotone on both prompts, pause more" reading should be treated as withdrawn: it was measured on a build where every accepted token was decoded twice.

**Output identity.** The binary announces the trade-off itself (`DSpark direct verifier-state commits enabled; greedy output may differ...`), and that is what I see: on counting all three speculative arms diverge from the plain-greedy stream; on prose only the default diverges, while both reduced-scheduler arms stay byte-identical. Prompt-dependent, as was predicted in #658.

**Protocol** (unchanged, so the arms stay comparable to the earlier table): 5 replicas per arm, `purge` before each run, arms alternated inside a replica, warm-up run discarded, a cell discarded when a single stall above 40 ms shows up in the per-token `execute` profile or `prop_setup` exceeds 200 ms, value = max over surviving cells because the fault is one-sided. To be unambiguous about that last part, since it is the step that decides the numbers: the **top two** surviving cells of each arm agree within **0.02–0.19%**, and that agreement is the confirmation I require before taking the max as the value — a single cell is not one. Across *all* surviving cells of an arm the spread is naturally wider, up to **0.88%** (prose, `DS4_DSPARK_SCHEDULER=0`), because the contaminant only ever adds time and never removes it. This machine was noisier than usual today (`audiomxd` at 76% CPU): 4 cells of 21 discarded on counting, 7 of 22 on prose.

I've run into this a few times across both b0309611041655f4e45671cfd9c9886aff161406 (I was running Cuda 13.01) and 84cc882352757baf628a1776badf7cc54d584e28 (Updated to Cuda 13.3.1) - but on sm_120 instead of GB10

Each crash follows the same pattern: DS4 already had a long Codex session resident on the GPU, then received a request it could not continue from that live state. An unrelated prompt the first time and a shorter “rewound” version of the session the second time. DS4 saved or evicted the old context and began rebuilding the new one from token zero.

In both cases, that cold replay worked normally until it reached exactly 32,768 tokens. The next chunk launched a CUDA kernel that accessed memory outside its valid range, producing Xid 13 and permanently poisoning that process’s CUDA context.

So this is not a general 32K context limit; the server has successfully processed other prompts far beyond 32K. The apparent trigger is the transition from a large live session to a different replayed context, combined with the 32K chunk boundary—likely stale or incorrectly sized GPU state during the reset/replay path. Disk-KV activity happens around the transition, but the evidence does not yet prove that the cache files themselves cause the bug.

Found and fixed a case where this PR's key never matches: **blocks injected *before* the user's own content** (Claude Code's `<system-reminder>` placement), as opposed to appended blocks (OpenCode's `<environment_details>`).

## Symptom

M3 Ultra, Metal, MXFP4 Flash 0731, this PR merged on `84cc882`. Turn 1 user content is `<system-reminder>...</system-reminder>\n` + document; turn 2 replays history without the block. The remember side works (`transient live checkpoint remembered ... stripped=4260`), but turn 2 still misses (`live kv cache miss ... common=9 reason=token-mismatch`) and pays the full reprefill.

## Root cause (byte-level, from `--trace` rendered prompts)

`strip_transient_blocks()` consumes separator whitespace only **before** a stripped block. A prepended block's trailing separator newline stays in the key:

```text
key kept:  ...<｜User｜>\nHere is a document excerpt...
turn 2:    ...<｜User｜>Here is a document excerpt...
```

One leftover `\n` right after the user-turn marker, so `byte_prefix_match` fails at that byte forever.

## Fix that worked here

Consume trailing whitespace after the block too, symmetric with the existing leading-side logic:

```c
         buf_append(&out, p, keep);
         stripped = true;
         p = close;
+        while (*p && isspace((unsigned char)*p)) p++;
     }
```

Same safety argument as the PR's own: a wrong guess only produces a visible key that never byte-matches and falls back to the existing full-reprefill behaviour; a match is still verified byte-for-byte against the rendered request, so no incorrect KV reuse is possible.

## After the fix

| metric | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| turn 2 TTFB | 2.59 s | **0.24 s** |
| turn 2 prefill | 1,342 tokens (full) | 10 tokens (`thinking live continuation match=visible-prefix cached=1371 prompt=1381`) |

Appended-block scenarios keep working (the existing test assertions in `./ds4_test --server` all pass with the change), and adjacent stripped blocks separated by whitespace now collapse cleanly as well.
